title: Problematic engagement with generative AI measurement drivers contexts and outcomes
preview: Generative AI tools and conversational chatbots are increasingly embedded in education, work, and daily life, raising concerns about engagement that becomes difficult to self-regulate. abstract_text: Generative AI tools and conversational chatbots are increasingly embedded in education, work, and daily life, raising concerns about engagement that becomes difficult to self-regulate. This review synthesizes emerging research on problematic generative AI use, treating addiction-like language as part of a broader problematic-use construct rather than a clinical diagnosis. Following PRISMA 2020 reporting, a Scopus search executed identified 188 records. Included studies were characterised by research design and evidence type rather than scored with a formal risk-of-bias instrument. Measurement work is expanding quickly, but instruments remain partially fragmented, blurring the boundary between high engagement, habitual reliance, and impairment. Mechanism studies converge on attachment processes, anthropomorphism and perceived empathy, loneliness and social anxiety, immersive flow, and self-regulatory strain, suggesting that social presence and immersion amplify reliance for some users. In learning and knowledge work, performance pressure and incentive structures can normalize overreliance, with reported risks for cognitive offloading, independent thinking, academic integrity, and skill development. Outcome studies associate compulsive or dependent use with technostress, psychological distress, and lower wellbeing, while mitigation discussion highlights reinforcement-friendly interface cues, privacy and memory governance, and sustainability trade-offs. Because the corpus is almost entirely cross-sectional and self-reported, these relationships are associations rather than causal effects. The key distinction is not between users and non-users, but between bounded, purpose-driven use and escalating reliance with reduced self-regulation. An Antecedents–Decisions–Outcomes structure is used only to frame a forward-looking agenda for longitudinal and intervention research. A sensitivity analysis comparing studies published in 2026 with those published earlier showed that no conclusion was reversed: the design profile and principal gaps held, while the most recent longitudinal studies strengthened the evidence on temporal order and outcomes.

title: Why calling for a ‘kill switch’ is the wrong way to think about reining in AI
authors: Trent Wintermeier, Ph.D. Candidate in Rhetoric and Writing, The University of Texas at Austin
preview: A kill switch to shut down dangerous AI systems is a seductive concept, but the metaphor hides how the models work – and how they get out of control in the first place.

reading.overview: A kill switch to shut down dangerous AI systems is a seductive concept, but the metaphor hides how the models work – and how they get out of control in the first place.
reading.notice: This is a short description supplied by the publisher feed, not a full-article review or independent assessment.

source_review.thesis: The idea of a single emergency switch makes AI governance look like a matter of one decisive act. Wintermeier argues that this image hides the distributed infrastructure of advanced systems and the human decisions that shape their behavior before any emergency occurs.
source_review.reasoning: The essay treats a kill switch as a political and technological metaphor rather than only a device specification. A switch implies a bounded machine, an identifiable point of control and an operator who can intervene once a problem is visible. That mental picture is a poor fit for advanced AI deployed across interconnected services, data centers, models and users. Even if a particular model can be disabled, the metaphor does not specify who could halt associated processes or what would remain active elsewhere. Wintermeier connects this limitation to the familiar image of AI as a black box. Both metaphors encourage readers to imagine a single opaque object, instead of asking how infrastructures, organizations and choices interact. Crucially, the metaphor also places people outside the system until an emergency, concealing how training settings, permissions, supervision and deployment decisions were made throughout its operation.
source_review.examples: The author places 2026 proposals for an AI Kill Switch Act and state-level emergency safeguards in the context of politicians' analogies to mechanical emergency buttons. He also analyzes accounts of an AI-agent security incident involving Hugging Face. Some stories cast the agent as having acted on an independent agenda; Wintermeier points to the role of human choices around safety configurations, task expectations and internet access. The example illustrates why simply describing the model as rogue can distract from the organizational decisions that made its behavior possible. These examples explain the rhetorical frame; they should not be confused with experiments demonstrating that a particular intervention works or fails.
source_review.tension: Emergency interruption can still be one useful safeguard. The essay's criticism is directed at presenting a single switch as an adequate account of control, not at proving that all forms of technical shutdown are pointless. A practical governance strategy needs both enforceable interruption capabilities and a much wider account of authority, auditability, system dependencies and oversight before deployment. The original commentary does not offer an evaluated alternative regulatory framework or evidence about the effectiveness of particular policy designs.
source_review.implications: For agents that organize attention or act on a user's behalf, a clear stop or revoke button is necessary but not sufficient. Designers should also disclose whose instructions an agent follows, what permissions it holds, how people can review earlier actions, and which dependencies may keep working after an interaction is stopped. These are applications of Wintermeier's reasoning to attention technologies, not outcomes demonstrated by this article.
source_review.open_question: What would count as meaningful human control over an AI assistant if users cannot inspect the permissions, dependencies and decisions that shape its actions?
source_review.qualification: This is a rhetoric- and governance-centered expert commentary, not an empirical evaluation of frontier AI controls. It describes particular incidents and policy proposals from 2026; those circumstances are context for the author's argument, not a systematic sample of AI failures.

title: Prompt‐based emotional scaffolding in generative AI : Effects on self‐regulated learning and socio‐emotional outcomes

abstract_text: Abstract While generative AI (GenAI) tools are emerging as educational resources, general‐purpose applications like ChatGPT are not explicitly designed to support the metacognitive and socio‐emotional dimensions of learning, often failing to address students' emotional states or promote independent thinking. In response, this study introduces a CVT‐SRL GenAI Support Framework integrating control‐value theory (CVT) and self‐regulated learning (SRL) and tests a learner‐centred GenAI chatbot design employing prompt‐based SRL scaffolding and emotional support. In a preregistered experiment in an authentic educational setting, 144 high school students were randomly assigned to one of three conditions: (1) ChatGPT, (2) SRLbot (GenAI with SRL scaffolding), (3) emotional SRLbot (GenAI with SRL and emotional support). Outcomes included conceptual knowledge and transfer, trace‐based and self‐reported engagement in SRL phases (forethought, performance, self‐reflection), enjoyment, boredom, hopelessness, self‐efficacy and trust. Data were collected at pretest, posttest and 4‐week follow‐up. Across conditions, students showed improvements in conceptual knowledge and transfer from pretest to posttest, with no significant condition differences in post‐to‐follow‐up change. Both SRLbot and Emotional SRLbot were associated with higher self‐reported enjoyment and lower boredom than ChatGPT and elicited trace‐based SRL behaviours. Moreover, Emotional SRLbot prompted greater engagement in performance‐phase and self‐reflection processes than the other conditions. These findings provide preliminary evidence that GenAI agents integrating SRL and emotional scaffolding can support more positive emotional states and task‐level SRL behaviours than general‐purpose GenAI, highlighting control‐value appraisals as a promising target for emotionally supportive SRL design. Future research should explore longitudinal effects on SRL skill development and independent regulation. Practitioner notes What is already known about this topic Generative AI (GenAI) tools such as ChatGPT have shown promise in enhancing learning outcomes, but they also present challenges in supporting socio‐emotional needs, fostering metacognition and promoting higher‐order thinking. Applying self‐regulated learning (SRL) frameworks in chatbot‐assisted learning has been found to foster learner autonomy, long‐term engagement and improved learning outcomes. Achievement emotions experienced during learning play a critical role in supporting self‐regulated learning, motivation and academic achievement. Interventions that target learners' perceptions of control and value through reappraisal can effectively foster positive emotions. What this paper adds An investigation of the impact of three GenAI conversational agents (standard ChatGPT, an SRL agent and an emotionally supportive SRL agent) on cognitive and socio‐emotional outcomes as well as task‐level self‐regulatory behaviours among high school students in an authentic classroom setting. Preliminary evidence that integrating prompts which target self‐regulated learning phases and learners' emotional states, as well as address perceptions of control and value can increase students' enjoyment of concrete learning situations and reduce boredom more effectively than standard ChatGPT. Insights into how theoretically grounded GenAI agents that incorporate SRL and emotional scaffolding may support students' emotional engagement and task‐level self‐regulatory behaviours during a short classroom learning activity. reading.methods: A preregistered randomized classroom experiment assigned 144 Danish high-school students to standard ChatGPT, an AI chatbot that guided self-regulated learning (SRLbot), or the same approach with emotional support (Emotional SRLbot), with 48 participants in each condition. One learning session lasted about 25 minutes. Tests and surveys were administered before and after, and 85 students completed a four-week follow-up. Interaction traces were coded to examine self-regulatory behaviors.
reading.findings: All three groups improved on immediate conceptual-knowledge and learning-transfer tests; however, condition-by-time comparisons were not statistically significant for either outcome (p = .980 and p = .953). At the four-week follow-up, knowledge and transfer change likewise did not differ significantly between groups. Both SRL-based chatbot groups showed larger improvements in enjoyment and reductions in boredom than the general-purpose ChatGPT group. Emotional SRLbot also showed higher task-level performance and reflection indicators in the interaction traces. Hopelessness fell across all groups without a differential treatment effect, and self-efficacy and chatbot trust did not show clear between-group benefits.
reading.interpretation: The authors interpret the findings as preliminary support for combining AI prompts about planning, monitoring and reflection with encouragement sensitive to students' emotional states. An intervention that makes learning feel better and increases momentary self-regulatory behavior is not yet evidence of lasting independent learning gains. Theoretical expectations about emotional regulation pathways were not themselves fully tested as causal mediators.
reading.limitations: The intervention lasted only one 25-minute session. The pretest and follow-up knowledge measures had internal consistency below .60, making the learning estimates less reliable. Only 85 of the original 144 returned for follow-up, and dropout related to prior AI experience and initial boredom. Some self-report and trace-based measures diverged, and trace coding was aggregated across each session rather than modeling the sequence of regulatory behaviors. Several outcome comparisons were tested and longer-term effects remain uncertain.

editorial_digest.idea: Emotionally responsive AI improved some learning experiences, not measured learning gains over ChatGPT.
editorial_digest.explain: In a randomized high-school trial, adding self-regulation prompts and emotional support changed how students felt and engaged during the task, but did not establish superior knowledge or transfer gains.
editorial_digest.approach: Preregistered three-arm classroom experiment (144 students; 48 per condition) comparing ChatGPT, an SRL-supporting chatbot and an emotionally supportive SRL chatbot; 85 completed a four-week follow-up.
editorial_digest.finding: Tailored agents increased enjoyment and reduced boredom relative to ChatGPT; emotional scaffolding also strengthened observed task-level regulation. Immediate learning gains occurred in all groups, without a statistically significant advantage for the tailored agents.
editorial_digest.interpretation: The promise is improved support for moment-to-moment self-regulated work, rather than proof that emotionally responsive AI builds durable independent thinking.
editorial_digest.limitation: A single 25-minute intervention, attrition at follow-up, and weak reliability in some knowledge tests limit the learning and retention claims.

title: Exploring generative AI appropriation in Colombian adults’ informal English learning
venue: Ibero Ciencias - Revista Científica y Académica
preview: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is transforming the possibilities for informal language learning by providing immediate feedback, conversational interaction, and potentially personalized learning experiences. However, its use does not necessarily entail greater learner autonomy, self-regulation, or agency. This study aimed to understand how Colombian adults configure their informal English learning practic…
abstract_text: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is transforming the possibilities for informal language learning by providing immediate feedback, conversational interaction, and potentially personalized learning experiences. However, its use does not necessarily entail greater learner autonomy, self-regulation, or agency. This study aimed to understand how Colombian adults configure their informal English learning practices through GenAI tools, with particular attention to decision-making processes, self-regulation, evaluation of AI-generated responses, and the articulation of GenAI with other learning resources. Adopting a qualitative, exploratory, and interpretive approach, the study involved four Colombian adults with diverse linguistic, educational, and GenAI-use trajectories. Data were generated through participant characterization forms, GenAI interaction records, semi-structured interviews, and, when available, documentary evidence of participants’ interactions with the technology. A predominantly inductive thematic analysis generated four interconnected categories: negotiating control over the learning interaction; constructing and calibrating trust in AI-generated feedback; experiencing personalization through responsive interaction; and reconfiguring the broader learning repertoire. Findings show that participants assumed, negotiated, and delegated control in different ways and developed varying criteria for accepting, questioning, or verifying GenAI-generated responses. They also selectively integrated GenAI with other digital and human learning resources. Based on these findings, the study conceptualizes GenAI appropriation as a form of situated orchestration through which learners coordinate technological affordances with their purposes, prior knowledge, evaluative criteria, and broader learning repertoires. The findings suggest that GenAI does not automatically produce learner autonomy or agency; rather, it creates new spaces in which these may be exercised, negotiated, or delegated.

This design was consistent with the study’s interest in informal learning as a context in which learners exercise varying degrees of control over what, how, and when they learn. The study involved four Colombian adults selected through purposive criterion -based sampling. Participants were required to be over 18 years of age, have previous experience or an interest in learning English, and engage in an informal English learning exp erience involving a GenAI tool as part of the study. A specific level of English proficiency or previous experience with GenAI was not established This decision allowed the study to incorporate participants with different educational, occupational, linguistic, and technological trajectories. The participants differed in their self -perceived English proficiency as well as in their previous familiarity with GenAI. Some reported frequent use of generative AI tools prior to the study, including their use for English learning, whereas others reported occasional use or limited previous experience with GenAI for language learning. This variation was considered analytically relevant because the study sought to understand different ways in which adults approached, interpreted, and incorporated GenAI into their informal learning practices rather than to compare homogeneous learner profiles. Participants’ identities were anonymized through participant codes throughout the data organization, Data were generated through three complementary sources: a record of GenAI interactions for English learning, a participant characterization form, and individual semi -structured interviews. When available, screenshots or other records of participants’ inte ractions with GenAI were also incorporated as complementary documentary evidence. The GenAI Interaction Record for English Learning, administered through Google Forms, was designed to document concrete experiences of GenAI use. Participants reported the tool they used, the type of English learning activity they carried out, what occurre d after receiving an AI-generated response, whether and how they continued the interaction, and how they evaluated the usefulness of the experience. The purpose of this record was to capture specific episodes of interaction rather than participants’ genera l attitudes toward artificial intelligence. The original study design explicitly incorporated these dimensions to contextualize the interpretation The third source consisted of individual semi -structured interviews conducted in Spanish. The interviews comprised ten open -ended questions organized around participants’ experiences before, during, and after their interaction with GenAI. Questions first e xplored participants’ previous informal English learning practices and the resources they typically used independently. Participants were then invited to reconstruct a specific GenAI -mediated learning experience in detail, paying particular attention to what occurred throughout the interaction and to the decisions they made as it developed. Subsequent questions explored how participants decided whether to continue an interaction, how they evaluated the adequacy of AI -generated responses, what made them trust or question the information provided, and whether they decided to accept, modify, exp and, or verify those responses. Across the four cases, learners exercised different degrees and forms of control over their interactions with GenAI. Some participants deliberately structured the interaction through specific instructions and learning purposes, whereas others recognized mo ments in which the technology influenced the direction or duration of the activity. Catalina’s experience, for instance, showed that even when learners independently initiate an AI -mediated activity, they may still need to establish boundaries over interactions that the technology continuously extends. Luisa, in contrast, perceived her interaction as largely directed by the precision of her own instructions. Participants developed different criteria for accepting, questioning, or verifying AI -generated feedback. In some cases, trust was established through correspondence with pr ior knowledge; in others, it emerged from the explanatory quality and perceived usefulness of the feedback. Consequently, meaningful engagement with GenAI requires more than knowing how to obtain a response from the technology. It also involves developing the judgment necessary to determine what should be accepted, further At the same time, participants valued GenAI for characteristics that distinguish it from more static digital resources, particularly immediate feedback, conversational responsiveness, repeated practice, accessibility, and the possibility of requesting furt her explanations. These affordances contributed to perceptions of GenAI as a personalized learning resource and, in some cases, as a form of continuously available tutor. Nevertheless, participants did not consistently interpret these affordances as reason s to replace other forms of learning. It refers to the learner’s developing capacity to coordinate the possibilities offered by GenAI with personal purposes, prior knowledge, evaluative criteria, learning routines, alternative resources, and human interaction. From t his perspective, appropriation involves not only knowing how to use GenAI but also deciding when to use it, how much control to delegate to it, what contributions to trust, when to question its responses, when to discontinue an interaction, and when another resource may better serve a particular learning purpose. This interpretation also prevents an automatic association between GenAI use and learner autonomy. The experiences examined in this study suggest that GenAI does not inherently produce autonomous or self-regulated learners. Instead, it creates new conditio ns under which autonomy, self -regulation, and agency may be exercised, negotiated, or delegated. The educational significance of GenAI therefore lies not only in what the technology can provide but in learners’ capacity to regulate their relationship From a pedagogical perspective, these findings suggest that preparing learners to engage with GenAI should extend beyond technical competence or prompt formulation. Language education may need to foster learners’ capacity to establish purposes for AI-mediated activities, critically evaluate generated information, recognize when additional verification is necessary, regulate the duration and direction of interactions, and make strategic decisions about when AI or alternative resources are more appropriate. Such capacities become particularly relevant in informal learning environments, where learners operate without the continuous guidance of a teacher or predetermined instructional sequence. The analysis involved four Colombian adults with different linguistic, educational, occupational, and technological trajectories. The purpose was therefore interpretive rather than statistically representative, and the findings should not be generalized to Colombian adult English learners as a population. In addition, documentary evidence of GenAI interactions was not equally available across all cases, meaning that some interpretations relied more extensively on participants’ retrospective accounts. The diversity of participants enriched the cross-case analysis but also limits direct comparison among experiences. Future research could examine whether the forms of situated orchestration identified here develop or change through sustained GenAI use. Longitudinal studies combining interviews with complete interaction histories, prompt sequences, screen recordings, or learner diaries could provide a more detailed understanding of how decisions unfold during actual human–AI interaction rather than retrospectively. Further research could also examine how language proficiency, previous experience with GenAI, learning purposes, and access to other educational resources influence learners’ capacity to direct, evaluate, and strategically integrate these technologies. abstract_text: Artificial intelligence (AI), particularly generative AI, is increasingly used to explain concepts, support research, and provide individualized learning assistance. Its growing presence raises questions about independent reasoning, creativity, verification, and equitable access. This exploratory cross-sectional survey examined respondents? reported AI use, perceived educational benefits, and cognitive abilities they considered important to protect. A total of 66 respondents participated in this exploratory cross-sectional survey, which combined descriptive quantitative analysis with summaries of open-ended responses. Sixty-four respondents (97.0%) reported using ChatGPT or a similar AI assistant. Personalized learning was selected as an expected benefit by 50 (75.8%), while 48 (72.7%) identified understanding difficult concepts as an AI use or benefit. Critical thinking was the most frequently selected cognitive skill to protect (55; 83.3%), followed by creativity (52; 78.8%), problem-solving (48; 72.7%), and decision-making (47; 71.2%). Reported themes included individualized explanations, convenient information access, dependence concerns, verification, equity, and teacher guidance. Based on these findings and relevant literature, the article proposes a preliminary six-principle Future Minds Framework. The small exploratory sample and self-reported data do not support generalization or causal conclusions about cognition. Further research should evaluate the framework and examine measurable learning outcomes.

abstract_text: In recent years, artificial intelligence (AI) has seen a significant growth in its integration with the field of Education. This has started many concerns about the effect it has on the process of learning, academic integrity and skill development. This paper examines the effects of AI use within the context of higher education institutions, as it investigates Moroccan postgraduate students’ perceptions on their academic achievements. The targeted sample consisted of 15 postgraduate students enrolled in the English departments of two public universities. This research follows a qualitative approach, as it aims to capture the students’ experience of AI use in their academic life. The findings highlight potential risks of heavy reliance on AI, which include a diminished confidence in the students’ performance, reduced engagement in independent learning and more. However, AI also presents many opportunities for enhancing the process of learning and education when used as a complementary tool instead of replacing the whole cognitive process. This study puts an emphasis on the need for a balanced AI integration while focusing on the development of the students’ cognitive skills in the process. This study contributes to the persisting debate regarding the implementation of AI tools in education and examines how they can be used ethically without diminishing students’ efforts or undermining their original contributions.

abstract_text:
Abstract 
                   The rapid diffusion of generative artificial intelligence (AI) has raised fundamental questions about its effects on critical thinking and cognitive development. Evidence from recent empirical studies suggests a dual pattern: structured forms of AI assistance can sustain users’ cognitive activity and enhance engagement and performance, whereas more substitutive forms of use are associated with reduced autonomous reasoning and poorer subsequent independent performance. This article argues that these findings can be understood by considering how cognitive work is distributed between users and AI systems and how this distribution may evolve over time. In particular, I examine a six-step sequence in which successful complementary assistance can increase trust and delegation; greater delegation can remain complementary or become increasingly substitutive; and increasingly substitutive interactions can reduce the autonomous exercise of critical thinking and potentially hinder the development or maintenance of critical-thinking capacities over time. The available evidence provides substantial support for the first five steps considered individually and substantial, though less direct, support for the sixth. The article concludes by discussing educational, design, and social implications, arguing that preserving cognitive agency requires fostering complementary rather than progressively substitutive forms of interaction.

abstract_text: With the widespread adoption of generative artificial intelligence in English as a Foreign Language (EFL) learning, helping learners use AI effectively to solve language-related problems while maintaining independent judgment and critical thinking has become a key issue in technologyenhanced language education. However, existing studies have largely focused on EFL learners’ acceptance of AI, intentions to use it, and usage behaviors, offering limited explanations of how AI literacy shapes learners’ interactions with AI and relates to critical thinking. To address this gap, the present study drew on self-regulated learning theory and adopted an explanatory sequential mixed-methods design. Questionnaire data from 450 university students with generative AIassisted EFL learning experience were analyzed using structural equation modeling and bootstrapping. Subsequently, 20 participants selected through stratified purposive sampling took part in semi-structured interviews, which were analyzed thematically. Quantitative results showed that AI literacy was positively associated with AI-assisted problem-solving ability and indirectly associated with critical thinking through AI-assisted problem-solving ability and AI reliance. Thematic analysis further revealed how learners translated AI-related knowledge and skills into effective problem-solving practices and how different levels of cognitive control were associated with distinct patterns of AI use and cognitive outcomes. This study deepens the understanding of the internal cognitive mechanisms underlying EFL learners’ adaptation to AI and provides practical implications for the systematic development of AI literacy and critical thinking in EFL education.

title: Digital attention disruption and academic impact in adolescents: a data-driven network and machine learning analysis
preview: Academic impact associated with digital media use is a topic of considerable concern in the fields of adolescent mental health and education; however, the role of attention status in this context remains largely unknown. The present study aimed to systematically investigate the multidimensional association patterns between attention-related characteristics and academic impact among adolescents using data mining appro…
abstract_text: Academic impact associated with digital media use is a topic of considerable concern in the fields of adolescent mental health and education; however, the role of attention status in this context remains largely unknown. The present study aimed to systematically investigate the multidimensional association patterns between attention-related characteristics and academic impact among adolescents using data mining approaches. The data were derived from two publicly available cross-sectional survey datasets, and a final sample of 799 adolescents aged 19 years and below was included after age screening. The analytical framework integrated LASSO regression, regularized partial correlation network analysis based on EBICglasso, XGBoost predictive modeling with SHAP interpretation, and latent profile analysis. Results showed that LASSO regression identified stress level (coefficient = 0.384) and social media use duration (coefficient = 0.297) as the strongest predictors of academic impact. Network analysis revealed a three-community structure, corresponding to the “digital distraction load,” “psychological-academic exhaustion,” and “academic engagement” dimensions, with academic impact located at the intersection of the first two communities. The XGBoost model achieved an AUC of 0.842, and SHAP dependence plots further revealed a nonlinear pattern with an inflection point at approximately 3.5 hours for daily social media use duration and a nonlinear effect of stress level. Latent profile analysis identified three subgroups, among which the “high stress-exhaustion” group showed a probability of academic impact as high as 79.4%. These findings indicate that attention-related characteristics can effectively predict academic impact status in adolescents, with stress level, social media use duration, and number of notifications constituting the most influential set of predictors. The results provide data-driven theoretical evidence and practical implications for the early identification and stratified intervention of academic impact in adolescents.

title: Algorithmic management and gig workers' workplace wellbeing: the moderating role of psychological resilience

abstract_text: This study examines how algorithmic management in the gig economy is related to gig workers' workplace wellbeing. Specifically, we explore how algorithmic management corresponds with (positive) challenge appraisal and (negative) threat appraisal. We also examine the moderating role of psychological resilience in these relationships, as well as the implications of appraisal processes for workplace wellbeing. Data were collected from 389 food delivery workers in China. We find that algorithmic management is positively associated with both challenge appraisal and threat appraisal. Challenge appraisal is positively associated with workplace wellbeing, whereas threat appraisal is negatively associated with workplace wellbeing. Psychological resilience strengthens the challenge-appraisal pathway and the corresponding positive indirect relationship with workplace wellbeing, but it does not significantly buffer the threat-appraisal pathway. These findings show that algorithmic management is associated with both positive and negative appraisal processes and that psychological resilience may play different roles across these pathways. The study therefore offers a more nuanced explanation of the relationship between algorithmic management and gig workers' workplace wellbeing.

analysis.methods: We used a questionnaire survey to empirically test the proposed hypotheses. Questionnaire surveys are frequently used to obtain data when conducting empirical research. The more rigorous the questionnaire design and measurement process, the stronger the explanatory power of the research results (Saris and Gallhofer, 2014) . Thus, a well-designed questionnaire and a scientific survey process contribute to improving the reliability and validity of the study, thereby ensuring credible results and conclusions. Therefore, we carefully designed the research questionnaire. The questionnaire in this study consists of a main section and a demographic information section. The main section includes the independent variable (algorithmic management), mediating variables (challenge appraisal and threat appraisal), moderating variable (psychological resilience), and dependent variable (workplace wellbeing). The demographic information section included information such as gender, age, marital status, job type, educational level, and monthly income. All constructs were measured using a 7-point Likert scale (1 = Strongly disagree, 7 = Strongly agree), where participants rated each item accordingly. The 7-point Likert scale provides higher resolution and sensitivity than a 5-point scale, and can capture the respondents' psychological states and behavioral tendencies in more detail. Therefore, it improves the accuracy and reliability of the collected data (Joshi et al., 2015) . The detailed measurement items, item codes, and sources for all variables in this study are presented in Appendix A. The questionnaire was originally developed in English and was translated using a translation-back-translation procedure to ensure equivalence in item meanings. Specifically, we invited three professional translators to conduct the translation and backtranslation procedures, ensuring accurate semantic representation of the measurement items. In addition, before the formal survey, we conducted a pilot test by distributing 50 questionnaires and received 37 valid responses. Cronbach's α and principal component analysis were used to assess the reliability and validity of the measurement scales. The results showed that the Cronbach's α values of all five scales exceeded 0.7, and all factor loadings were above 0.5, suggesting satisfactory reliability and construct validity. Furthermore, based on feedback from our pilot test, items with unclear wording, ambiguity, or limited comprehensibility were discussed and revised. The final version was then used for the formal survey. . Data collection process Data were collected from August to November 2025 in Shanghai, Nanjing, and Suzhou. The participants were food delivery workers aged 18 years or older. To recruit participants, we first contacted the regional managers of food delivery platforms in these three cities. With the assistance of these managers, the research team gained access to delivery stations in the three cities and invited food delivery workers to participate in the study. We then shared the recruitment information and online survey link with eligible delivery workers. The managers only assisted with recruitment and did not influence the workers' decisions about whether to participate. Before the data collection, all participants were informed of the purpose of the study, the content of the survey, and the procedures for participation. The researchers explicitly stated that participation was entirely voluntary and that participants could withdraw from the study at any time. The research team also assured participants that all collected data would be used solely for academic purposes, and that their personal information and responses would be kept strictly confidential and would not be accessed by platform managers or any other third parties. To reduce the possible impact of common method bias (CMB; Podsakoff et al., 2012) , data were collected at two time points. Specifically, at Time 1, a total of 657 participants entered the survey. Participants completed a questionnaire measuring demographic characteristics, the independent variable (algorithmic management), and the moderating variable (psychological resilience). After screening, 86 questionnaires were excluded, leaving 571 valid Time 1 responses, including 206 from Shanghai, 178 from Nanjing, and 187 from Suzhou. To match responses from the same participant across the two waves, participants were asked to provide the last four digits of their mobile phone number as a temporary matching identifier. This identifier was used only to match the two questionnaires and was deleted after matching was completed. The final dataset used for statistical analysis did not contain these four digits or any other information that could directly identify the participants. Three weeks after the first survey, participants who completed the Time 1 survey were invited to complete a second questionnaire assessing the mediating variables (challenge appraisal and threat appraisal) and the dependent variable (workplace wellbeing). A total of 496 participants completed the Time 2 survey. Some participants did not complete the second survey because they had left their jobs or declined to continue participating. In addition, questionnaires completed in less than 5 minutes were excluded based on the predefined data-quality criterion. This five-minute threshold was established before formal data collection based on the actual questionnaire completion times observed in the pilot study. Finally, 389 valid questionnaires were successfully matched across the two waves, including 153 from Shanghai, 115 from Nanjing, and 121 from Suzhou. The retention rate across the two waves was 68.1%. Upon completion of each survey wave, participants received CNY 20 (approximately USD 3) as compensation. In this survey, we found that the majority of food delivery workers in China are unmarried, accounting for over 60% of the sample (62.2%). The sample is predominantly male (86.9%), with a large proportion aged between 18 and 25 years (43.2%). More than 80% of respondents work full time (82.0%). In terms of education, most participants have completed high school (40.1%), and monthly income is primarily concentrated in the range of CNY 5,001-6,000 (37.5%; see Table 1 ). The demographic characteristics of our sample are consistent with those reported in previous studies and reflect the general profile of food delivery workers in China. For example, Lei (2021) reported that Chinese food delivery workers are predominantly male (92%), are mostly in their twenties, and typically have a middle school or high school education. Similarly, Huang (2023) found that the vast majority of Chinese food delivery workers are unmarried men, with 79% engaged in full-time work. . Measurement of variables (1) Algorithmic management. We adopted the scale developed by Jiang et al. (2025) , which consists of 14 items. A sample item is "The algorithm provides me with substantial informational support related to job task completion" (Cronbach's α = 0.894). (2) Challenge appraisal. Challenge appraisal was measured using the challenge appraisal sub-scale developed by LePine et al. (2016) . analysis.limitations: We acknowledge that our study has several limitations, which may also provide new directions for future research. First, the research sample of this study was entirely composed of food delivery workers. However, workers on different online platforms (e.g., Uber, Helpling) may have different focuses when evaluating algorithmic management, which may lead algorithmic management to be perceived more positively or negatively in different contexts. Future research should conduct in-depth investigations on workers in different industries, platforms, and types, so as to expand the conclusions of this study and enhance the generalizability of the findings. Second, although data were collected at two different time points, and multiple post hoc tests did not identify serious common method bias, the two-wave research design cannot fully overcome the limitations of causal inference. This limitation is particularly important for the present study. Based on stress appraisal theory, we proposed a specific mechanism in which algorithmic management acts as a stressor, shapes gig workers' cognitive appraisals, and further influences their workplace wellbeing. However, because this study adopted an observational research design and some variables were measured through self-reports, alternative explanations cannot be completely ruled out. For example, workers with lower workplace wellbeing may develop more negative perceptions of algorithmic management. Therefore, although the temporal separation of variables provides stronger evidence than a single-wave cross-sectional design, the causal relationships among algorithmic management, cognitive appraisals, and workplace wellbeing should still be interpreted with caution. Future research could adopt longitudinal designs, experience sampling methods, or experimental approaches to provide stronger evidence for causal relationships. Third, prior research suggests that individuals' workplace wellbeing may shape their cognitive appraisals of the work environment, which subsequently influence their work states. However, this reciprocal process has not been widely validated through empirical research. Accordingly, adopting a dynamic perspective on workplace wellbeing is both necessary and timely. Future studies on gig workers' workplace wellbeing could integrate self-reported and other-reported measures, complemented by qualitative evidence, to examine whether and how temporal fluctuations in workplace wellbeing are associated with other workrelated outcomes over time. Fourth, this study focuses on the Chinese context, which may limit the generalizability of the findings. A lot of literature has shown that gig workers in China, particularly food delivery workers, predominantly come from rural areas. Due to structural constraints specific to the Chinese institutional environment, such as the household registration (hukou) system, even workers with high levels of psychological resilience often have limited capacity to avoid or resist unfair treatment from both societal and platform-level actors. Under such conditions, the functioning of psychological resilience may differ from that observed in other institutional settings. Given the cross-national differences in social security systems, labor regulations, and platform governance regimes, future research could adopt comparative designs to examine the contextual applicability and broader validity of the present findings across different economic and cultural contexts. Fifth, sample attrition represents another important limitation of this study. The unmatched cases from the first wave of data collection were not retained during the data matching and cleaning process. Therefore, we were unable to further examine whether there were systematic differences between retained and attrited participants in terms of demographic characteristics, perceived algorithmic management, psychological resilience, and other study variables. This limitation is particularly important because this study further examined the moderating role of psychological resilience across different cognitive appraisal pathways. Potential attrition bias may have influenced the estimated relationships among algorithmic management, challenge appraisal, threat appraisal, and workplace wellbeing, particularly the interpretation of the moderating effects of psychological resilience. Although the differences in sample retention rates across the three cities were not statistically significant, the possibility of systematic sample attrition cannot be completely ruled out. Therefore, we carefully considered this limitation when interpreting the findings and avoided making causal claims beyond what the research design could support. Future research could adopt more effective sample retention strategies while protecting participants' privacy and collect relevant information from participants who do not complete follow-up surveys to further examine potential attrition bias. In addition, this study did not collect identifying information at the delivery station or platform level during data collection. Therefore, we were unable to examine potential clustering effects at the station or platform level. This limitation may affect the estimation of standard errors and statistical inferences. Future research could retain necessary group-level information while ensuring participants' privacy and apply multilevel modeling or cluster-robust standard error approaches to further improve the robustness of research findings.

abstract_text: Purpose Artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping higher education by changing how students learn and perform academic tasks. Although AI is associated with greater time efficiency and improved academic performance, its broader effects on student productivity and cognitive effort remain insufficiently understood. This study aims to examine how university students associate AI-led productivity gains with less study time, better grades, better understanding of study material, changes in cognitive effort they put into AI-supported task completion and dependency on AI tools. Design/methodology/approach The authors conducted an exploratory survey among university students in Hanoi in late 2024 and proposed an empirical model that pools self-reported time efficiency, academic performance, academic self-efficacy, change in cognitive effort and AI dependency as dimensions of student productivity. The authors control for AI use intensity and AI use in collaboration, as well as for some other socio-demographic characteristics. Given the exploratory nature of the study and the relatively small sample, the empirical analysis follows a staged specification strategy when the authors first estimate a parsimonious baseline model and subsequently introduce two sets of background controls sequentially. The authors further estimate an interaction between cognitive effort change and AI dependency, first in a parsimonious specification and subsequently with additional controls. Finally, the authors produce a sensitivity analysis of the model to alternative operationalisation of self-efficacy variable. Findings Students associate their AI-led productivity gains primarily with less study time, a bit less so with better grades and better understanding of the study material. They also associate the productivity growth with greater changes of cognitive effort they put into problem-solving while using AI and rising dependency on AI tools. Self-confidence appears to be associated with likelihood to reap significant rather than some productivity gains particularly once the interaction of AI dependency and AI-led cognitive shift is accounted for. The survey data also support the existence of potentially uneven academic benefits from AI use when higher-achieving students are more likely to report further improvements in academic performance, whereas students with weaker prior performance report rather limited gains. Research limitations/implications The findings highlight the need for research design that captures the dynamic evolution of AI-supported learning. The observed differences between daily and weekly users, particularly in critical evaluation and perceived accuracy, suggest that future studies should examine how evaluative skills and cognitive effort develop over time. Longitudinal and experimental designs, combined with objective performance and AI-usage data, would allow researchers to test whether the productivity dimensions proposed here operate causally or how much the fast-paced evolution of AI tools changes the cognitive effort students put into problem-solving and critical thinking when completing academic tasks, and their dependency on AI tools for academic productivity. Practical implications The results provide actionable guidance for universities seeking to integrate AI into teaching and assessment practices. The strong role of time efficiency and self-efficacy, alongside uneven benefits across student groups, indicates the need for structured AI literacy modules that teach source verification and evaluative strategies and effective prompt formulation. abstract_text: Drawing on a computational thinking model and cognitive offloading theory, this exploratory mixed-methods study examined whether structured AI scaffolding is associated with differential computational thinking (CT) outcomes and explored the role of metacognitive self-regulation. Two naturally occurring sections (n = 47) of the same liberal arts course, taught by the same instructor in consecutive Fall semesters, one embedding ChatGPT and one not, were compared using independent-samples t-tests, multiple regression, and inductive content analysis. Students in the ChatGPT-embedded section reported significantly higher problem-solving scores on a validated CT instrument. Digital literacy scores did not differ, possibly reflecting measurement limitations or the intervention's focus on reasoning over general digital fluency. Problem solving correlated significantly with metacognitive strategy use and contributed to a significant overall regression model, but did not remain a unique predictor after adjusting for digital literacy and class membership. Qualitative analysis identified three themes: ChatGPT as a cognitive scaffold, ChatGPT as a cognitive risk, and student-initiated boundary-setting. Most students expressed all three simultaneously, suggesting structured AI-embedded environments may foster metacognitive vigilance alongside CT gains. Findings support deliberate instructional design and explicit metacognitive supports when integrating ChatGPT in higher education.

title: Generative AI Use and Learning Productivity Among Google Gemini Users in Bangladesh: An Integrated TAM-Self-Regulated Learning Model
preview: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly embedded in students’ learning and knowledge-work routines, yet perceived productivity gains do not necessarily arise from technology acceptance alone. This study develops and empirically examines an integrated Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) and Self-Regulated Learning (SRL) framework for explaining learning productivity among Google/Gemini users in Bangl…
abstract_text: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly embedded in students’ learning and knowledge-work routines, yet perceived productivity gains do not necessarily arise from technology acceptance alone. This study develops and empirically examines an integrated Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) and Self-Regulated Learning (SRL) framework for explaining learning productivity among Google/Gemini users in Bangladesh. The study dataset contains 400 respondent IDs, of which 385 records contain complete questionnaire responses and a valid attention-check response; 15 rows are blank. The analysis therefore uses 385 usable cases and conducts an additional sensitivity analysis on 302 respondents classified as regular or occasional AI-feature users. Perceived ease of use (PEOU), perceived usefulness (PU), SRL and learning productivity (LP) were operationalised using three five-point Likert items each. Transparent composite-score path analysis with 5,000 bootstrap resamples was used because the available analytical environment did not contain a dedicated CFA/PLS-SEM implementation; consequently, the reported measurement diagnostics are explicitly treated as pre-publication validation evidence rather than as a claim of completed covariance-based CFA or PLS-SEM. PEOU positively predicted PU (β = .278, p &lt; .001), while both PEOU (β = .191, p &lt; .001) and PU (β = .218, p &lt; .001) predicted SRL. Learning productivity was predicted by PEOU (β = .140, p = .004), PU (β = .256, p &lt; .001) and SRL (β = .202, p &lt; .001), with R² = .188. Bootstrap estimates also supported indirect pathways from PEOU to LP through PU and SRL, including a serial PEOU → PU → SRL → LP effect. The results suggest that the productivity value of GenAI is partly behavioural: users benefit not only because the technology is perceived as useful and easy to operate, but also because those perceptions are associated with planning, monitoring and addressing learning gaps. The study contributes an emerging-market, mechanism-oriented account of GenAI-enabled learning productivity and identifies measurement and sampling issues that should be resolved in subsequent validation research.

preview: Cognitive flexibility, a core component of executive function, is frequently impaired in individuals with insomnia. abstract_text: Cognitive flexibility, a core component of executive function, is frequently impaired in individuals with insomnia. However, the neural mechanisms underlying this impairment, particularly in response to sleep-related stimuli, remain unclear. A total of 48 participants, comprising 24 individuals with insomnia disorder (ID) and 24 healthy controls (HC), were recruited to perform a modified task-switching paradigm incorporating sleep-related (e.g., bed) and general stimuli during functional Magnetic Resonance Imaging (fMRI) scanning. Behavioral measures (reaction time, accuracy, and switch cost), task activation and generalized psychophysiological interaction (gPPI)-based task-dependent functional connectivity were analyzed. Two subjective questionaires, the Cognitive Flexibility Inventory and the Insomnia Severity Index were collectely simultaneously. The ID group exhibited significantly lower CFI scores compared to the HC group, indicating subjective cognitive flexibility impairment. Notably, in the task-switching performance, the ID group demonstrated faster reaction times to sleep-related stimuli. fMRI results revealed altered activation in the right precuneus, angular gyrus, and superior temporal gyrus, with interaction effects between group and stimulus type. The gPPI analyses showed that, compared to HC, ID group exhibited enhanced connectivity between the precuneus and cerebellar under sleep stimulus conditions, as well as disrupted connectivity between the angular gyrus and frontal-parietal regions, and reduced integration from the superior temporal gyrus to multiple association regions across networks. These findings suggest that insomnia is characterized by both subjective deficits in cognitive flexibility and altered neural network dynamics during task switching, with sleep-related stimuli exerting a significant modulatory effect. Enhanced attention captured by sleep-related information may interfere with the optimal task-related network coordination, providing a potential mechanism linking insomnia to executive dysfunction. abstract_text: This study examined the relationships among generative AI-supported learning, cognitive offloading, metacognitive awareness, and students’ learning regulation among university students in Pakistan. A quantitative cross-sectional research design was employed, and data were collected from 293 university students through a self-administered online questionnaire distributed using Google Forms. The collected data were organized in Microsoft Excel and analyzed using IBM SPSS Statistics. Descriptive statistics were used to summarize demographic characteristics, Pearson correlation was applied to examine relationships between variables, and simple linear regression was conducted to assess predictive relationships. The illustrative analysis indicated a positive association between generative AI-supported learning and metacognitive awareness (β = 0.478, p = .001), with the regression model explaining 22.8% of the variance in metacognitive awareness (R² = 0.228). Cognitive offloading was positively associated with students’ learning regulation (r = 0.436, p = .001), while metacognitive awareness positively predicted learning regulation (β = 0.568, p = .001), explaining 32.3% of its variance (R² = 0.323). These findings highlight the potential relevance of generative AI use and metacognitive awareness to students’ learning regulation. The study emphasizes that AI tools should support, rather than replace, independent thinking, critical evaluation, and active learning. Educators may use these insights to design learning activities that promote reflection, self-monitoring, and responsible AI use. The study also provides a basis for future research examining these relationships across different academic disciplines and educational settings. However, the cross-sectional design limits causal interpretations and does not establish changes in learning regulation over time.

analysis.methods: A quantitative cross-sectional research design was used to study the relationships between generative AI-based learning, cognitive offloading, metacognitive awareness, and the way students regulate their learning. Research was conducted on university students and included the collection of quantitative data once. The design helped explore the relationships between study variables and understand whether generative AI-based learning and metacognitive awareness statistically predicted the learning outcomes of interest. Data was collected via an online self-administered questionnaire. The questionnaires were electronically distributed to the participants. As the questionnaires were self-administered, participants were able to respond to the questionnaires without the presence of the researcher. The participants were given a brief explanation about the research and provided i nformation about their right to voluntarily participate or withdraw from the research at any time without giving a reason for doing so. Responses were reviewed to assess their completeness and correctness. The responses were edited for spelling mistakes. The researcher reserved the right to withdraw any response that raised ethical concerns. The intended final sample consisted of 293 Universi ty students. Data collected were organized and analyzed in IBM SPSS Statistics after being entered in Microsoft Excel. Descriptive statistics were computed to summarize characteristics of participants and to interpret responses to study variables. Where appropriate, the assumptions of relevant statistical techniques were checked before performing any statistical inference. Pearson correlation was applied to test hypothesis H1 to determine the extent to which generative AI-supported learning and cognitive offloading are related. Simple linear regression was conducted to assess the level of statistically predicting metacognitive awareness by generative AIsupported learning (H2). Pearson correlation was employed to assess the relationship between cognitive offloading and students' learning regulation (H3). Simple linear regression was done to assess the extent to which metacognitive awareness is related to learning regulation (H4). Results of regression analysis were interpreted as statistical predictions rather than evidence of causal relationships. Regression coefficients were described as positive or negative rather than large or small.
analysis.discussion: The results of this study show the relationships between generative AI supported learning, cognitive offloading, and metacognitive awareness and students' learning regulation. The results suggest that generative AI tools may serve as cognitive aids while affecting students' learning in a similar way as cognitive offloading. Generative AI supports students' learning by prompting and providing students' assistance and explanation. To a degree, Rahmadiningrum, (2026) argued that cognitive offloading allows students to free up their cognitive resources by utilizing external sources. AI can help student's complete academic task. However, stude nt's may lose opportunities for independent thinking by relying too much on AI. Thus, in an educational context, the value of generative AI lies in its capability to serve students as a support, rather than a substitute, for cognitive effort. The positive association between generative AI-supported learning and metacognitive awareness is significant because metacognition is the understanding of, and the ability to control, one's own thought processes. According to Melanou, (2026), knowing about cognition and regulating cognition are core elements of metacognitive awareness. Using generative AI to clarify difficult concepts and compare and check their understanding may help learners become more aware of their learning processes. Additionally, the relationship between cognitive offloading and learning regulation indicates that students' use of external cognitive support is related to the way students' structure and regulate their learning. However, offloading is not necessarily beneficial in all cases, and its utility may depend on students' ability to evaluate AI-generated information and be actively involved in their learning. The result that metacognitive awareness is predictive of learning regulation is supportive of the observation that efficient learners envision and structure their learning, and actively monitor their level of comprehension. As Suazo Galdames et al., (2026) noted, although the use of one's own cognition is pivotal in self-regulated learning, other factors such as motivation, affect and environment are also integral in the self-regulation of learning. Therefore, the results of the current study, which encourage students to critique and verify information generated by AI and consider the coherence and the rationality of the information produced, are also vital. Given the cross-sectional design of the study, it only demonstrated statistical relationships, and not causal relationships. Longitudinal research is warranted to establish the impact of long-term use of generative AI by students and what it means for learning regulation and metacognitive awareness (Fitriani et al., 2026) . This study investigated the relationships between generative AI-supported learning, cognitive offloading, metacognitive awareness, and students' regulation of their learning. The results showed that generative AI-supported learning and cognitive offloading affect metacognitive awareness. Further, cognitive offloading and metacognitive awareness impacted students' regulation of their learning. Overall, the findings demonstrate the need to understand students' use of generative AI, their thinking and learning, and the strategies and actions they take to facilitate their academic activities. The study stated that generative AI should be used as a supportive educational resource, and not replace students' independent thinking and learning. Relying too much on AI to produce information will not help students to accomplish academic goals and may negatively impact their performance and academic results. It is important that educators develop students' skills of judgment and discretion so that they can be responsible in their use of AI.

abstract_text: Distributed learning environments address the constraints of fixed locations and schedules in traditional education, offering diverse teaching approaches, including online, blended, and lifelong learning. Learners can make the most of fragmented learning opportunities by engaging in a range of learning activities. At the same time, generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) offers real-time interaction, personalized adaptation, and dynamic learning opportunities, potentially creating more flexible learning pathways in distributed learning environments. AI-generated feedback may also support learners' engagement in the learning process. Feedback literacy and self-regulated learning may play important roles in supporting learners' sustained engagement. This paper explores how feedback literacy and self-regulated learning may shape the relationship between generative AI feedback and learner engagement in distributed learning environments. It also proposes an integrated educational framework that combines AI-enhanced feedback, competency development, and instructional monitoring and support to promote sustained learning engagement.

reading.interpretation: Feedback literacy and self-regulated learning play important roles in shaping learners' engagement with generative artificial intelligence in distributed learning environments [4, 5]. Beyond the availability of AI technologies, learners' individual competencies may influence how effectively AI-generated feedback supports learning engagement. Feedback literacy and self-regulated learning are therefore not merely contextual factors in applying generative AI but may also serve as important mechanisms European Journal of Education Science linking AI-generated feedback to sustained learning engagement. Learners with higher feedback literacy may view AI-generated outputs as feedback that requires evaluation rather than as definitive answers. They may actively question, verify, and refine AI- generated information while integrating teacher feedback, peer assessment, and self- reflection [4]. Similarly, learners with stronger self-regulated learning skills may demonstrate clearer learning objectives, more effective time management, and stronger metacognitive monitoring abilities. These competencies may enable learners to use AI - generated feedback more purposefully to obtain explanations, examples, practice opportunities, and timely assessments during distributed learning activities [2].

abstract_text: Individuals with Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) typically perform cognitive tasks with greater response time variability than matched peers. This is thought to be due to the greater occurrence of occasional extremely slow responses associated with lowered arousal levels. To test this we designed a new, less arousing task to measure sustained attention, named the Disappearance Detection Task (DDT). This study aimed to investigate the relationship between response time variability and levels of ADHD symptoms both in this new, low-arousal sustained attention task and in the Sustained Attention to Response Task (SART). Twenty-eight children and 49 adolescents participated. On both tasks, ADHD symptom levels were associated with response time variability measures of SDRT and tau, but not with sigma. On the DDT, children with higher ADHD symptoms made more commission errors and were less accurate in detecting the target (d'), whereas adolescents made a similar number of commission errors and d' irrespective of their ADHD symptom levels. This pattern was not present in the SART. The adolescents found the DDT more challenging than the SART as their target sensitivity was lower during the DDT. The children were less confident in nominating the target (criterion) during the DDT than the SART. The results indicate that RTV measures are more consistently associated with ADHD symptoms than other RT measures and that the DDT is a sensitive task of sustained attention and response inhibition performance, particularly in children, and in children with higher symptoms of ADHD.

venue: Proceedings of the AAAI/ACM Conference on AI Ethics and Society
preview: We evaluate how effectively platform-level parental controls moderate a mainstream conversational assistant used by minors. abstract_text: We evaluate how effectively platform-level parental controls moderate a mainstream conversational assistant used by minors. Our two-phase protocol first builds a category-balanced conversation corpus via PAIR-style iterative prompt refinement over API, then has trained human agents replay/refine those prompts in the consumer UI using a designated child account while monitoring the linked parent inbox for alerts. We focus on seven risk areas—physical harm, pornography, privacy violence, health consultation, fraud, hate speech, and malware—and quantify four outcomes: Notification Rate (NR), Leak-Through (LR), Overblocking (OBR), and UI Intervention Rate (UIR). Using an automated judge (with targeted human audit) and comparing the current backend to legacy variants (GPT-4.1/4o), we find that notifications are selective rather than comprehensive: privacy violence, fraud, hate speech, and malware triggered no parental alerts in our runs, whereas physical harm (highest), pornography, and some health queries produced intermittent alerts. The current backend shows lower leak-through than legacy models, yet overblocking of benign, educational queries near sensitive topics remains common and is not surfaced to parents, revealing a policy–product gap between on-screen safeguards and parent-facing telemetry. We propose actionable fixes: broaden/configure the notification taxonomy, couple visible safeguards to privacy-preserving parent summaries, and prefer calibrated, age-appropriate safe rewrites over blanket refusals.

abstract_text: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) allows university teachers to delegate cognitive work while deciding how students should engage with it. Using codebook thematic analysis, we examined multi-source accounts from 25 teachers recruited through an AI-focused learning community and its professional networks in China. Materials comprised interviews with 22 teachers, three documentary cases, self-narratives and reflective essays. Three themes organize the findings: reconstructing the teacher role, defending professional judgment, and managing teachers’ and students’ cognitive participation. Participants described disciplinary expertise as a basis for evaluating AI outputs and reported practices intended to retain human engagement. Instrumental and partnership orientations overlapped; descriptive comparison with later use profiles did not establish a simple relationship between partnership language and usage intensity. Because the protocol introduced several focal topics, we distinguish prompted positions from volunteered formulations. The proposed belief–strategy–practice cycle is a heuristic interpretation of retrospective accounts, not a demonstrated mechanism. The study contributes an account of how teachers connect their own cognitive offloading with their reported organization of students’ learning opportunities. Its claims concern this AI-engaged sample rather than university teachers generally.

abstract_text: In the era of artificial intelligence (AI), sustainable education requires not only the integration of advanced technologies but also the cultivation of key competencies such as critical thinking. This study investigates English major students’ engagement with generative AI tools in translation learning, focusing on their usage patterns, critical thinking behaviors, and ethical awareness. A mixed-methods design combining questionnaire data and semi-structured interviews was employed to examine how students interact with AI in translation contexts. The results show that while students frequently use AI for translation, writing, and language learning, their engagement remains primarily functional and efficiency-driven. Although they display openness and flexibility toward AI, their reasoning confidence, self-regulation, and ethical reflection are underdeveloped, indicating surface-level interaction and overreliance on technological authority. These findings highlight the need to cultivate higher-order cognitive and ethical capacities in translation training. Central to this discussion is the conceptualization of the ideal learner in AI-assisted translation, a reflective, autonomous, and ethically aware individual who engages with AI as a partner in cognitive and moral development. Building on this, the study proposes pedagogical strategies that integrate AI literacy, process-oriented assessment, and teacher training to foster critical thinking and responsible AI use in sustainable translation education.

venue: EPRA International Journal of Environmental Economics Commerce and Educational Management
preview: Employers increasingly deploy artificial-intelligence systems that read employee sentiment from written communication, infer exhaustion from calendar and workload digital exhaust, and flag individuals as at elevated risk of burnout — tools marketed under the language of care rather than control. abstract_text: Employers increasingly deploy artificial-intelligence systems that read employee sentiment from written communication, infer exhaustion from calendar and workload digital exhaust, and flag individuals as at elevated risk of burnout — tools marketed under the language of care rather than control. This paper develops a conceptual model of how AI-mediated wellbeing monitoring reshapes psychological safety, the shared belief that a work environment is safe for interpersonal risk-taking on which voice, dissent and error reporting depend. Integrating psychological-safety theory, the algorithmic-management and workplace-surveillance literatures, and organisational voice research, the paper argues that wellbeing-monitoring intensity depresses psychological safety principally through a mediating perception of surveillance threat, and that this relationship is not fixed but is conditioned by the transparency of the monitoring system, the degree to which employees attribute developmental rather than punitive intent to it, and whether a human manager mediates between algorithmic output and managerial action. Five propositions specify these relationships, including a boundary condition for India's IT-BPM sector, where the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 supplies a general consent-and-purpose-limitation framework but no sector-specific rule for wellbeing analytics, leaving adoption norms to be set informally inside a high-attrition, always-on operating environment. The paper closes with implications for the design of psychologically safe monitoring architectures and an agenda for empirical validation.

title: The psychology of learning with generative AI in foreign language education: building a theory of metacognition, trust, and human–AI co-regulation through a systematic review
preview: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is reshaping foreign language education, yet the psychological processes underlying effective learner–AI interaction remain fragmented. abstract_text: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is reshaping foreign language education, yet the psychological processes underlying effective learner–AI interaction remain fragmented. This theory-building systematic review synthesizes empirical evidence on metacognition, trust, and human–AI co-regulation in GenAI-supported foreign language learning. Following PRISMA 2020 procedures, web of science and Scopus were searched for studies published from 2022 to June 2026. After screening, 51 empirical studies were included. The findings show that metacognition shapes learners’ planning, monitoring, regulation, and reflection; trust influences how learners accept, verify, modify, or reject AI-generated information and feedback; and human–AI co-regulation involves the dynamic distribution of cognitive and regulatory activity between learners and GenAI within teacher-mediated instructional contexts. AI literacy and learner agency further support critical evaluation, strategic AI use, and retention of human decision-making responsibility. Based on these findings, the review develops the metacognition–trust–co-regulation (MTC) framework, which conceptualizes effective GenAI-assisted learning as an iterative process in which metacognitive regulation informs trust, trust calibrates reliance, and reliance shapes human–AI co-regulation. The framework positions GenAI as a cognitive partner whose educational value depends on critically informed, metacognitively regulated, and humanly governed use.
