abstract_text: Generative artificial intelligence (GAI) is increasingly integrated into higher education, creating opportunities for flexible and personalised learning while raising questions about AI-supported learning. This study examines whether students’ attitudes toward GAI mediate the relationships between perceived ease of use (PEU), perceived usefulness (PU), and perceived Generative AI support for self-regulated learning (GAI-SRL). A cross-sectional survey was conducted with 264 undergraduate students at a public university in Indonesia. Data were analysed using partial least squares structural equation modelling (PLS-SEM). PEU and PU were positively associated with attitudes toward GAI, while attitudes were positively associated with perceived GAI support for self-regulated learning. PEU and PU also showed significant direct relationships with GAI-SRL, and their indirect relationships through attitudes were significant, indicating partial statistical mediation. These findings suggest that students’ attitudes toward GAI constitute an intermediate statistical pathway linking technology-related perceptions with perceived GAI support for self-regulated learning. The study extends technology acceptance research by positioning attitudes toward GAI within a learning-oriented framework and highlights responsible, learner-centred use of GAI while preserving students’ learning agency.

Data were collected through an online questionnaire during the first semester of the 2025/2026 academic year. A total of 278 questionnaires were returned. During the predefined eligibility screening procedure, 9 responses were excluded because the personal information provided could not be verified as indicating active undergraduate student status. A further 5 responses were excluded because the respondents reported very limited use of Generative AI for academic learning and therefore did not meet the study's predefined eligibility criterion concerning prior experience with Generative AI. Thus, 14 responses were excluded and 264 valid responses were retained for the final analysis. The final sample consisted of 112 male students (42.4%) and 152 female students (57.6%), with a mean age of 20.8 years (SD = 1.34). Participation was voluntary, and before completing the questionnaire, respondents were informed about the purpose of the study and provided electronic informed consent. Respondents' names and student identification numbers (NIM) were collected solely for the purpose of verifying active undergraduate student status. These identifying data were not included in the analytical dataset and were deleted before statistical analysis. Accordingly, the statistical analyses were conducted using de-identified data, while responses were treated confidentially. Data analysis was conducted using SmartPLS 3.0 following a two-stage PLS-SEM procedure. The first stage involved assessment of the measurement model, followed by evaluation of the structural model and mediation relationships. Given the cross-sectional research design, all estimated relationships were interpreted as statistical associations rather than causal effects (Hair et al., 2019) . The measurement model was assessed in terms of internal consistency reliability, convergent validity, and discriminant validity. Internal consistency reliability was evaluated using Cronbach's Alpha (CA) and Composite Reliability (CR). Convergent validity was assessed using indicator outer loadings and Average Variance Extracted (AVE). Discriminant validity was examined using the Fornell-Larcker criterion and the Heterotrait-Monotrait Ratio (HTMT). The structural model was evaluated using path coefficients, coefficient of determination (R²), collinearity assessment, effect sizes (f²), predictive relevance (Q²), and out-of-sample predictive assessment using PLSpredict. Effect size f² was used to assess the contribution of each exogenous construct to the explained variance of the endogenous construct. Predictive relevance was examined using the blindfolding procedure, with positive Q² values interpreted as evidence of predictive relevance. PLSpredict was additionally used to assess out-of-sample predictive performance using the resulting Q² predict values. Mediation effects were assessed through indirect effects estimated using bootstrapping with 5,000 resamples. The indirect effects of PEU and PU on GAI-SRL through ATT were examined using the bootstrapped estimates and confidence intervals. Consistent with the cross-sectional design, statistically significant indirect effects were interpreted as evidence of statistical mediation within the proposed model rather than evidence of a temporal or causal mechanism. Because the predictor, mediator, and endogenous constructs were measured using self-report items within the same online questionnaire and at the same measurement occasion, the potential for common-method variance was considered. Several procedural safeguards were applied, including voluntary participation, electronic informed consent, confidentiality of responses, and de-identification of the analytical dataset. Names and student identification numbers were collected only to verify active student status and were deleted before statistical analysis. The analytical dataset therefore did not contain direct personal identifiers. The outer and inner VIF values reported in the structural model were used to assess statistical collinearity and were not treated as a formal test of common-method bias. Therefore, the VIF results should not be interpreted as demonstrating the absence of common-method variance. Given the single-source, self-report measurement approach, the possibility of common-method variance cannot be completely excluded and is considered in the interpretation of the findings.

preview: The growing use of generative AI writing assistants, such as ChatGPT, in ESL/EFL academic contexts has sparked debate about their influence on self-regulated learning (SRL). abstract_text: The growing use of generative AI writing assistants, such as ChatGPT, in ESL/EFL academic contexts has sparked debate about their influence on self-regulated learning (SRL). This systematic review examines 41 empirical studies published between 2021 and March 2026 to evaluate how university students engage with AI tools in relation to SRL. Guided by PRISMA 2020 standards, the review synthesises quantitative, qualitative, and mixed methods research through narrative analysis, drawing on Zimmerman’s (2000) three phase SRL model and metacognitive regulation theory. Three central patterns emerge. First, SRL phases are unevenly addressed: the performance phase dominates (92.7% of studies), while forethought (58.5%) and self-reflection (51.2%) receive less attention, suggesting an incomplete regulatory cycle. Second, AI demonstrates a dual role in metacognitive regulation, facilitating monitoring, evaluation, and revision (68.3%), yet also contributing to cognitive offloading and reduced learner agency (14.6%), with 17.1% of studies reporting mixed outcomes. Third, pedagogical design is critical: structured approaches that integrate AI literacy, guided feedback, and teacher mediation consistently enhance SRL, whereas unguided use yields weaker results. The evidence base remains limited by its concentration in Asian contexts (73.2%), reliance on self-report data, and absence of longitudinal designs, restricting claims about sustained competence. Overall, the review concludes that generative AI can strengthen self-regulated academic writing when embedded in intentional pedagogical frameworks that activate all SRL phases; without such alignment, AI may improve immediate performance but hinder the development of lasting regulatory skills.

Many studies lack explicit theoretical grounding, and even when SRL is referenced, it is not consistently applied across all phases (Banihashem et al., 2025) . Contextual imbalances further constrain the field, with research concentrated in specific regions and predominantly on higher-education writing tasks (Chung & Wan, 2025; Zhang et al., 2025) . Furthermore, while writing has received disproportionate attention, other language skills essential for academic success, such as speaking, listening, and vocabulary development, remain critically underexplored in the AI-SRL literature (Kanont et al., 2024; Rahnuma, 2025) . Collectively, these limitations demonstrate that, despite the growing volume of research, the field remains insufficiently developed to support robust and generalisable conclusions. This study employed a systematic literature review design guided by the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) 2020 framework to ensure transparency, methodological rigour, and reproducibility (Page et al., 2021) . The PRISMA framework provides a structured procedure consisting of sequential phases that enhance the credibility and replicability of systematic reviews. The present review synthesises empirical research on the role of generative AI writing assistants in shaping self-regulated learning (SRL) among ESL/EFL university students engaged in academic writing. A review protocol was developed before conducting the study to guide the search, screening, and analysis procedures; however, it was not formally registered, which is acknowledged as a limitation affecting transparency.
analysis.discussion: This review examined how generative AI writing assistants influence self-regulated learning (SRL) in ESL/EFL university students' academic writing. By integrating the findings with prior scholarship, the discussion demonstrates that while existing literature provides important conceptual claims about AI and SRL, the empirical evidence both supports and complicates these assumptions, particularly when interpreted through Zimmerman's (2000) SRL model and metacognitive regulation theory. A central point of convergence between the literature and the findings lies in the selective operationalisation of SRL. As highlighted in the literature review (de Mooij et al., 2025; Molenaar et al., 2023; Lan & Zhou, 2025) , prior research tends to privilege the performance phase while neglecting forethought and self-reflection. The present findings empirically confirm this pattern. Most studies focus on monitoring, strategy use, and interaction with AI during writing, with far fewer examining planning or reflective processes. This alignment suggests that SRL has often been adopted as a partial framework, applied primarily where learner-AI interaction is observable. However, the findings extend the literature by showing that this imbalance is not merely conceptual but systematically embedded in research design, reinforcing a view of SRL that is reactive rather than cyclical. In Zimmerman's terms, the regulatory loop is truncated, limiting opportunities for learners to internalise strategies across phases. The findings also provide a more nuanced perspective on the debate surrounding metacognitive regulation, which the literature positions as the central mechanism through which AI influences learning (Schraw & Dennison, 1994, as cited in Banihashem et al., 2025; Lan & Zhou, 2025) . Consistent with studies emphasising AI's affordances (Nguyen et al., 2024; Nikolopoulou, 2024) , the results show that learners frequently engage in monitoring and evaluation when interacting with AI, using it to identify weaknesses, refine arguments, and generate alternatives. This supports the claim that AI can function as a metacognitive scaffold, extending learners' capacity to regulate their writing. However, the findings also substantiate the counter-argument in the literature that AI may lead to externalisation of metacognitive processes (Kanont et al., 2024; Lan & Zhou, 2025) . Evidence of cognitive offloading, uncritical acceptance of AI outputs, and reduced monitoring effort indicates that metacognitive activity may be performed but not internalised. This extends prior critiques by demonstrating that the tension between enhancement and externalisation is not theoretical but empirically observable across multiple studies. In this sense, the findings refine the literature by introducing a critical distinction between metacognitive engagement as behaviour and metacognitive development as competence, a distinction that has remained largely implicit in previous work. The review further advances the literature on generative AI as a pedagogical tool, which has been characterised by competing assumptions of empowerment and dependency (Nikolopoulou, 2024; Tekir, 2026) . The findings suggest that both perspectives are valid, but incomplete when considered in isolation. Rather than being inherent properties of AI, supportive and hindering effects are shown to be contingent on pedagogical conditions, a point that aligns with but also extends earlier calls for more attention to instructional design (Lan & Zhou, 2025). Studies incorporating structured interventions, such as AI literacy training, guided workflows, and teacher mediation, demonstrate stronger SRL outcomes, whereas unguided use is associated with surface-level engagement. This reinforces the argument that AI should not be conceptualised as an independent variable, but as a pedagogically mediated artefact whose impact depends on how it is embedded within learning environments. Importantly, the findings also speak directly to the methodological limitations identified in the literature review (Banihashem et al., 2025; de Mooij et al., 2025; Xu et al., 2026) . The dominance of self-report measures and short-term designs is confirmed, raising concerns about the validity of claims regarding SRL development. While many studies report improvements in strategy use or writing performance, the evidence suggests that these gains may reflect situated task support rather than durable competence, reinforcing the performance-competence divide highlighted in prior research. The limited use of process-oriented methods further constrains the field's ability to capture SRL as a dynamic and evolving process. The findings deepen the literature's critique of contextual and geographic concentration (Chung & Wan, 2025; Zhang et al., 2025) . The strong clustering of studies in Asian higher education contexts is not only confirmed but also shown to shape the evidence base itself, limiting the generalisability of conclusions. Notably, the absence of studies from African contexts is particularly significant, given the region's linguistic diversity and differing levels of digital infrastructure. This suggests that current understandings of AI-supported SRL may reflect contextspecific dynamics rather than universal patterns, an issue acknowledged in the literature but insufficiently addressed empirically. The discussion demonstrates that the findings both validate and extend existing scholarship. While prior research correctly identifies the potential of generative AI to support SRL, it underestimates the extent to which this support is uneven, context-dependent, and pedagogically mediated. title: Beyond accuracy: extracting reaction-time biomarkers of sustained attention and cognitive flexibility from the UCancellation task

abstract_text: Cancellation tasks are widely used measures of attention but are conventionally scored by metrics such as mean accuracy or concentration scores, disregarding the temporal structure of responding. Here, we derive two reaction-time (RT) biomarkers from our tablet-based UCancellation task in 388 young adults: intra-individual RT variability (RTV), a marker of sustained attention, and switch cost, an index of cognitive flexibility from transitions between two different task's target categories. Because consecutive targets are separated by a variable number of scanned distractors, both are confounded by search effort, which we remove with a scanning-load (p) correction framework. RTV behaved as a scored individual-difference measure: correction improved reliability and convergent validity against TOVA low-frequency RTV (n = 373), and a cross-target composite was the most reliable index. Switch cost behaved as a within-task phenomenon whose sign reversed with load—large and positive when targets were adjacent, reversing as scanning load increased—consistent with inhibition of return. Together, these metrics show that RT structure within a brief cancellation task carries attentional information that standard metrics alone does not capture.

abstract_text: This study explored how English writers differ in their engagement with generative AI tools for writing, focusing on perceived cognitive effort and critical thinking, and examined how learner profiles differed in their perceived confidence in AI-assisted writing, evaluative skill, and automation orientations. A total of 540 university-level English writers completed a questionnaire integrating self-regulated learning phases and AI literacy dimensions. Latent profile analysis identified four distinct learner profiles that reflected varying levels of self-reported AI confidence, evaluative skill, and willingness to automate writing. The profiles ranged from traditional self-reliant writers to critical evaluators and AI-enthusiastic but uncritical users. Subsequent weighted analyses revealed that, while general AI writing confidence did not vary substantially across profiles, significant group differences emerged in AI content evaluation and willingness to automate. Learners with high critical-thinking breadth demonstrated stronger evaluative competence and a more cautious adoption of AI, whereas those with high training experience exhibited greater confidence and openness to use. Multinomial logistic modeling further showed that formal AI or critical thinking training predicted membership in high-engagement profiles, whereas dependency tendencies negatively predicted critical user orientation. These findings suggest that learners’ orientations toward AI-assisted writing are shaped less by access or usage frequency and more by the interplay between critical literacy, metacognitive regulation, and perceived control.

abstract_text: Aim of the study: This study aimed to investigate the impact of the use of AI tools on academic engagement and critical thinking among university students in Karachi. Methodology: The study used a preliminary exploratory mixed-methods design with a sample of 165 bachelor’s students, selected through equal stratified randomization from seven public universities on University Road, Karachi, Pakistan. The study used a self-administered questionnaire with 36 closed-ended and 3 open-ended questions to collect data. The tool showed strong overall reliability, as indicated by Cronbach’s alpha (α = 0.753). Findings: Results revealed a significant but negative relationship between AI use and academic engagement (r = -.402), and regression analysis demonstrated that AI use was associated with a 91.7% decrease in critical thinking (R² = .917, β = -.958). Moreover, academic engagement and critical thinking were positively related (r = .369). Thematic analysis identified three themes: academic use of AI, benefits of AI, and challenges of AI, which fully corroborated the quantitative findings. Conclusion: The study concludes that uncontrolled reliance on AI significantly weakens students’ critical thinking and academic engagement; however, AI can be helpful and efficient for academic tasks, and excessive reliance on it could hinder the development of vital cognitive skills. The study suggests promoting balanced AI use, integrating research and inquiry into academic practice, and raising awareness of AI ethics education. Besides, there is an urgent need to make AI literacy obligatory in Pakistani university curricula and to provide formal training in the ethical use of AI to all faculty and students.

abstract_text: Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly used by university students not only to locate information, but also to explain concepts, organize ideas, and complete academic tasks. This article examines the psychological processes that may explain why such use can support learning in some situations while reducing students' intellectual involvement in others. A conceptual literature review was conducted by bringing together foundational work on Distributed Cognition, Extended Mind, Cognitive Load, Student Engagement, and the ICAP Framework with recent studies on GenAI in education. Sources were selected for their relevance to cognitive offloading, cognitive engagement, and academic integrity. The review suggests that the educational consequences of GenAI depend less on its mere use than on how cognitive work is divided between students and the system. Offloading routine demands may free resources for evaluation and reflection, whereas delegating core reasoning may weaken engagement and make academic products less representative of students' own understanding. On this basis, the Educational Cognitive Transformation Model (ECTM) is proposed to connect learning transformation, cognitive offloading, redistribution of cognitive activities, cognitive engagement, learning quality, and academic integrity. ECTM is offered as a conceptual proposition that still requires empirical testing.

abstract_text: This study examines the relationship between digital distraction and academic self-regulation among distance education students. Digital distraction is defined as the interruption of academic tasks caused by the frequent use of digital devices and platforms, which negatively affects attention, concentration, and academic performance. In this context, self-regulation is a key process that enables learners to plan, monitor, and adjust their behavior to optimize learning outcomes. Theoretical models, such as Pintrich’s framework, emphasize the importance of goal setting, time management, and reflection on learning strategies. A quantitative, correlational, and cross-sectional study was conducted with 200 Psychology students enrolled in the SUAyED program. Data were collected through an adapted version of the Motivated Strategies for Learning Questionnaire (MSLQ) and the Digital Distraction Scale (DD). Results indicate that students with higher self-regulation skills— particularly in Control Beliefs and Time and Environment Management—showed lower levels of digital distraction. Moreover, older students exhibited greater self-regulation and less susceptibility to distractions. These findings highlight the importance of enhancing self-regulation skills and fostering a mindful use of technology in distance learning environments

abstract_text: This study examines how undergraduate students integrate generative AI tools into home exams and how these practices relate to self-regulated learning (SRL) and academic performance. Using a mixed-methods design, we analyzed exam responses, self-reports, and performance data from 891 students enrolled in BA-level qualitative methodology courses (2023–2024). Students were permitted to use AI if they disclosed their usage. Three modes of AI engagement were identified: instrumental (task completion with minimal evaluation), ideational (idea generation and selective integration), and reflective (critical evaluation and feedback-driven refinement). At a general level, AI use was associated with increased efficiency and somewhat higher performance than non-use. However, these aggregate patterns masked substantial variation across modes of use. Instrumental use was associated with weaker performance in some tasks, including definition tasks where reliance on generic AI-generated responses did not align with course-specific criteria. In contrast, reflective engagement with AI was associated with stronger and more consistent performance. Interpreted through an SRL framework, these findings suggest that outcomes of AI use depend on how students regulate its use. Rather than uniformly supporting or undermining learning, AI appears to amplify differences in students’ self-regulatory capacities. This highlights the importance of supporting students in developing skills for critical and reflective engagement with AI.

analysis.methods: The study was conducted in the "Introduction to Qualitative Methods" course offered to undergraduate students in the Faculty of Social Sciences at the University of Eastern Finland. The compulsory course is taken in the second or third year by students in social sciences, health and social management, business, geography, and open university. Instruction and assessment were conducted in Finnish (quotes are translated into English). The dataset is based on a home exam consisting of three tasks. The first task asked students to define a key concept in qualitative research. To receive the maximum score, students had to provide an accurate definition, elaborate on it using course materials, and contextualize it within qualitative research. The second task assessed students' ability to apply a qualitative analysis method to a short dataset. High-scoring responses included an appropriate research question, a description of the selected method, a clear account of the analytical process (coding and theme development), and a coherent interpretation of findings. The third task required students to evaluate the methodological and ethical aspects of a research setting. Full credit required identifying strengths and limitations in relation to research questions, data collection, analysis, and ethics. Emphasis was placed on internal consistency, that is, recognizing how individual design choices combine into a coherent qualitative approach. The study used authentic course data, meaning that assessment was conducted by the course instructor as part of the normal course process, and the research began only after grading had been completed. Consequently, inter-rater reliability was not calculated. However, the use of a structured rubric and the re-evaluation of a subset of responses supported consistency in grading. Students received information about the research via the course page and email, and those who declined participation were excluded. The study complied with the EU General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR, 2016/679) and the Finnish Data Protection Act (1050/2018). All data were pseudonymized prior to analysis. The dataset includes home exam materials from 413 students in 2023 and 478 students in 2024 (total N = 891). We used five types of data: exam answers, platform log data, exam results, self-reported AI use, and course feedback (Table 1 ). Each dataset served a distinct role within a mixed-methods design. Exam answers, self-reports, and feedback formed the basis for qualitative analysis of AI use, while performance (points and grades) and log data (completion time) supported quantitative analysis of outcomes and efficiency. After course completion, we compiled all exam data into a spreadsheet containing exam year, submission time, task scores, total points, final grade, and self-reported AI use. Anonymous course feedback was not linked to individual students and was analyzed separately. The qualitative analysis focused on exams in which students reported AI use. We conducted a thematic analysis to identify patterns in AI use (Braun & Clarke, 2021) . The coding proceeded in four steps: 1) inductive coding of self-reports, 2) identification of recurring patterns, 3) deductive coding of exam responses with cross-validation to self-reports based on created criteria, and 4) deductive coding of course feedback. We identified three modes of AI use: instrumental, ideational, and reflective. In self-reports students described instrumental use as editing or directly adapting AI-generated text, ideational use as using AI for idea generation, and reflective use as evaluating their writing with AI tools. The first author conducted the initial inductive coding, after which the third author reviewed coding. Rather than conducting independent blind coding, the review process focused on evaluating the conceptual coherence of the categories, discussing ambiguous cases, and refining category boundaries. Particular attention was given to distinctions between instrumental and ideational use, which were less clearly differentiated than reflective use. Specifically, some students used AI primarily for improving language, grammar, or structure while leaving the substantive content largely unchanged. After discussion, these cases were classified as instrumental use because AI functioned mainly as an editing tool rather than as a source of ideas or reflective feedback. Because many self-reports were brief, we developed additional classification criteria (typical indicators) to support the following deductive coding. To refine these criteria, we compared a sample of student responses from each mode with example answers generated by ChatGPT 3.5, which was used by 85% of the students, and with established indicators of AI-generated text (Simon, 2023) . We focused on three dimensions: 1) content (superficial analysis, contextual misalignment, generic responses and factual inconsistencies in relation to course materials), 2) structure (formulaic organization, weak logical connections, mechanical use of transitions, and similar structural patterns across task types), and 3) style (overly formal tone, overly polished appearance, generic or vague wording, repetitiveness, lack of personal voice). Instrumental use was coded when AI-generated content formed the primary basis of the response with minimal modification. Ideational use was coded when AI outputs were selectively integrated into student-authored text. Reflective use was coded when AI was used primarily to refine students' own responses. In ambiguous cases, classification was based on the dominant pattern across content, structure, and style indicators. Together, we used these steps to develop the coding scheme (Appendix 1). In the final stage of qualitative analysis, by using a coding scheme, we deductively coded exam responses and open-ended course feedback. We then added AI modes to the spreadsheet, coding each exam response as non-use, instrumental, ideational, or reflective. Because AI use varied across tasks (Table 2 ), analyses were conducted at the task level, with each task treated as an independent observation. Where aggregated performance measures were used, these were calculated by combining task-level scores. We then conducted quantitative analysis by linking modes of AI use to performance (points and grades) and efficiency (completion time). First, the quantitative analysis focused on differences in results between students who used AI and those who did not. The differences were studied using a non-parametric U test due to unequal group sizes and non-normal distribution of scores. To study the possible differences in exam results between students in different modes of AI, the Kruskal-Wallis test was used. The quantitative part of the study was conducted using Jamovi software. In this dataset, insights into self-regulated learning are drawn from materials produced in an authentic course context rather than from students' explicit reflections on their learning. Within the SRL framework, the decision to use AI as a resource (and for which tasks) was interpreted as part of the forethought phase. Exam performance reflected the performance phase, and self-reports represented selfreflection. Course feedback further illuminated metacognitive reflections and motivational and emotional aspects across all phases. analysis.discussion: Our findings suggest a gradual normalization of AI use in academic settings, reflected in increased uptake and more positive attitudes, aligning with prior research indicating generally neutral or positive student perceptions of AI in education (Ardelean & Edit, 2023; Jinchuña Huallpa et al., 2023) . However, ethical concerns persisted, particularly regarding whether AI-assisted exam work constitutes genuine learning. Similar student concerns have been identified in contexts AI use may compromise fairness and skill development (Chaudhry et al., 2023) . Overall, the findings challenge the notion of students as uniform adopters of AI. Instead, attitudes and emotions toward AI differ, shaping how and whether students use LLMs in academic tasks. This variation underlines the need for more nuanced, context-sensitive accounts of AI use in authentic learning situations. This study shows that students' use of AI in academic tasks is not uniform but varies in meaningful ways. We identified three modes of AI use-instrumental, ideational, and reflective-and found that these are associated with different levels of engagement and performance. Students who engaged more evaluatively with AI tended to demonstrate stronger and more consistent outcomes, while more instrumental use was sometimes associated with weaker performance, especially in tasks requiring contextualization and critical interpretation. Taken together, these findings indicate that the role of AI in learning depends on how students use it. AI is not inherently beneficial or harmful; rather, its effects depend on how students regulate its use. In this sense, AI makes students' self-regulatory capacities more visible and potentially more consequential. This highlights the importance of supporting students in developing the skills needed to use AI thoughtfully and critically, so that it contributes to meaningful learning rather than mere task completion.
analysis.limitations: This study has several limitations. First, the data were collected during the early stages of widespread generative AI adoption, when many students were still experimenting with the technology. As a result, the proposed categorization of AI use should be considered an initial framework, open to further refinement. In addition, the study was conducted in the context of home exams, which represent a specific assessment setting. Comparisons to more complex academic tasks, such as thesis writing, should therefore be made with caution, as students may employ multiple AI strategies across extended projects and use a wider range of tools. Second, the study is based on naturally occurring data without experimental control. Consequently, self-regulated learning processes were inferred rather than directly measured. The analysis relies primarily on self-reports, which varied in detail and did not include prompts, limiting insight into actual AI interactions. This may have affected the classification of AI use, particularly in distinguishing between ideational and reflective modes. In addition, it is possible that some students did not disclose their AI use, which could lead to under-or overestimation of differences between groups. As AI models evolved rapidly during data collection (2023-2024), differences in tool capabilities may have influenced the effectiveness of certain usage strategies. And variation in exam tasks across sessions may also affect comparability, despite the use of a shared grading rubric. A further limitation concerns interpretation. As an observational and mainly qualitative study, the findings indicate associations rather than causal relationships. In particular, students who engaged in more evaluative or reflective forms of AI use may already have differed from others in terms of prior ability, motivation, or self-regulatory capacity. This makes it difficult to disentangle whether differences in performance are related to AI use itself or to underlying student characteristics. The study is also limited by its theoretical framing. Although selfregulated learning provided a useful framework for identifying differences in students' AI use, the aim was not to measure or validate SRL processes as such. Consequently, the findings primarily, and somewhat simplistically, draw attention to students' self-regulation in integrating AI as a learning resource. Alternative theoretical perspectives, such as deep learning or digital literacy, might have provided greater insight into the learning processes themselves or the critical skills required to use AI tools. Both of these aspects deserve further exploration. Thus, the study provides only partial access to students' learning processes. While self-reports and feedback offer useful insights, they do not capture students' internal motivations, planning strategies, or realtime decision-making. In particular, motivational factors such as task value, goal orientation, and self-efficacy were not directly measured, even though the findings suggest they play an important role in shaping AI use. Given the complexity of motivation as a research domain, future studies would benefit from employing methods specifically designed to capture these dimensions more systematically. The findings cannot be generalized statistically to all higher education contexts where students use generative AI for written assignments. The study is based on an authentic teaching situation, with all its inherent imperfections, and it began as a qualitative and conceptual process to which quantitative elements were added later on. The findings should therefore be interpreted as indicative rather than definitive. However, the consistency of the identified patterns across two academic years suggests that the distinction between instrumental, ideational, and reflective AI use may have relevance beyond the specific course examined here. Despite these limitations, the study highlights the complex and nonuniform role of AI in educational settings. Drawing on authentic assessment context, longitudinal design spanning two academic years, and triangulated data, the study provides a robust account of how students engage with AI in practice. The findings suggest that the pedagogical value of AI depends less on the tool itself and more on how students regulate its use within learning processes. The findings may inform educational decision-making in several ways. First, they suggest that educational interventions should focus not only on whether students use AI, but also on how they use it. Second, instruction on AI literacy should emphasize critical evaluation, adaptation, and reflection rather than task completion. Third, assessment practices may benefit from rewarding contextualization, critical thinking, and reflective engagement, which appear to distinguish higher-performing forms of AI use. Future research should examine how instructional approaches and targeted support can help students engage with AI in ways that sustain autonomy, critical thinking, and deep learning.

abstract_text: Generative AI (GenAI) tools entered higher education classrooms faster than the field was able to study their effects on learning. One concern is that GenAI may displace the critical thinking and AI literacy that students will need after graduation. This paper reports a Design-Based Research pilot of a GenAI-assisted critical thinking framework, in which ChatGPT was used as a thinking partner in an undergraduate research methods and statistics course during Spring 2025 (N = 14). The mixed-methods design combined pre- and post-intervention measures of statistical learning (AASCDM), AI literacy (MAILS), and critical thinking (WGCTA) with instructor field notes, student artifacts, and student-AI interaction logs. Pre-post tests showed gains on every AASCDM dimension and on eight of nine MAILS dimensions, while WGCTA percentiles did not change. Qualitative analysis identified four themes: the ways students positioned the LLM (as answer generator, validator, or co-thinker); the depth of student engagement (procedural vs. conceptual); occasional humanizing of the tool; and the role of curriculum design in shaping each of the prior three. Read together, the findings indicate that one semester of GenAI-assisted instruction can move domain learning and self-reported AI literacy but does not move standardized critical thinking, and that the modal student-LLM relationship is one of validation instead of dialogue. We end with design principles for the next iteration of the framework and implications for research on adaptive and personalized learning.

abstract_text: Background/ problem: The rise of artificial intelligence (AI) use in education has sparked debate about its potential association with students’ critical thinking, while existing studies have reported inconsistent findings. Objective/ purpose: This study examined how AI dependency affects students’ critical thinking disposition through the mediating roles of cognitive fatigue and engagement. Design and Methodology: A cross-sectional survey was conducted among 639 university students in Java, Indonesia, using convenience sampling design. Data were collected through an online questionnaire and analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling (SEM-PLS). Results: The findings show that AI dependency does not directly affect students' critical thinking disposition (β = .05, p = .31). Instead, cognitive fatigue (β = -.60, p = .00) and engagement (β = .36, p = .00) significantly mediate the relationship in contrasting ways. On one hand, AI dependency increases cognitive fatigue, which subsequently weakens students' critical thinking disposition. On the other hand, AI dependency promotes engagement, which in turn strengthens critical thinking disposition. Conclusion and Implications: These findings suggest that AI dependency influence students’ critical thinking disposition indirectly through contrasting cognitive and behavioral pathways. From a behavioral-science perspective, modifiable student–AI interaction behaviors shape these outcomes. Educators should promote reflective AI engagement, require independent verification of AI-generated outputs, and design learning activities that maintain students’ responsibility for reasoning and decision-making. Strategies that limit cognitive offloading, uncritical acceptance of AI outputs, and excessive dependency help prevent cognitive fatigue and support students’ critical thinking disposition.

abstract_text: This study examined students’ AI literacy, perceived learning benefits, and ethical awareness following participation in a structured, AI-integrated classroom activity. The study also investigated the relationships among these constructs and examined whether perceived learning benefits mediate the relationship between AI literacy and ethical awareness. In addition, the study explored whether students’ responses differed according to gender, prior AI experience, and frequency of AI use. The study involved 104 undergraduate students who participated in a hands-on classroom activity over two academic semesters. Students used generative AI tools, including ChatGPT, Google Gemini, and Microsoft Copilot, to prepare and deliver short lessons to their classmates, followed by discussions addressing responsible and ethical AI use. Data were collected using a structured questionnaire measuring AI literacy, perceived learning benefits, ethical awareness, and related aspects of students’ experiences. Overall, students reported positive perceptions of the learning experience. They strongly agreed that AI made learning easier and more enjoyable (M = 4.29), saved time on academic tasks (M = 4.27), and helped improve the quality of their work (M = 4.09). AI literacy was positively correlated with perceived learning benefits (r = 0.559, p .05). The findings suggest that students’ AI literacy is associated with greater perceived learning benefits and ethical awareness. Furthermore, the study examines the potential mediating role of perceived learning benefits in the relationship between AI literacy and ethical awareness. These findings highlight the importance of structured, meaningful classroom activities that encourage students to actively engage with, evaluate, and take responsibility for AI-generated content rather than relying on AI outputs passively.

reading.findings: The empirical findings provide support for the relationships among the three measured constructs: AI literacy, perceived learning benefits, and ethical awareness. The observed correlations were statistically significant (r = 0.559, p < .001; r = 0.386, p < .001; and r = 0.472, p < .001, respectively). Mediation analysis indicated a statistically indirect association between AI literacy and ethical awareness through perceived learning benefits (Indirect effect = 0.194, 95% CI [0.051, 0.361]), with a non-significant direct effect (β = 0.165, p = .091). These findings support the empirically tested relationships among the measured variables, while critical thinking and co-creation remain theoretical components of the conceptual framework. As presented in Table 4 , participants reported high levels across all three domains. AI Literacy scored (W.A = 3.81, SD = 0.908), with the highest-rated item being understanding how AI assists in lesson preparation (W.A = 4.01), followed by critical thinking about AI-generated content (W.A = 3.84), and active engagement (W.A = 3.56). Perceived Benefits scored very high (W.A = 4.215, SD = 0.874). Students rated "AI made learning easier and more enjoyable" highest (W.A = 4.288), followed by time savings (W.A = 4.269), and improved quality of work (W.A = 4.087). Ethical Awareness scored high (W.A = 4.103, SD = 0.846). The highest-rated item was commitment to responsible AI use (W.A = 4.279), followed by understanding ethical use after the activity (W.A = 4.183), and support for institutional guidelines (W.A = 4.067). Chi-square Goodness-of-Fit tests confirmed significant deviations from uniform distribution across all domains ( p < .001). To examine the mediating role of Perceived Benefits (M) in the association between AI Literacy (X) and Ethical Awareness (Y), Hayes' PROCESS Macro (Model 4) was utilized with 5,000 bootstrap samples. reading.interpretation: The results indicate a statistically significant indirect association between AI Literacy and Ethical Awareness through Perceived Benefits, while the direct association between AI Literacy and Ethical Awareness was not statistically significant. These findings are consistent with the interpretation that the association between AI Literacy and Ethical Awareness may operate indirectly through Perceived Benefits. However, given the cross-sectional design, these findings are correlational and should not be interpreted as evidence of a causal pathway. Higher levels of perceived AI Literacy were associated with higher Perceived Benefits, which were in turn associated with higher Ethical Awareness. The aim of this study was to analyze the influence of the class activity based on the application of generative AI on the AI literacy, learning benefits perceived by undergraduate students, and their ethical awareness. The findings have shown a statistically significant indirect effect of the AI literacy on the ethical awareness via the perception of learning benefits, as hypothesized in the proposed theory. This relationship is in line with-but does not prove-the possible process through which AI literacy is associated with the perception of the usefulness of AI, which is further associated with perceived learning benefits (savings in time, improvement in quality, pleasure) and, finally, with ethical awareness. This finding aligns with Self-Determination Theory (Ryan and Deci, 2000) . When students experience competence through perceived benefits, they are more likely to internalize responsible behaviors. To examine the mediating role of Perceived Benefits (M) in the association between AI Literacy (X) and Ethical Awareness (Y), Hayes' PROCESS Macro (Model 4) was utilized with 5,000 bootstrap samples. The results revealed the following: Path A (X → M): AI Literacy was significantly and positively associated with Perceived Benefits (β = 0.538, p < .001), explaining 31.2% of its variance. Path B (M → Y): Perceived Benefits was significantly and positively associated with Ethical Awareness (β = 0.360, p < .001), after controlling for AI Literacy. Direct association (X → Y): The direct association between AI Literacy and Ethical Awareness was not statistically significant after accounting for Perceived Benefits (β = 0.165, p = .091). Indirect effect (X → M → Y): The indirect effect was statistically significant (Effect = 0.194, BootLLCI = 0.051, BootULCI = 0.361). Because the bootstrap confidence interval does not include zero, the results provide evidence consistent with an indirect mediation pathway. The results showed that after the AI activity, students had good AI literacy (M = 3.81), very good perceived benefits (M = 4.22), and good ethical awareness (M = 4.10). Students said that AI helped them save time (71.2%), improved their ability to solve problems (71.2%), and strengthened their critical thinking (62.5%). At the same time, some students worried about incorrect AI outputs (54.8%) and plagiarism (35.0%). This shows that students have a balanced and thoughtful view of AI tools. The statistical analysis also showed that students who had used AI before the activity had higher perceived benefits (p = .003) and higher ethical awareness (p = .005). However, gender and academic level did not make any difference in the results. Also, how often students used AI was linked to all three areas (p < .01). This means that using AI more often helps students build better skills and awareness.
analysis.discussion: The results indicate a statistically significant indirect association between AI Literacy and Ethical Awareness through Perceived Benefits, while the direct association between AI Literacy and Ethical Awareness was not statistically significant. These findings are consistent with the interpretation that the association between AI Literacy and Ethical Awareness may operate indirectly through Perceived Benefits. However, given the cross-sectional design, these findings are correlational and should not be interpreted as evidence of a causal pathway. Higher levels of perceived AI Literacy were associated with higher Perceived Benefits, which were in turn associated with higher Ethical Awareness. The aim of this study was to analyze the influence of the class activity based on the application of generative AI on the AI literacy, learning benefits perceived by undergraduate students, and their ethical awareness. The findings have shown a statistically significant indirect effect of the AI literacy on the ethical awareness via the perception of learning benefits, as hypothesized in the proposed theory. This relationship is in line with-but does not prove-the possible process through which AI literacy is associated with the perception of the usefulness of AI, which is further associated with perceived learning benefits (savings in time, improvement in quality, pleasure) and, finally, with ethical awareness. This finding aligns with Self-Determination Theory (Ryan and Deci, 2000) . When students experience competence through perceived benefits, they are more likely to internalize responsible behaviors. It also supports Expectancy-Value Theory (Eccles and Wigfield, 2002) , where value beliefs (perceived benefits) mediate the relationship between competence beliefs (AI literacy) and behavioral outcomes (ethical awareness). Notably, the insignificant direct effect (β = 0.165, p = .091) together with the significant indirect effect suggests that AI literacy does not have a direct association with ethical awareness when learning gains are controlled for. This implies several important implications for teaching practice: instructors must not rely on the belief that the mere teaching of AI techniques fosters responsible conduct. Students must also experience and value the benefits of AI use.
analysis.limitations: • First, the sample (N = 104) came from only one university, and students were chosen based on convenience. This means the results may not apply to all students. • Second, the study used self-reported answers, which may not be completely accurate (common method bias; Podsakoff et al., 2003) because students might answer in a way they think looks good. • Third, there was no control group, so we cannot say for sure that the activity caused the results. • Fourth, the study measured outcomes right after the activity. We need follow-up studies to see if the gains in literacy, benefits, and awareness last over time, • Fifth, although the study included open-ended questions, a systematic qualitative analysis was not conducted. Therefore, the study should be characterized as predominantly quantitative, with qualitative data used for exploratory purposes only. Future research should employ rigorous qualitative methods such as thematic analysis (Braun and Clarke, 2006) or in-depth interviews to capture richer insights into students' experiences, • Sixth, the study's findings are based on self-reported data, which may be subject to social desirability bias or inaccurate recall. Future studies should incorporate objective measures of student performance and AI interaction behaviors (Podsakoff et al., 2003) .

abstract_text:
The new generation of digital assistance programs, including generative artificial intelligence
(GenAI), is increasingly shifting from information retrieval to the generation of explanations,
arguments, code, abstracts, and solutions. The extent to which GenAI support of human
cognition can extend human capacity versus supplant critical cognitive processes underlying
knowledge and skill formation has been a longstanding psychological question. This narrative
review focuses on foundational research on cognitive offloading and on peer-reviewed studies of
GenAI published through September 05, 2026. A structured narrative search for experimental,
meta-analytic, and mixed-methods studies on memory, learning, critical thinking, creativity,
perceived effort, trust, and dependence on GenAI was complemented by a search of crosssectional and qualitative studies that provided early characterization of emerging constructs of
dependence on GenAI. Evidence does not support a simple positive or negative effect of GenAI
on human cognition. GenAI-supported offloading of cognitive functions such as memory
retrieval, processing, and learning can reduce the required cognitive capacity and support high
performance across a variety of tasks, including memory-based and GenAI-supported academic
tasks. However, the same cognitive offloading can, in some cases, reduce the quality of
subsequent encoding, and recent studies on GenAI show a consistent performance-learning
dissociation. While support that enables high performance when support is available can carry
over to later unsupported performance, the gain is typically small, nonexistent, or even negative.
Studies of support provided under instructional control indicate that retaining learner-generated
nodes or restricting direct-answer substitutes for generators can support later independent
performance better than unlimited support. It remains to be determined what the independent
contribution of explanation, verification, revision, and fading support is. Nevertheless, findings
from emerging dependence research correlate with indicators of academic stress, performance
expectations, anxiety, and self-efficacy. However, currently available evidence does not support
claims of irreversible cognitive decline. A key finding of this review is that whether GenAI is
used at all is less critical than which functions are offloaded, which are maintained, and the
extent to which users remain epistemically responsible for the resulting output. Implications are
developed for education, knowledge work, tool design, and longitudinal research.

abstract_text: Digital devices can function simultaneously as learning resources and sources of distraction, making their educational consequences dependent on how and why they are used. This qualitative descriptive study examines parents’ accounts of students’ digital-device use, focusing on academic use, digital distraction, time and attention management, social interaction, and parental mediation. Primary data were derived from parent interviews and interpreted thematically, while relevant peer-reviewed literature was used to contextualize the findings. The results indicate that digital devices can extend access to learning materials, support homework completion, and enable learning beyond the classroom. However, unstructured recreational use, particularly gaming, social media, and entertainment, was associated in parents’ accounts with reduced study time, fragmented attention, and diminished face-to-face interaction. Because the study did not employ objective achievement scores, the findings do not establish a causal effect on academic achievement. Instead, they identify learning conditions through which device use may support or undermine student outcomes. The study contributes an interpretive framework that distinguishes on-task from off-task use and positions parental mediation as a contextual mechanism. Educational guidance should therefore emphasize the quality and purpose of device use rather than screen duration alone.

abstract_text: This quantitative predictive-correlational study determined whether digital distraction and study habits were associated with and jointly predicted critical thinking skills in English among Grade 7 learners of Bigaan National High School, Division of Surigao del Sur. Thirty-six learners with complete and valid responses participated through purposive selection of the grade level followed by an attempt at total enumeration. Digital distraction and study habits were measured through an adapted and contextualized Digital Distraction and Study Habits Questionnaire, while critical thinking was assessed using a researcher-made Grade 7 English Critical Thinking Skills Test. Weighted means, standard deviations, rank ordering, frequency and percentage distributions, Pearson product-moment correlations, and multiple linear regression were used. Digital distraction was very high, while study habits were moderate. The mean critical thinking score was 21.0286 out of 50 (42.06%), with performance concentrated in the Developing and Beginning levels. Digital distraction was significantly and negatively related to critical thinking, whereas study habits were significantly and positively related to critical thinking. The combined regression model was significant, F (2, 32) = 10.12, p = 0.000393, explaining 38.75% of the variance in critical thinking scores (R² = 0.3875). The findings indicate that managing digital distraction and strengthening structured study routines are relevant school-based directions for supporting higher-order English reasoning.

reading.interpretation: Grade 7 learners in the study exhibited very high digital distraction, moderate study habits, and generally low-to-developing critical thinking performance in English. Off-task phone use and notification-driven interruption were the most prominent forms of distraction, while time management and planning represented the weakest study-habit area. The findings therefore describe a learning context in which frequent digital interruption coexists with only moderately established study routines and difficulty in higher-order English reasoning. abstract_text: In the educational context, generative artificial intelligence (AI) challenges traditional conceptions of language, authorship, and knowledge. Given this, the main objective of this article is to identify the metacognitive strategies employed by participants in a study group regarding the use of generative artificial intelligence in their daily lives and in their teaching practices. This is a qualitative, exploratory-descriptive study conducted with 12 participants at a private higher education institution in southern Brazil between February and June 2025. Data collection was carried out via a questionnaire with open-ended questions, administered following readings, theoretical discussions, and experiences with generative AI. Data analysis was conducted using the content analysis method (Bardin, 2016). The results reveal that collective practices enhanced the teachers’ metacognitive awareness. This process allowed for the problematization of naturalized discourses and the shared construction of meanings. It is concluded that metacognitive development is central to teachers adopting a critical stance toward generative AI, promoting a more ethical, situated, and transformative pedagogical practice.

analysis.methods: This study adopts a qualitative, exploratory-descriptive methodological approach. Qualitative research investigates subjects' practices and interactions in everyday life. According to Flick (2009) , qualitative research is necessary because most everyday phenomena are too complex to be explained in isolation. If empirical studies were designed exclusively around cause-and-effect relationships, he argues, all complex objects would need to be excluded. Qualitative research is therefore grounded in the idea of discovering the new and developing empirically based theories. As Flick (2009, p. 20) notes, "qualitative research is of particular relevance to the study of social relations due to the pluralization of life spheres, which calls for new sensitivity in empirical studies." 10 This means qualitative research engages with the deeper layer of relationships, processes, and phenomena that cannot be reduced to the operationalization of variables. Its essential features thus include the choice of methods and theories, the recognition and analysis of different perspectives, researchers' reflections as part of the knowledge production process, and a diversity of approaches and methods. This investigation has an exploratory-descriptive scope. Sampieri, Collado, and Lucio (2013) explain that exploratory studies aim to examine an underexplored research topic, unfamiliar phenomena, or existing themes from new perspectives. Their value lies in enabling more comprehensive research within a particular context. Similarly, Gil (2018) argues that descriptive research aims to survey a population's opinions, attitudes, and beliefs about a given phenomenon without analyzing the relationships between variables. Its main purpose is to accurately describe the phenomenon under investigation, rather than to understand why it manifests in a particular way. Having outlined the nature of the study, we now describe the participants, instruments, and procedures used for data collection and analysis. The study group comprised 20 members, of whom 12 voluntarily agreed to take part in the research. Of these participants, 10 identified as female and 2 as male, with ages ranging from 20 to 60 years. Their educational levels included 2 undergraduate students, 4 master's students, 3 doctoral students, and 3 individuals who already held a doctorate. Their fields of training and professional practice spanned Education, Psychology, and psychopedagogical clinical practice. Data were collected in July 2025, immediately after the semester of study concluded, using an online questionnaire comprising 5 open-ended questions addressing participants' perceptions of artificial intelligence, current teaching practice, and their views on the content produced by these tools. It is worth noting that, to ensure compliance with ethical research principles, the study was approved by the Institution's Research Ethics Committee for Studies Involving Human Subjects (CAAE No. 60949522.7.0000.0020). Furthermore, participants' identities were protected through anonymization, with each participant identified by a letter followed by a number (P01 for Participant 1, P02 for Participant 2, and so on). Data analysis was based on the content analysis method proposed by Laurence Bardin (2016) , understood as a set of techniques for grasping the meanings underlying discourse. This method comprises the stages of pre-analysis, material exploration, and the treatment and interpretation of results. During the pre-analysis stage, a preliminary reading of the empirical material was conducted, allowing for initial familiarization with the data, the formulation of hypotheses, and the identification of indicators relevant to the investigation. During the material exploration stage, the data were coded-that is, organized and systematized into smaller units of meaning to enable their classification, articulation, and interpretation (Bardin, 2016) . Rather than following a strictly inductive approach, coding was guided by categories defined a priori-awareness, self-regulation, and autopoiesis (Mayor, Suengas, and Marques, 1995) . Fragments of meaning extracted from participants' responses were thus analyzed in light of these categories and grouped according to their conceptual proximity to each. This coding process revealed the metacognitive strategies that participants mobilized during the investigation; to clarify this process, Table 1 presents representative excerpts organized by these categories. Regarding enumeration rules (Bardin, 2016) , the frequency of occurrence of recording units was adopted as the analytical criterion. This means that each time a participant expressed an idea aligned with one of the predefined categories (metacognitive strategies), one occurrence was counted. A higher incidence of elements related to the metacognitive strategy of awareness was observed (25 occurrences), followed by control (16 occurrences), and, less frequently, autopoiesis (6 occurrences). This finding points to a progressive movement in participants' metacognitive development, in which expanding awareness of AI use precedes and sustains processes of regulation and, subsequently, the reframing of pedagogical practices. Table 2 presents the frequency of recording units identified in participants' responses. Based on the distribution of occurrences by participant presented in Table 2 , the data were then organized by total frequency and percentage for each category, as shown in Table 3 . With the data organized in this way, it becomes possible to proceed to the interpretive analysis stage, seeking a deeper understanding of the meanings participants attributed to their practices and reflections throughout the study.
analysis.results: The analysis of participants' responses reveals the mobilization of metacognitive strategies across three a priori categories: awareness, control, and autopoiesis. This points to a progressive formative process within the group under study. The data indicate a predominance of the metacognitive strategy of awareness (53.2%), showing that participants significantly expanded their understanding of generative AI use and expressed perceptions and attitudes adopted when using it. Initially, most participants had already been using these tools in an exploratory way, driven by curiosity or a desire to streamline everyday tasks, often reflected in practices such as asking 'random questions' (P02; P11) or using the tool as an extension of search engines (P02; P10; P11). Similarly, P10 reports using AI out of 'curiosity' and to generate 'ideas for extra activities,' reinforcing the exploratory nature of this initial contact and a still largely unsystematic form of appropriation. These responses reinforce that, with the popularization of tools such as ChatGPT, there has been a significant increase in the everyday use of artificial intelligence, particularly as a resource for searching, organizing, and quickly producing information. As Santaella (2023) argues, these interactions continuously generate data linked to human activities-including experiences, relationships, and ways of thinking-highlighting how deeply integrated these technologies have become into contemporary social life. At the same time, a significant portion of participants already used AI in a more structured and intentional way, particularly in academic and professional contexts. Reported practices included identifying articles for research purposes (P03), teaching and research activities (P04), designing assessments and rewriting texts (P05), using AI as a professional resource for filtering information (P07), and supporting academic research (P08; P12). The case of P09, who works as a teacher and researcher in Europe, points to an already highly diversified prior use, suggesting a more advanced level of appropriation of these tools. In her words: […] these tools are employed for multiple purposes: the drafting and revision of academic texts […] support for qualitative data analysis, the design of research instruments, lesson preparation, and the production of accessible and inclusive teaching materials […] (P09). This positioning reveals not only technical familiarity, but also a broad understanding of AI's potential and limits within the educational context. This perspective aligns with Moura and Carvalho (2023) , who argue that artificial intelligence can serve as a tool for collaboration and innovation, supporting teachers' work and mediating learning. More broadly, Accoto (2020) notes that the emergence of generative AI ushers in a new configuration of humantechnology relations, in which not only are connections expanded, but cognitive functions themselves may be reconfigured, enabling more complex forms of creation, analysis, and problem-solving. The author nonetheless stresses the need to maintain a critical stance toward these technologies, particularly regarding their ethical and epistemological implications. Perceptions of risk associated with AI use also emerged, as noted by P03, who mentions "uncertainty about research sources," and by P04, who acknowledges "how much algorithms can do with our data." These statements show that participants moved beyond simply using these technologies to also questioning their broader implications. Taken together, these findings indicate that participants mobilized the metacognitive strategy of awareness to recognize their individual characteristics, the specific demands of tasks, and the conditions under which they used AIthereby guiding more appropriate choices. As Mayor, Suengas, and Marques (1995) emphasize, awareness of situations and contexts constitutes the initial, foundational stage of the metacognitive process, since it allows subjects to intentionally access their goals, the strategies they will use to achieve them, and their characteristics as learners and, in this case, as users of generative AI tools. The metacognitive strategy of control (34%) reflects the adoption of more intentional strategies for using AI tools, such as filtering AI-generated information, validating content, using tools more ethically and carefully, and formulating prompts with greater precision. These elements point to the activation of cognitive control mechanisms, through which subjects deliberately plan, monitor, and adjust their actions-reflecting a more elaborate level of metacognitive functioning. Empirical evidence supports this process. abstract_text: The call for papers for the 2025 PESA conference referenced our ‘increasingly pluralistic, post-truth, post-reality and divided world’ and the ‘existential problems’ that we face—noting climate change, AI, populism and the decline in ethical and reasoned discourse. The assumption contained in the call was that equipping young people with the ability to engage in reasoned deliberation is more pressing than ever before. And certainly, educating for critical thinking—thoughtfulness, coherence, rationality—is often held up as a silver bullet to heal our seemingly ailing and divided world. Perhaps rightly so. But here, I apply some critical thinking to the claim. Drawing on many years of involvement in teaching philosophy and ethics at the tertiary level, I reflect on what teaching critical thinking skills can, and cannot, achieve. I question the pervasive ‘crisis’ framing in education, suggesting that constant existential rhetoric can leave students anxious and less resilient and I argue for some guiding principles: teach students how to think, not what to think; and guard against ideological narrowing, ensuring critical thinking is genuinely open to diverse perspectives, including those that make us uncomfortable. Rather than a cure-all, critical thinking should be taught as a discipline grounded in humility, charity, and the courage to engage with difference. Its power lies not in solving every societal problem, but in equipping students to reason together in good faith—even when the stakes are existential.

abstract_text: Purpose This study aims to examine how customers perceive and engage with generative artificial intelligence (GenAI)-enabled services provided by small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), with a particular focus on value co-creation and well-being outcomes. While prior studies have mainly investigated GenAI adoption from the firm perspective, this research shifts attention to customer-level psychological and experiential mechanisms in an emerging economy context. Design/methodology/approach Drawing on service-dominant logic and Sustainable Development Goal 3, the study adopts a quantitative approach. Data were collected from 180 Vietnamese consumers, predominantly educated youths aged 18–24, who had prior experience with GenAI-powered services offered by SMEs. Partial least squares structural equation modeling was used to test the proposed hypotheses. Findings The results indicate that perceived knowledge about GenAI and perceived marketplace influence are positively associated with customers’ value co-creation behavior. Value co-creation is positively associated with both value-in-use and emotional well-being. In addition, value-in-use is positively associated with perceptions of social well-being, whereas emotional well-being is not significantly associated with social well-being. Originality/value This study extends GenAI research by moving beyond firm-level adoption to examine customer-centric outcomes in SME service contexts in an emerging economy. It highlights perceived knowledge and marketplace influence as critical antecedents of value co-creation and demonstrates how AI-enabled services contribute to social value primarily through functional value-in-use rather than emotional pathways.

It may also reflect a theoretical misalignment, as affective responses often occur at an individual level, whereas social well-being reflects evaluative, relational and ethical considerations. This study makes several important contributions to the literature on GenAI, value co- creation and social impact within the context of SMEs. First, this study advances the social impact literature by providing empirical evidence on how customers experience and derive value from GenAI-enabled services. It establishes that social impact in AI-mediated SME contexts is not solely a technological outcome, but a human-centered process shaped by customer perceptions, engagement and co-creation behaviors (Baabdullah, 2024; Dwivedi et al., 2023). The findings show that GenAI can serve as a social enabler when customers perceive transparency, control and personalization, reinforcing the idea that responsible AI deployment in SMEs can enhance community trust and shared well-being. title: Born into the Algorithm: Global Law, Cognitive Autonomy, and Children’s Rights in the Age of Artificial Intelligence
preview: Children born today enter a world in which artificial intelligence systems collect, categorize, and predict from the moment of birth, often before any digital engagement and well before the capacity to consent. Existing legal frameworks address children primarily as platform users defined by an age threshold or as natural persons without operational protection during incapacity, and none adequately addresses the new…
abstract_text: Children born today enter a world in which artificial intelligence systems collect, categorize, and predict from the moment of birth, often before any digital engagement and well before the capacity to consent. Existing legal frameworks address children primarily as platform users defined by an age threshold or as natural persons without operational protection during incapacity, and none adequately addresses the newborn as a rights-bearing subject of algorithmic systems from the moment of birth. This paper proposes sovereignty-in-trust as the doctrinal frame within which children’s rights attach at birth and are held in trust during the period before consent capacity, with cognitive autonomy as the substantive content of what is held. The framework is derived from a literature review of the established provisions of the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child, read with the Committee’s General Comments, supported by data-protection and AI-governance instruments in the European Union, and refined through the supported-decision-making framework of the Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities. The paper highlights four key failure modes in current frameworks: regulatory overload, commercial monetization, dependence on political will, and the limitations of current doctrinal structures. It outlines five legal measures to enhance resilience: mandatory disclosure during neonatal data collection, a bankruptcy-proof restriction on transferring data from minors, automatic deletion or anonymization of identity data not explicitly retained, a safeguard against predictive profiling without prior consent, and ongoing ethical reform and liability across the AI product lifecycle. The paper advocates that the United Nations Committee on the Rights of the Child issue a new General Comment specifically addressing children’s rights in algorithmic systems, with dedicated provisions for the period before children have the capacity to give consent. The doctrinal objective is not to establish a new right but to articulate the operational form of existing rights as they apply to a subject who is currently unable to exercise them at the moment they attach.

analysis.methods: The study used a cross-sectional survey design. Convenience sampling was used to administer paper-and-pencil questionnaires to undergraduate students at universities in mainland China during the 2024–2025 academic year. After data screening for completeness and inattentive responding, 421 valid questionnaires were retained for analysis. Of these participants, 128 (30.4%) identified as male and 293 (69.6%) as female. The sample comprised 116 first-year (27.6%), 101 second-year (24.0%), 164 third-year (39.0%) and 40 fourth-year (9.5%) students, drawn from a range of disciplines.
