analysis.discussion: This study set out to test a moderated mediation model linking generative artificial intelligence use to university students’ self-reported critical thinking, with GenAI feedback literacy as the mechanism and reflective thinking as a boundary condition. Three findings stand out. First, GenAI use was positively related to critical thinking, both directly when modelled alone and through GenAI feedback literacy when both were entered together. Second, the inclusion of feedback literacy reduced the direct effect to non-significance and accounted for nearly three-quarters of the total effect, a pattern consistent with feedback literacy as a principal mechanism. Third, the model was conditional on reflective thinking: at low reflective thinking the link was direct and the indirect path was not significant, whereas at high reflective thinking the indirect path through feedback literacy strengthened and the direct path disappeared. Read together, these results are consistent with a dual-route interpretation of the inconsistent existing evidence on GenAI and critical thinking, in which the structure of the association is sensitive to learner disposition. Each finding warrants discussion. Before turning to each finding, one interpretive boundary should be made explicit. Critical thinking was measured with the critical analytical skills sub-scale of the Chinese Critical Thinking Scale, on which students rate their own habitual analytical behaviour. The outcome therefore represents self-reported critical analytical skills, not critical-thinking performance demonstrated on a task, a test or an expert-rated piece of work. Self-reports of this kind capture students’ perceptions of how they approach problems rather than the observed quality of their reasoning, and they share a method with the self-reported predictors. Accordingly, where we write that GenAI use, feedback literacy or reflective thinking “predicts” critical thinking, the claim is that these variables are associated with higher self-rated analytical skill in a cross-sectional model, not that they produce better critical-thinking performance. This boundary applies to every finding discussed below. Generative AI is rapidly becoming part of the cognitive infrastructure of higher education, and a settled empirical answer to whether its use is associated with stronger or weaker critical thinking has remained elusive. The present study reframes the question. In a cross-sectional sample of Chinese undergraduates, GenAI use was positively associated with self-reported critical analytical skills, but the association was largely indirect: it was carried by students’ capacity to interpret, judge and act on AI-generated feedback, and its structure depended on students’ reflective stance. At low reflective thinking the association was direct and modest; at high reflective thinking it ran through feedback literacy, yielding a stronger indirect association. If these associations reflect the hypothesised causal ordering, a question that longitudinal and experimental designs must settle, the cognitive dividend of GenAI is unlikely to come from access alone, and universities that pair AI integration with explicit feedback-literacy training and reflective pedagogical practises may be better placed to convert ubiquitous AI use into the analytical capacity that higher education is meant to cultivate. The moderated mediation model presented here offers a tractable framework for the next wave of empirical work on GenAI and higher-order cognition.
analysis.limitations: Several limitations bound the study’s claims. First, the cross-sectional design precludes causal inference. All variables were measured concurrently, so the mediation and moderated-mediation estimates describe patterns of association that are consistent with the hypothesised ordering but cannot establish it; reverse or reciprocal orderings (for example, students with stronger analytical skills making heavier or more sophisticated use of GenAI, or feedback literacy shaping use rather than the reverse) are equally compatible with the data. Although PLS-SEM with bootstrapped indirect effects and theoretically motivated path direction is well suited to estimating complex models, the findings should be replicated using longitudinal panel data or randomised intervention designs that track how GenAI use, feedback literacy and reflective thinking co-evolve over time. Second, the sample is drawn from Chinese universities and is skewed female (69.6%); cross-cultural and gender-balanced replications are needed to assess generalisability across educational systems with different assessment cultures and AI-policy environments. Third, all measures are self-reported, and the outcome in particular represents self-reported critical analytical skills rather than demonstrated critical-thinking performance. Although the study’s common-method-bias diagnostics did not flag a serious problem, behavioural and performance-based measures of critical thinking and feedback engagement (e.g., analyses of think-aloud protocols, log data from AI interactions, expert ratings of student work) would strengthen inference ( Fan et al., 2025 ). Fourth, critical thinking was operationalised through the analytical-skills sub-scale of a Chinese instrument; future studies could examine the model with broader operationalisations covering inference, evaluation, explanation and self-regulation ( Facione, 2011 ) and across disciplines, since GenAI’s affordances and risks may differ between, say, the humanities and STEM. Relatedly, the dual-route interpretation in this study rests on the pattern of moderation, not on direct observation of cognitive processing; the study did not measure whether students engaged with GenAI outputs shallowly or deeply, and process-tracing methods such as interaction logs, think-aloud protocols or eye-tracking are needed to test the proposed routes directly. Fifth, the incremental fit indices of the item-level measurement model fell below conventional thresholds, as is common with long instruments such as the 39-item GenAI-SFLS ( Kenny and McCoach, 2003 ; Shi et al., 2019 ); future work could refine the GenAI-SFLS for shorter administration without losing dimensional coverage. Finally, GenAI tools are evolving rapidly, and the empirical model captures a snapshot of usage patterns at a given moment; tracking the moderated mediation structure across model generations and modalities (text, voice, multimodal agents) is an important agenda for the field.

title: From digital companionship to capability building: reframing conversational artificial intelligence and older adults' psychological wellbeing in active aging
preview: The rapid diffusion of conversational artificial intelligence (AI) has reshaped the landscape of digital interaction in later life, with growing attention to its implications for older adults' mental health and wellbeing. abstract_text: The rapid diffusion of conversational artificial intelligence (AI) has reshaped the landscape of digital interaction in later life, with growing attention to its implications for older adults' mental health and wellbeing. Existing research has predominantly interpreted conversational AI through the lens of digital companionship, emphasizing its capacity to simulate social presence, reduce loneliness, and provide emotional support. While this perspective captures important affective outcomes, it offers a limited account of the developmental processes through which AI engagement may influence psychological wellbeing in aging populations. This conceptual analysis proposes a shift from a companionship-oriented paradigm to a capability-building perspective grounded in the Capability Approach. It argues that the primary value of conversational AI lies not in its ability to substitute social interaction, but in its potential to expand older adults' cognitive, emotional, social, and digital capabilities. Building on this argument, this paper develops an AI-Augmented Active Aging Framework that explains how conversational AI affordances, responsiveness, personalization, accessibility, and availability, interact with personal, social, environmental, and system-level conversion factors. Under supportive conditions, these affordances may facilitate cognitive, emotional, social, and digital capability formation, thereby supporting autonomy, competence, social integration, and active aging. Under adverse conditions, however, conversational AI may contribute to capability erosion through over-reliance, cognitive offloading, reduced human contact, or diminished autonomous judgment. The framework therefore emphasizes heterogeneous and conditional outcomes rather than assuming uniform benefits across older adults.

title: Structure-Aware Rendering: How Code Reveal Shapes Programmers' Visual Attention

abstract_text: AI coding interfaces present generated code either all at once or token-by-token. These rendering strategies reflect model generation rather than how programmers actually read code: selectively, non-linearly, and guided by the structure. We argue that code rendering is a first-class interaction primitive that shapes how programmers read and understand code. To explore this design space, we introduce structured rendering, a technique that reveals code in semantically meaningful chunks derived from its syntactic hierarchy, exposing high-level structure before low-level details. To isolate rendering effects on visual attention, we conducted an eye-tracking study with 53 participants comparing static, character-based, and structured rendering. Our findings show that rendering alters visual attention and reading behavior: dynamic rendering induces fewer but longer fixations and more sustained focus, while structured rendering further guides attention toward semantically meaningful units and supports high-level understanding. We release the anonymized dataset with an interactive demo (https://codegaze.vercel.app/) to support future research.

abstract_text: Purpose of Review: To synthesize recent literature on the relationships between generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) use and adolescents' mental health, with particular attention to problematic use and psychiatric vulnerabilities. Recent Findings: Emerging evidence suggests associations between GenAI use and a range of adolescent mental health outcomes, including depression, anxiety, psychosis-related experiences, externalizing behaviors, eating disorder risk, and suicidality. Problematic patterns of use, including dependency and emotional reliance, may be particularly relevant among adolescents with preexisting psychiatric vulnerabilities. Current evidence suggests that these relationships may be bidirectional: psychological distress can motivate GenAI use for companionship, emotional support, or escape, while problematic use may reinforce maladaptive beliefs, displace real-world relationships, and amplify existing vulnerabilities. However, evidence remains predominantly cross-sectional, limiting causal inference. Summary: GenAI may interact with and amplify underlying psychiatric vulnerabilities during adolescence, highlighting the importance of understanding patterns and motivations of use. Pediatricians and other clinicians caring for adolescents could consider not only the frequency of GenAI use but also motivations for use, problematic dependency, and socioemotional reliance. Identifying high-risk usage patterns of GenAI through longitudinal research, particularly among youth with preexisting psychiatric risks, may inform the development of tailored screening, intervention, and prevention strategies.

Adolescents with or at risk for a variety of mental health concerns may be particularly vulnerable to adverse outcomes associated with GenAI use and dependency, which could, in turn, exacerbate existing symptoms and underlying susceptibilities. Figure 1 presents an integrated conceptual framework for understanding the relationship between GenAI use and various forms of adolescent psychopathology. These emerging patterns have implications for pediatric practice because pediatricians and other clinicians caring for adolescents are well positioned to ask about GenAI use in the context of routine psychosocial and digital media assessment. To this end, clinicians could consider incorporating a brief GenAI dependency assessment (see Table 1 as an example) designed to evaluate general dependency across diverse contexts and platforms [78] . abstract_text: The importance of critical thinking when using generative AI in personal, professional, and educational contexts is widely acknowledged by scholars, educators, and politicians. There are contradictory hypotheses regarding the influence of AI on critical thinking, and research thus far has produced mixed results. In this paper, we present a critical scoping review of 80 research papers from Human-Computer Interaction (HCI) that study critical thinking with or about AI, focusing on how “critical thinking” is defined, measured, and how the papers claim critical thinking to be influenced by AI, according to current HCI research. Our findings demonstrate that critical thinking is rarely defined in HCI research about AI, and there are fundamental construct and criterion validity challenges in this line of research. We present a research agenda for more theory-grounded empirical research in critical thinking with or about AI, based on cognitive-psychological, philosophical, or educational research traditions.

analysis.discussion: The goal of this section is to lay out potential paths forward. We first describe the general challenges that pervade the study of critical thinking with or about AI in HCI research. We then outline some potential approaches to meet these challenges, both by looking at exemplars from the corpus, and then by revisiting the three theoretical traditions and what these might be able to offer in terms of designs of future studies. In this paper, we presented a scoping review of 80 research papers that empirically studied critical thinking in the context of using AI, a new but increasingly popular topic in HCI, and found that the included studies were highly heterogeneous in terms of their definitions of critical thinking and their studies of it. The studies are conducted especially in the USA, with students as participants, and using LLMs as the AI technology. Most of the studies evaluate a system designed to influence critical thinking, and most are based on short-term interventions and attitudinal rather than behavioral assessment. Several observations about the corpus indicate construct validity challenges, such as a lack of clear and/or shared definitions of critical thinking and how this is assessed, especially in the question of perceived versus demonstrated critical thinking. A majority of the studies in the corpus rely on selfassessment as a measure of critical thinking; in fact, self-assessment measurements account for half (25 of the total 50) of the submissions that claim that AI has a primarily positive influence on people's critical thinking ability. Of the studies that base their assessment on a demonstrated effect of AI on critical thinking specifically, only 10 submissions provide explicit and reproducible criteria for how their assessment is made. We also identified potential criterion/content validity challenges, and a notable absence of in vivostudies or studies which focus on professionals rather than students. This means that it is difficult to know whether the studies actually predict or explain the type and scope of critical thinking we may be interested in assessing. Finally, we suggested some ways forward for HCI research that attempts to evaluate the influence of AI on critical thinking, based on the three theoretical foundations of cognitive psychology, philosophy, and education. We suggest that future studies of critical thinking in the context of using AI could make even clearer contributions by making explicit, at least, what their definition of critical thinking is, how they evaluate the influence, and finally, why their chosen method can reasonably be believed to measure what it is intended to measure.
analysis.limitations: A main limitation of this review is the possibility of misrepresenting the actual body of research about "critical thinking and related concepts." Searching with keywords is inherently reductionist, and our search is likely to have missed some existing work. Because we limited our search to the specific term "critical thinking" (as opposed to related terms such as "decision-making," "critical evaluation," or "reflective thinking"), we may have excluded work using a different terminology. However, as described in the methodology, this scoping review is about critical thinking-other definitions would be a matter for different (systematic rather than scoping) reviews. A second limitation is our focus on the HCI domain and our venue-based definition of this domain. Our search was confined to the ACM Digital Library, the International Journal of Human-Computer Interaction, and International Journal of Human-Computer Studies as representative for HCI work. Outside these databases, there is likely HCI-work to be found. Most importantly, we have not reviewed work from psychology or education, which could topically be characterized as at least HCI-adjacent research. However, our intention with this review was to bring attention to the gaps of work conducted in the domain of HCI. We believe that because this field draws upon many psychological and educational traditions, it is important to articulate more clearly which foundations are drawn upon in individual work. A third limitation is that we did not perform any quality assessment of the articles included in the corpus. When we report "claimed influence," it should not be interpreted as evidence for proven influence. A fourth limitation is that extraction of data was performed primarily by the first author. This may have biased the judgment in cases where decisions had to be made between assigning one category or another. We deem the influence of this acceptable, considering our focus was on relatively objective categorizations and not qualitative analysis. Finally, the rapidly evolving research area makes it likely that the corpus will become outdated or misrepresentative relatively fast. We do believe our scoping review merits further systematic review of work in this area. Especially the heterogeneity of the studies in terms of use of the term "critical thinking," their divergent focus on critical thinking with/about AI, and their varying levels of detail about data used as basis for the conclusions warrant this.

Researchers and commentators frequently label this experience “attention fragmentation” (AF), yet the term is used loosely in the literature and has not been formally distinguished from adjacent constructs such as distraction, multitasking, attention span, task-s…
abstract_text: The proliferation of notification-driven, multi-device digital environments has produced widespread everyday experiences of scattered, discontinuous focus. Researchers and commentators frequently label this experience “attention fragmentation” (AF), yet the term is used loosely in the literature and has not been formally distinguished from adjacent constructs such as distraction, multitasking, attention span, task-switching, mind-wandering, and smartphone addiction/compulsive use. No dedicated, psychometrically validated scale for AF currently exists; where researchers have needed to quantify AF, they have relied on proxy measures built for other purposes — most recently a reverse-scored trait-mindfulness scale (Bayaskar &amp; Sharma, 2026). This manuscript (a) proposes a formal operational definition of AF grounded in the interruption and attentional-control literatures, (b) systematically differentiates AF from six related constructs and the instruments used to measure them, (c) documents a genuine, current, and specific measurement gap, (d) proposes a tentative five-dimensional structure to guide item generation, and (e) outlines a three-phase empirical program: item development, exploratory factor analysis, and confirmatory factor analysis with convergent, discriminant, and incremental validity testing for developing and validating an Attention Fragmentation Scale (AFS). This manuscript reports no new empirical data; it establishes the conceptual and methodological foundation for the validation studies that follow.

abstract_text: With the rapid development of generative artificial intelligence, AI feedback in EFL writing instruction has gained increasing attention. Grounded in social cognitive theory and self-regulated learning theory, this mixed-methods study compared AI-mediated and teacher-mediated feedback delivery modes and examined their relationships with writing performance, learning motivation, and self-regulated learning among 120 s-year English majors at Henan Normal University. A 16-week quasi-experimental pretest-posttest-delayed test design was combined with semi-structured interviews. Repeated measures ANOVA and mediation analysis (PROCESS macro) were used for quantitative analysis; thematic analysis was applied qualitatively. abstract_text: This study explored the lived experiences of high school students using ChatGPT in mathematics learning through a student engagement framework and the interpretive lens of Self-Determination Theory (SDT). Using a descriptive phenomenological design, data were gathered from 58 students through eight focus group discussions and analyzed using Colaizzi's method. The findings revealed that participants described ChatGPT as shaping their engagement in multiple ways. Students valued its accessibility, immediate feedback, and step-by-step explanations, which they described as supporting their participation, conceptual understanding, and confidence in learning mathematics. Emotional engagement was reflected in students' experiences of psychological safety and perceived support, while cognitive engagement was reflected in participants' perceptions that ChatGPT supported their understanding and critical evaluation of AI-generated responses. However, participants also reported disengaging experiences, including overreliance on ChatGPT, reduced interaction with teachers and peers, challenges in using mathematical symbols, and concerns regarding inaccurate responses. These findings suggest that participants perceived ChatGPT as creating both opportunities and constraints for meaningful mathematics learning. Interpreted through SDT, participants' accounts reflected experiences that may be interpreted as supporting or frustrating psychological needs related to autonomy, competence, and relatedness. This study contributes to the growing literature on AI-assisted learning by integrating student engagement and SDT to provide a nuanced understanding of students' experiences. The findings underscore the importance of guided AI use, critical evaluation, teacher support, and collaborative learning to promote meaningful and sustainable engagement in mathematics.

abstract_text: Effective collaboration and communication are vital to developer productivity and well-being, yet remain constrained by human factors such as attention, intrinsic motivation, and interpersonal accountability. These constraints are particularly vital for developers identifying with Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD), who navigate persistent environmental barriers in modern hybrid workplace settings. While developers with ADHD frequently rely on collaborative copresence practices (such as body doubling or pair programming) to support executive function, the recent emergence of agentic AI coding assistants has begun reshaping these collaborative dynamics. To investigate how developers with ADHD engage in human and AI-based copresence practices, we conducted semi-structured interviews with 14 software engineers with ADHD. Our findings reveal that while traditional human-human copresence provides critical social support and onboarding structure, it forces developers to constantly manage professional reputation and sacrifice personal privacy. Conversely, developers leverage emerging human-AI copresence to maintain accountability and cognitive flow without the social anxiety, performance judgment, or surveillance associated with human observation. Based on these empirical insights, we map developer copresence practices onto core dimensions of Goffman's copresence theory and Forsgren et al.'s SPACE framework of developer productivity, and provide design recommendations for AI-based tools that promote inclusive collaboration for developers with ADHD.

abstract_text:
Abstract 
                 Drawing on cognitive offloading theory and levels-of-processing theory, this study examined how conversational artificial intelligence (AI) learning support is related to university students’ critical thinking. Survey data from 426 students were analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling and fuzzy-set qualitative comparative analysis. The results revealed two contrasting pathways. Conversational AI learning support was positively associated with both scaffolded cognitive offloading and substitutive cognitive offloading. Scaffolded cognitive offloading was positively associated with post-response deep processing, whereas substitutive cognitive offloading was negatively associated with it. Post-response deep processing was further positively associated with critical thinking. The moderating effect of AI evaluation literacy was not significant. The configurational results provided supplementary evidence that high critical thinking was more likely to occur when scaffolded cognitive offloading was present and substitutive cognitive offloading was low. These findings suggest that conversational AI may be more closely associated with critical thinking when learners continue to verify, question, reflect on, and revise AI-generated responses rather than simply accept them.

The PLS-SEM results showed opposite scaffolding and substitution pathways, and the fsQCA results provided supplementary evidence that high critical thinking was more likely when scaffolded offloading was present and substitutive offloading was low. The findings should be interpreted cautiously because CT explained variance was modest and AEL moderation was nonsignificant. Overall, the findings suggest that conversational AI may have greater educational value when learners are encouraged to verify, question, compare, reflect on, and revise AI-generated responses rather than simply accept them.
reading.limitations: Several limitations should be acknowledged. First, the sample was mainly drawn from one university, so future studies should test the model across educational stages, disciplines, and institutions. Second, the cross-sectional self-report design limits causal interpretation; experimental designs, behavioral indicators, or longitudinal tracking would support stronger causal interpretations. Third, future work could compare text-based and multimodal tools and examine how interaction turns, feedback types, and prompt strategies shape cognitive offloading and critical thinking (Hutler et al., 2025) . Finally, the measurement of AI evaluation literacy, especially AEL1, should be refined.

title: Freirean Pedagogy for Equitable Assessment, Decolonial Governance, and Cognitive Wellbeing in the Age of Artificial Intelligence: A Systematic Review
preview: The rapid integration of generative artificial intelligence into higher education has outpaced the development of pedagogical frameworks and institutional policies, raising fundamental questions about the purposes of education in an algorithmic age. abstract_text: The rapid integration of generative artificial intelligence into higher education has outpaced the development of pedagogical frameworks and institutional policies, raising fundamental questions about the purposes of education in an algorithmic age. Paulo Freire’s critical pedagogy offers a powerful lens for interrogating the epistemological, ethical, and political dimensions of AI-mediated education, yet its application remains fragmented across disciplinary boundaries. This systematic review followed the PRISMA 2020 guidelines and employed a systematic literature search across the Scopus database, supplemented by backward and forward citation tracking. The search strategy combined terms related to Freirean pedagogy and liberating education with terms related to artificial intelligence, yielding a final corpus of 15 peer-reviewed open access journal articles published between 2021 and 2026, within the 2020–2026 eligibility window. Data extraction and thematic synthesis were conducted using the PEO framework, and risk of bias was assessed using appropriate tools. The synthesis identified four thematic clusters: epistemological foundations for critiquing algorithmic neutrality; redesign of assessment and governance practices; intersectional and decolonial dimensions of algorithmic harm; and psychological consequences of cognitive offloading. Key findings reveal that uncritical AI integration reproduces the banking model of education, systematically marginalizes nondominant epistemologies, and risks eroding critical thinking through cognitive debt. A critical framework organized around recognition, voice, and power, operationalized through credibility, comprehensibility, and control, is proposed. Freirean pedagogy retains transformative relevance when translated into design principles, governance mechanisms, and evaluative criteria that challenge algorithmic reductionism and center epistemic justice, relational agency, and collective liberation. The framework offers actionable guidance for equitable assessment redesign, participatory governance, and psychologically sustaining pedagogies in AI-mediated higher education.

A fourth significant finding addresses the psychological and cognitive consequences of uncritical AI integration, revealing that the primary risk is not academic dishonesty but the cumulative erosion of critical thinking, ethical reasoning, and professional judgment through chronic cognitive offloading. Watts (2025) develops the concept of "cognitive debt," drawing on cognitive load theory and neuroscientific evidence to demonstrate that uncritical AI use results in skill decay and diminished capacity for independent judgment. Crimmins et al. (2026) empirically substantiate these concerns, finding that faculty resistance to AI reflects a form of "pedagogical care," a principled commitment to preserving the epistemic struggle through which genuine understanding is forged, and that faculty frame academic integrity as the preservation of judgment and meaning-making rather than rule compliance. Alqarni (2025) contributes a psychometric instrument, the Artificial Intelligence-Critical Pedagogy Scale, validated with 800 teachers, which identifies four dimensions of critical pedagogical competence and provides a measurable pathway for professional development. The synthesis thus establishes that the primary ethical imperative is the deliberate design of learning experiences that sustain cognitive engagement, metacognitive reflection, and durable mental models. Finally, the synthesis converges on a reconceptualization of learner agency as fundamentally relational, contextually situated, and organized around recognition, voice, and power, which collectively constitute the conditions for genuine participation and collective liberation. Omodan & Ngubane (2026) articulate this most systematically, insisting that agency depends on being treated as a credible knower (recognition), having channels to shape meaning and criteria (voice), and holding decision rights over data and learning pathways (power). Young et al. ( 2021 ) complement this through their emancipatory organizing processes, emphasizing role freedom, mutual learning, and the identification of alternative futures as prerequisites for synergistic human-machine partnerships. Karatsiori et al. (2026) extend this vision to the planetary scale, urging institutions to move beyond neoliberal metrics and embrace a values-based pedagogy grounded in care, shared responsibility, and epistemic humility. The synthesis thus arrives at its definitive conclusion: the future of liberating education in the algorithmic age depends not on technological sophistication but on the sustained, collective cultivation of critical consciousness that alone can subvert algorithmic domination and reclaim education as a practice of freedom. analysis.discussion: This systematic literature review has demonstrated that Paulo Freire's philosophy of liberating education retains its critical and transformative relevance in the age of artificial intelligence, provided that it is operationalized through concrete design principles, governance mechanisms, and evaluative criteria that challenge algorithmic reductionism and centre the dignity, agency, and epistemic authority of learners. The synthesis reveals that uncritical AI integration reproduces the "banking model" of education, positioning learners as passive consumers of machine-generated outputs rather than active co-constructors of meaning, while simultaneously amplifying existing inequalities along axes of language, gender, caste, and geography. However, the reviewed literature also demonstrates that these risks are not inevitable; they are products of specific design choices and governance failures that can be contested and reconfigured through deliberate, justice-oriented intervention. The study proposes a critical framework organized around three interlocking principles, recognition, voice, and power, operationalized through the CCC checkpoints of credibility, comprehensibility, and control, which translate epistemic justice theory into actionable design and governance for AI-mediated education. The practical implications are clear: institutions must move beyond reactive surveillance toward systemic frameworks that prioritize infrastructure-based equity, transparent collaboration, and institutional scaffolding, while investing in faculty development that cultivates critical AI literacy and dialogical pedagogy. Ultimately, the future of liberating education in the algorithmic age depends not on the sophistication of predictive models but on the sustained, collective commitment to cultivating critical consciousness, redistributing epistemic authority, and reclaiming education as a practice of freedom, a commitment that must guide the redesign of curricula, assessments, pedagogies, and institutional structures in the years ahead. analysis.limitations: The present synthesis, while offering a comprehensive critical framework for understanding AI-mediated education through the lens of Freirean critical pedagogy, is subject to several important limitations that must be acknowledged to appropriately contextualize its contributions and guide its application. First, the framework developed in this synthesis remains conceptually robust yet empirically unvalidated. As Espartinez (2026) explicitly acknowledges in his systemic framework, the model constitutes a "theoretically grounded hypothesis rather than an empirically established model," pending validation through prospective implementation studies. Similarly, Watts (2025) frames his cognitive debt model as a conceptual proposition that requires quasi-experimental evaluation to establish its efficacy in diverse educational settings. This conceptual nature implies that the practical feasibility, scalability, and transformative potential of the proposed framework have not been tested through longitudinal, mixed-methods implementation research across varied institutional contexts. Second, the geographical concentration of the reviewed empirical studies introduces significant contextual limitations. The synthesis draws predominantly on research conducted in Australia, India, Indonesia, the Philippines, the United States, and the United Kingdom, with limited representation from Sub-Saharan Africa, Latin America, and other regions of the Global South where infrastructural conditions, colonial histories, linguistic diversity, and educational governance structures differ substantially (Espartinez, 2026; Joseph & Areepattamannil, 2025; Syamsiah & Aisyah, 2025) . Begum et al. (2025) demonstrates how algorithmic biases manifest distinctly in postcolonial, multilingual contexts, suggesting that findings from one national setting may not transfer directly to others without careful contextual adaptation. Third, the rapid and ongoing evolution of generative AI technologies imposes temporal limitations on the synthesis, as the specific tools, policy frameworks, and institutional practices analyzed in the reviewed literature may become outdated within short timeframes, necessitating continuous updating and periodic reassessment of the framework's relevance (Joseph & Areepattamannil, 2025; Laidlaw, 2026) . Fourth, the synthesis privileges institutional and academic perspectives, with limited direct incorporation of student voices, particularly those from the most marginalized communities who are most affected by algorithmic governance and epistemic exclusion. As Laidlaw (2026) explicitly acknowledges, future work must centre student voices and engage with non-Western epistemologies to enrich theoretical understanding and global applicability, a gap that constrains the framework's capacity to fully represent the lived experiences, resistance strategies, and agency of learners themselves. Fifth, the reliance on English-language publications, while methodologically necessary, introduces a linguistic bias that may exclude regionally specific scholarship published in other languages, thereby potentially underrepresenting Indigenous epistemologies, local pedagogical innovations, and grassroots resistance movements that are not mediated through global academic publishing circuits (Begum et al., 2025; Karatsiori et al., 2026) . These limitations do not invalidate the synthesis but rather underscore the provisional, situated, and contestable nature of its claims, demanding that readers exercise critical reflexivity in adapting its insights to their specific institutional, cultural, and political contexts.

abstract_text: AI coding assistants are rapidly transforming software development, but are known to produce insecure code. Prior work has measured whether AI-assisted developers produce secure code, but less is known about how they evaluate AI-generated code: whether they can identify vulnerabilities, what cues they use, and how trust shapes their decisions. This evaluation step is foundational to secure development with AI, whether using auto-complete, chat tools, or AI agents. As a first step, we conducted a remote observational study with 100 participants isolating this evaluation stage. Participants were tasked with producing secure and functional code for four C linked-list tasks. For each, participants were able to cycle through five AI-generated suggestions varying in security and functionality, select one, and edit their choice into a final submission. Participants also completed a post-study survey about their decision-making and perception of AI-generated code's security and 23 completed a more in-depth interview.

preview: This integrative literature review examines how generative artificial intelligence is shaping human thinking, cognitive processes and writing practices, with a focus on education across schools, universities, adult learning and professional settings. abstract_text: This integrative literature review examines how generative artificial intelligence is shaping human thinking, cognitive processes and writing practices, with a focus on education across schools, universities, adult learning and professional settings. It considers how AI-supported composing alters the ways writers plan, generate, organise, revise and evaluate text, and how these changes reshape cognition, agency, authorship and learning. Rather than treating generative AI simply as a tool for productivity, the review approaches it as a relational technology that mediates meaning-making and textual production, while reserving the language of intentional agency for human actors. Thirty-six publications, identified through a structured search of seven information sources reported in accordance with PRISMA 2020 and appraised using criteria matched to each form of evidence, were synthesised thematically. Albert Bandura’s social cognitive theory provides the analytical lens, particularly triadic reciprocal causation, self-efficacy, observational learning, self-regulation and human agency. The discussion develops a critical account that recognises clear benefits while flagging risks of cognitive offloading, uncritical trust, homogenised expression and weakened metacognitive control. Claims are calibrated to the type of evidence supporting them, and findings drawn from preprints, small samples and self-report designs are presented as preliminary. The review advances a hybrid account in which human and machine contributions to composing are entwined and argues that this entwinement makes deliberate human participation more rather than less necessary. It concludes by proposing guidelines for educators across sectors, together with the assessment conditions under which those guidelines can be verified.

editorial_notes.argument: Media quality cannot be reduced to screen-time totals or educational subject matter. Kucirkova argues that the rhythm of children's media shapes opportunities to reflect, understand a story and connect emotionally: constantly shifting cues may capture attention while leaving too little space to process.
editorial_notes.design_relevance: The relevant design question for focus interventions is not simply how long someone looks at a screen, but whether the interface permits uninterrupted interpretation, deliberate pauses, repetition and self-directed attention. This application to AI tools is a design implication, not a measured AI outcome.

abstract_text: The article examines the shift in the digital cultural ecosystem triggered by the widespread adoption of Generative AI. Historically, the platformization of cultural industries established an attention economy, where recommendation algorithms were essential for guiding users through overwhelming content catalogs. However, the recent influx of synthetic media has disrupted the dynamic, creating a synthetic tsunami that threatens cultural diversity, undermines user trust, and jeopardizes the livelihoods of human creators. Furthermore, this unchecked proliferation risks model degeneration for the AI systems themselves. To mitigate these economic and social tensions, Digital Service Providers are evolving their algorithmic policies. We analyze how platforms handle AI detection tools, transparent labeling, and adjusted recommendation guidelines to filter and distinguish human creations from automated content. Ultimately, this paper argues that platforms transition from a pure attention economy to a trust economy, actively protecting and highlighting human-made works to preserve the integrity and sustainability of the cultural value chain.

title: Beyond "ChatGPT Can Make Mistakes": Designing Interventions to Support Metacognitive Monitoring in AI-Assisted Work
preview: AI assistance places a metacognitive demand on users, who must judge their own competence and the system's. Yet designers lack comparative evidence on which interventions to choose, where to place them, and how to tell whether they worked. abstract_text: AI assistance places a metacognitive demand on users, who must judge their own competence and the system's. Yet designers lack comparative evidence on which interventions to choose, where to place them, and how to tell whether they worked. We elicited 30 interventions from 11 experts and, with prior work, organized them into a design space of time (when an intervention acts), level (whose competence is judged), and source (who supplies the monitoring cue). A between-subjects experiment (N = 917; 12 planning-and-organizing problems) compared a per-task reliability card, contrasting replies, pause points, and post-problem reflection against a baseline LLM assistant. Reliability cards and contrasting replies reduced estimation error and overconfidence and increased aggregate confidence discrimination. No task-performance improvement or average within-item discrimination gain was established. We contribute a shared vocabulary, a design space, and evidence that measured monitoring and task performance are separable design targets.

abstract_text: The rapid adoption of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has transformed how students access information, complete academic tasks, and manage their learning processes. This study examines the effects of GenAI use on students’ self-directed learning and critical thinking skills. It employs a qualitative approach based on library research. Data were collected from reputable journal articles, academic books, and institutional reports identified through Scopus, ScienceDirect, SpringerLink, Taylor & Francis, and Google Scholar. The literature was analyzed using thematic content analysis involving identification, selection, classification, synthesis, and interpretation. The findings demonstrate that GenAI can function as a personalized learning assistant by helping students identify learning needs, formulate learning goals, understand complex concepts, explore alternative perspectives, and obtain immediate feedback. Reflective and purposeful use of GenAI can strengthen students’ autonomy and promote interpretation, analysis, evaluation, inference, and problem-solving skills. However, passive and excessive use may lead to technological dependence, cognitive offloading, superficial understanding, violations of academic integrity, and uncritical acceptance of inaccurate or biased information. Therefore, the educational effects of GenAI are determined not only by the frequency of its use but also by students’ purposes, AI literacy, self-regulation, verification practices, and instructional design. This study highlights the conceptual relationship between GenAI use, self-directed learning, and critical thinking within an integrated analytical framework. Higher education institutions should position GenAI as a cognitive scaffold rather than a substitute for students’ intellectual effort. Universities should consequently develop responsible AI policies, authentic assessments, and AI literacy programs that emphasize fact-checking, ethical disclosure, reflective learning, and independent reasoning. Further empirical and longitudinal research is recommended to validate these relationships across disciplines and educational contexts.

title: Evaluating the Impact of Generative AI-Driven Adaptive Assessment Frameworks on Critical Thinking and Academic Integrity in Higher Education
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
preview: Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) adaptive assessment, in which the difficulty of questions, hints and feedback adjust to a learner’s live performance, is increasingly presented as a means of supporting personalised learning and critical thinking. At the same time, it may encourage cognitive offloading and create new academic-integrity concerns. This pilot study examines student perceptions of GenAI adaptive…
abstract_text: Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) adaptive assessment, in which the difficulty of questions, hints and feedback adjust to a learner’s live performance, is increasingly presented as a means of supporting personalised learning and critical thinking. At the same time, it may encourage cognitive offloading and create new academic-integrity concerns. This pilot study examines student perceptions of GenAI adaptive assessment, critical thinking, cognitive offloading, academic integrity and institutional readiness. The study combines secondary literature with a primary Google Form survey of 13 higher education students collected on 14 September 2026 through convenience sampling. Responses were analysed using frequencies, descriptive statistics, one-sample Wilcoxon signed-rank tests, sign tests, rank correlations and thematic coding. Respondents agreed that interactive AI hints improve the ability to break down multi-step problems (69.2%; p = .011) and that excessive reliance on real-time AI causes cognitive offloading (61.5%; p = .005). They also considered cognitive offloading in unmonitored work frequent (61.5%; p = .010). However, respondents were undecided on whether process-based adaptive assessment reduces ghostwriting, and they were divided on the clarity of institutional guidelines. As the sample is small, non-random and self-reported, the findings are indicative rather than generalisable. The study recommends adaptive systems designed around hints rather than final answers, assessment tasks requiring verification of AI outputs, process evidence and clear institutional rules on ethical AI use.

abstract_text: Children participate in increasingly AI-mediated environments. Drawing on children’s rights, philosophy of technology, cognitive science, and AI literacy research, this paper argues that exercising rights in these environments increasingly depends on metacognitive monitoring and control. This extends beyond narrower approaches to AI literacy focused primarily on technical knowledge and children’s safety. To that end, an alignment between rights-related concerns, metacognitive processes, and learning goals is established. This provides a preliminary conceptual basis for future research, curriculum development, and educational policy. The paper emphasises local adaptation, subject-embedded teaching, and learner diversity, including SEND. Furthermore, as AI systems and educational contexts continue to evolve rapidly, open educational resources are suggested as a particularly valuable model for collaborative refinement, localisation, and equitable access.

reading.interpretation: This paper has argued that children's AI literacy should not only be understood as technical competence or safe use, but as a rights-based educational concern. As AI systems increasingly participate in cognitive tasks previously performed by learners themselves, autonomy, critical judgement, and informed participation depend increasingly on how learners engage with these systems. Generative AI changes the educational problem by enabling complex cognitive offloading, obscuring underlying learning processes, and blurring the line between assistive tools and quasi-social interaction. Learners therefore require metacognitive regulation directed both towards their own thinking and towards AI systems, opening a new frontier for metacognitively oriented pedagogy. By bringing together children's rights, philosophy of technology, AI literacy, and metacognition, the paper explored how rights-related concerns in AI-mediated environments might be aligned with metacognitive capacities and translated into educational goals. While necessarily preliminary, this alignment offers a simple but robust conceptual basis for curriculum development, and educational intervention and future policy discussion. Because the conceptual framework is preliminary, it should be refined through empirical work, practitioner feedback, and local adaptation, with OER offering one practical model for doing so. As AI systems increasingly participate in cognitive tasks previously performed by learners themselves, autonomy, critical judgement, and informed participation depend increasingly on how learners engage with these systems. Learners therefore require metacognitive regulation directed both towards their own thinking and towards AI systems, opening a new frontier for metacognitively oriented pedagogy. By bringing together children's rights, philosophy of technology, AI literacy, and metacognition, the paper explored how rights-related concerns in AI-mediated environments might be aligned with metacognitive capacities and translated into educational goals. Because the conceptual framework is preliminary, it should be refined through empirical work, practitioner feedback, and local adaptation, with OER offering one practical model for doing so. abstract_text: The diffusion of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) across the creative industries has sharpened debates about automation, productivity, authorship, and the future of work. Attention has so far gravitated towards two poles: macro-level questions about job displacement, and technical questions about model performance and output quality. Much less has been said about how these systems are folded into the daily routines of professional work, and how that folding reorganises the conditions under which creative labour is performed, judged, and legitimated. This paper examines the incorporation of generative AI into advertising agencies, treated as strategic observatories of wider transformations in cognitive and creative labour. Drawing on a multi-method qualitative design that combines a scoping review with thirty-three in-depth semi-structured interviews with creative professionals, it traces how AI-assisted workflows are reorganised around selective delegation, cognitive offloading, iterative evaluation, orchestration, and what it terms curatorial labour: the emergent expertise of directing, evaluating, and taking responsibility for what algorithmic systems generate. Drawing on socio-technical accounts of distributed creativity, the paper argues that generative AI redistributes rather than replaces creative production, dispersing expertise, evaluative authority, and aesthetic judgment across human actors, machines, datasets, and commissioning organisations. It further argues that AI governance remains too model-centred and proposes a workflow-centred perspective on generative AI at work.

abstract_text: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is rapidly entering education, framed as a tool for efficiency and personalization. In this Perspective, we argue this obscures a deeper transformation. Schools are cognitive ecologies in which tools and social practices actively shape learning. GenAI restructures this ecology, redistributing epistemic labour, consolidating pedagogical functions, and reorganizing how knowledge is accessed, produced, and evaluated. Unlike most educational technologies, it is active, persistent, and generalist. We identify two enduring misalignments: a pedagogical gap between learning sciences and AI design, and a goal gap between measurable performance and developmental aims. Both gaps reflect logics already embedded within existing educational systems organized around efficiency, standardization, and control. GenAI does not introduce but risks entrenching and amplifying these gaps. Rather than accommodating GenAI through technical adjustments, we propose treating it as a diagnostic opportunity to redesign schooling for embodied, collaborative, and distinctly human forms of learning.

analysis.discussion: These considerations cannot be addressed by optimising individual tools or incrementally adjusting curricula. They require a broader reconfiguration. GenAI, precisely because it unsettles established assumptions about knowledge, authority, and learning, represents a catalytic opportunity to undertake it (for a summary, see Fig. 1 ). Fig. 1 Current Educational Logic vs Multitechnological Cognitive Ecology. This opportunity has precedent. The COVID-19 pandemic exposed the fragility of inherited educational arrangements with unprecedented clarity 31 , 33 . Yet, the prevailing response was restorative rather than transformative, focused on recovering what had been lost rather than reconsidering what might be built in its place 171 . Crises alone do not produce transformations, which require a prepared conceptual and practical vocabulary. The vocabulary for such a reconfiguration already exists. From Dewey’s learning by doing 172 to Papert’s constructionist vision of coding as epistemic practice 173 , from place-based education 174 to ‘Learning by Design’ 175 , 176 , from Bers’ framing of coding as a playground for young learners 177 to contemporary research on embodied learning environments 178 , and more powerfully, to Montessori’s prepared environment (e.g., refs. 93 , 179 – 182 , a rich lineage of educational theory and practice has long insisted that learning is most powerful when it is embodied, situated, collaborative, and materially grounded. What has been lacking is not the vision, but the institutional will, the technological ecology, and the socio-economic resources adequate to realise it. Realising it requires conceiving of education as a multi-technological cognitive ecology : a deliberately designed configuration of diverse material, social, and digital resources that jointly scaffold learning in ways consistent with what cognitive science tells us about human understanding 99 . Within such an ecology, no single technology dominates: low-tech, embodied, and collaborative tools are combined with digital and AI-based resources according to pedagogical aims rather than market logic. This framing also carries an eco-sustainable dimension that cannot be ignored. AI systems are among the most resource-intensive technologies ever deployed in educational contexts, with substantial energy, water, and infrastructural costs 183 . Introducing them into schools without accounting for these costs risks reproducing, at a larger scale, the same logic of resource exploitation that education is increasingly called upon to counter. A multi-technological ecological approach implies instead a principle of deliberate use: combining tools according to their pedagogical affordances, sharing resources across learners and generations, and treating AI as one component among many rather than as a default infrastructure: using, not abusing, the technological resources available 184 , 185 . Seen in this light, GenAI represents less a ready-made solution than a diagnostic catalyst. It exposes longstanding tensions between educational systems organised around efficiency and performance and the broader developmental aims education is meant to serve: agency, critical judgment, collaboration, and meaningful participation in shared epistemic practices. These tensions are not new: AI makes them impossible to ignore. Addressing them requires shifting the central question from how to integrate AI into existing schools to how schooling itself should be reimagined in light of what we know about cognition, learning, and the ecological conditions that sustain both. The answer, we suggest, lies not in the adoption of any single technology, but in the deliberate design of plural technological ecologies, combining embodied, social, material, and digital resources, that only together are capable of supporting the full range of human learning and development. AI is neither saviour nor threat. It is a stress test for education, exposing the limits of existing models and compelling a reconsideration of their aims, foundations, and ecological responsibilities. It is one tool among many. Above all, it is a catalyst for reimagining the technological arrangements that structure every day at school.

abstract_text: Industry 5.0 emphasises human-centric, sustainable, and resilient digital transformation, in which technology augments human skills and wellbeing. While the integration of generative AI into workplaces is rapidly reshaping job roles, this study investigates how organisations can guide employees from AI-related fear to fluency, achieving confident, ethical, and psychologically safe engagement with AI systems, and proposes a contextualised diagnostic tool for measuring organisational readiness. A mixed-methods design was used. Quantitatively, 217 professionals from AI-adopting organisations completed a nine-item online survey measuring psychological safety, innovation climate, skill confidence, leadership communication, policy understanding, training efficacy, and adoption outcomes, analysed using descriptive statistics and Pearson correlations. Qualitatively, 15 semi-structured interviews with mid-level managers across French, Indian, and American operating contexts were deductively coded against six a priori dimensions and triangulated against the survey findings. Qualitative accounts converged with quantitative patterns on the centrality of leadership translation and the insufficiency of generic training, while showing partial divergence on how explicitly managers themselves name psychological safety as a lever. The study finally proposes the AI Readiness Scan, a six-dimension diagnostic (psychological safety, intercultural contextualisation, regulatory compliance, skill confidence, change resilience, and leadership AI readiness), each grounded in an established measurement or theoretical literature, to help organisations act on evidence rather than assumption before and during AI transformation. The findings bridge psychological safety theory, responsible AI governance, and international labour considerations into an integrated, actionable framework for managers and policymakers navigating AI-driven digital transformation.

preview: Early stroke risk prediction offers an opportunity for timely interventions and may help reduce the clinical burden associated with stroke. abstract_text: Early stroke risk prediction offers an opportunity for timely interventions and may help reduce the clinical burden associated with stroke. Artificial intelligence (AI) provides medical practitioners with tools to analyse clinical biomarkers and predict a patient’s stroke risk. However, existing models lack interpretability and explainable decision support, limiting their adoption in clinical settings. This paper proposes a hybrid Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU)-TabTransformer architecture using cross-attention for stroke-status prediction. The proposed architecture comprises two stages. In the first stage (Model A), ordered feature-sequence representations from a GRU encoder are combined with concatenated categorical and numerical tabular features from a TabTransformer encoder. The model passes these distinct learned representations through cross-attention and linear projection layers before the final prediction. In the second stage (Model B), we augment our model with Large Language Models (LLMs) and Local Interpretable Model-agnostic Explanations (LIME) to provide per-sample, post hoc, human-interpretable explanations based on predicted probabilities. Experimental results show that both models achieve competitive sensitivity and accuracy values. In particular, the Synthetic Minority Over-sampling Technique (SMOTE) yielded a more balanced sensitivity–specificity trade-off, with a sensitivity of 74.00% and a specificity of 75.10%. Moreover, the model achieved an accuracy of 75.05% with SMOTE. An ablation study further shows that Cross-Attention offers better sensitivity and Receiver Operating Characteristic-Area Under the Curve (ROC-AUC), while Gated Fusion performs better on several other metrics. Additionally, age and average glucose level were the most influential stroke risk indicators, while Body Mass Index (BMI) and ever-married status were secondary model-attributed features. A two-factor repeated-measures Analysis of Variance (ANOVA) confirmed an interaction between model choice and the class-balancing technique used in stroke risk prediction systems. The Mistral + Hybrid GRU-TabTransformer architecture also recorded a mean inference time of 57.59s using few-shot prompting. Overall, the results provide a proof of concept for integrating hybrid GRU-TabTransformer with cross-attention and LLM-based explainability to support interpretable stroke risk prediction systems, pending robust external validation before deployment.

Purpose 
                     The rapid integration of Conversational Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) into higher education has sparked intense pedagogical debates regarding its impact on student cognition. This study aims to deconstruct the micro-level interactive processes through which university students engage with large language models (LLMs), mapping the systemic socio-technical mechanisms that shape, extend, or restrict the development of independent critical thinking skills. 
                   
                   
                     Design/methodology/approach 
                     Adopting an exploratory qualitative research paradigm, this study used a combination of purposive and maximum variation sampling strategies to recruit n = 55 undergraduate and postgraduate students across diverse disciplinary tracks (STEM, medicine, humanities and social sciences) at a public university. Data collection was executed through semi-structured depth interviews incorporating stimulated recall methodologies and live interaction histories. The qualitative texts were analyzed using Braun and Clarke’s inductive thematic analysis methodology guided by Grounded Theory coding protocols via NVivo, augmented by cross-dimensional matrix queries across student subgroups. 
                   
                   
                     Findings 
                     The analysis generated an integrated socio-technical framework comprised of four core themes. The Paradox of Cognitive Offloading vs Extension, where automated text consolidation yields significant efficiency dividends but risks fostering cognitive inertia and domain-specific skill atrophy, particularly in technical code and math execution. The Awakening of Algorithmic Discernment through Epistemic Vigilance, revealing that model imperfections, flawed logic and fabricated bibliographic citations serve as unexpected cognitive catalysts that disrupt passive trust and force active multisource validation loops. The Regulatory Role of Individual Prompt Literacy, distinguishing low-literacy single-turn commands from advanced interactive conditioning workflows that deconstruct complex problems; and the Scaffold Effect of Process-Oriented Pedagogical Interventions, demonstrating that instructor-imposed structural constraints create “desirable difficulties” that effectively preserve human cognitive agency. 
                   
                   
                     Research limitations/implications 
                     The research relies on qualitative self-reported reflections during depth interviews and represents a cross-sectional snapshot of rapid technological evolution. Future research should integrate objective backend telemetry data with multi-semester longitudinal tracking. 
                   
                   
                     Practical implications 
                     Grounded directly in empirical student interaction data, the paper provides an actionable blueprint for higher education governance, advocating for a transition from unenforceable prohibition policies toward structured “Critical Integration.” Key recommendations include rewriting curriculum assignments to evaluate process-oriented modification logs rather than final written products, embedding formal prompt literacy into core curricula and training students to deploy multisource triangulation protocols against digital hallucinations.

abstract_text: The rapid evolution of digital technologies has fundamentally reshaped consumer behavior, emphasizing the influence of digital environment factors on engagement and purchasing decisions. This study investigates the effects of interface design and notifications on online consumer behavior, highlighting their roles in facilitating both planned and impulse purchases. Interface design, encompassing visual aesthetics, navigation structures, and interactive features, directly impacts perceived ease of use, trust, and user satisfaction, thereby promoting engagement and transaction completion. Notifications, including push alerts, emails, and in-app messages, function as contextual cues that capture attention and prompt immediate action, with personalization and timing serving as critical determinants of effectiveness. Employing a mixed-method approach, data were collected from 450 active e-commerce users and analyzed using structural equation modeling to examine the relationships among interface design, notifications, and online purchasing behavior. Findings demonstrate that both interface quality and notification strategies significantly influence purchase intentions, with perceived ease of use and emotional response mediating and moderating these effects. The interaction between interface design and notifications underscores the importance of an integrated digital strategy. These results provide theoretical insights into digital consumer behavior and offer practical implications for e-commerce platforms aiming to optimize user experience, increase conversions, and enhance long-term consumer loyalty.

abstract_text: This reflective paper explores how Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) can function as a conversational partner for self-regulated learning in higher education, and how such use complicates assessment. Using an illustrative interaction with a GenAI chatbot based on a take-home examination question from cognitive science, ‘Do machines think?’, we apply the Structure of observed learning outcome (SOLO) taxonomy, to analyse qualitative differences in the structural complexity of the interaction itself. Our demonstration reveals that GenAI’s default output consistently remained at the quantitative, multistructural phase, producing polished but pedagogically thin responses, and that reaching the qualitative phase required repeated meta-level interventions from the learner, including requests for simplification and structured learning support. Critically, this process demanded the very self-regulatory skills the tool was expected to support. We introduce the concept of AI-interaction literacy to describe the capacity to steer, evaluate, and learn from iterative GenAI interaction, and argue that unguided use may disproportionately benefit already advantaged students. We conclude with three propositions: students should treat GenAI as a critical dialogue partner; teachers should explicitly teach AI-interaction literacy with attention to equity; and take-home assessments should emphasise evaluating knowledge at the qualitative phase of the SOLO taxonomy.

abstract_text: Introduction With the growing integration of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) into higher education, research attention must shift from the frequency of tool use to how these tools are used by learners. This study examines how GenAI literacy is related to learners' patterns of GenAI use and cognitive engagement during GenAI interactions. Methods Drawing on questionnaire data from a large, diverse international sample of academic learners (N = 848), hierarchical multiple regression analyses were conducted to examine the relationships between dimensions of GenAI literacy and actual usage behaviors. Cluster analysis was then used to identify learner profiles based on patterns of GenAI use, literacy, monitoring, and reliance. Results The findings indicate a dual role for critical-ethical awareness, a dimension of GenAI literacy that is associated with both monitoring GenAI outputs and using GenAI as a cognitive shortcut. Cluster analysis identified three learner profiles: Engaged and Literate users, who integrate monitoring and reliance; Uncritical Reliant users, who show high reliance but limited monitoring; and Skeptical Minimal users, who have low GenAI use but high reliance when they do engage. These patterns point to an “illusion of cognitive independence,” in which learners report high levels of independent thinking while engaging in cognitive offloading by relying on GenAI outputs without sufficient monitoring, particularly among Uncritical Reliant users. Discussion Collectively, these findings suggest that GenAI literacy does not necessarily reduce reliance on GenAI but instead shapes how learners combine monitoring with reliance. Conceptually, this positions GenAI literacy as a regulatory mechanism of human–AI interaction, extending self-regulated learning to contexts in which cognitive processes are distributed between learners and systems. These results highlight the importance of developing GenAI literacy as a practice of reflective and regulated use rather than focusing solely on increasing technology adoption.
