abstract_text: A rigorous, evidence-based pedagogical foundation for educators who wish to help students maintain and cultivate their critical thinking skills in the age of generative AI. The book provides an important overview of the cognitive impacts of offloading intellectual labor to AI, and defines and probes key concepts such as critical thinking, AI literacy, and meta-cognition. It contextualizes the challenge faced by educators by mapping the global state of AI literacy integration across K-12 and higher education, identifying how and where AI literacy is being taught, and where it is currently missing. The book reflects on best practices and evidence-based research from around the globe, providing educators with specific and actionable methods to help their students gain the skills, motivation and habits of mind to use AI more selectively and avoid offloading their cognitive capabilities. It also explores strategies for knowledge transfer and retention, featuring insights from diverse critical thinkers, and provides educators with guidance on designing “AI resilient” assignments and assessments and integrating education-focused AI models that effectively incentivize critical thinking and learning. This book is essential reading for educators - teachers, professors, and librarians – currently grappling with the challenge of preserving critical thinking in an age of pervasive AI and will be particularly useful to those teaching information literacy, media literacy, and digital literacy.

abstract_text: We investigated the effect of an acute partial sleep deprivation on upper limb dual-task performance. Through a within-subject design, we assessed participants' inhibitory control (Go/No-go task; GNG), sustained attention (Psychomotor vigilance test; PVT) and motor performance (finger tapping; FT) after one night of partial sleep deprivation (SD) versus one night of normal sleep (NS). After both SD and NS, participants underwent three single task (ST) conditions and two dual-task (DT) conditions in a counterbalanced order. We observed in 46 participants substantial differences between DT and ST performance, i.e., dual-task effects (DTEs), for both inhibitory control and sustained attention regardless of the sleeping conditions. Notably, more negative DTEs emerged after SD compared to NS only in GNG, but not in PVT. Overall, the present dual-task paradigm effectively elicited cognitive interference, revealing robust DTEs across cognitive tasks independent of sleep condition, and a selective sleep-deprivation effect only for inhibitory control under dual-tasking. Unveiling factors shaping dual-task performance in sleep-deprived situations provides novel insights into the implications of both sleep-disordered conditions and lifestyles entailing occasional sleep deprivation.

abstract_text: Many organizations seek to combine human expertise with explainable artificial intelligence (XAI), but they often overlook a core requirement for effective collaboration; humans must understand their own abilities. This understanding of one’s own abilities is referred to as metacognition, which captures how well individuals monitor and regulate their own decision making. In two experiments with real estate and lending professionals, we find that XAI improves human metacognition by reducing their overconfidence. As a result, experts can better delegate decisions to an artificial intelligence (AI) and interact with it more effectively, improving the collaborative performance. These effects occur primarily when XAI highlights differences between human reasoning and AI logic. Our findings demonstrate that metacognition is a key mechanism through which XAI affects decision outcomes and offer guidance for organizations deploying (X)AI under growing transparency and accountability mandates, such as those in the European Union Artificial Intelligence Act.

abstract_text:
Abstract 
                 This study examines the impact of social network use on the innovation performance of entrepreneurial firms, with particular emphasis on the mediating role of digital distraction. Drawing on an integrated perspective of network-based resource access and attention allocation, this research addresses a critical gap in understanding the dual effects of social networks in entrepreneurial contexts. A quantitative, cross-sectional survey was conducted among managers and employees of small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) in Jeddah, Saudi Arabia. Using stratified random sampling, data were collected from 375 respondents and analyzed through variance-based structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM). The findings reveal that social network use has a positive and significant effect on innovation performance. However, digital distraction negatively mediates this relationship, such that increased distraction weakens the beneficial impact of social networks on innovation outcomes. These results highlight the paradoxical role of social networks as both enablers of knowledge exchange and sources of cognitive interference. This study contributes to the entrepreneurship and innovation literature by integrating the bright and dark sides of social network use within a single model. Practically, the findings suggest that entrepreneurial firms should adopt structured policies and attention-management strategies to mitigate digital distraction while leveraging the benefits of social networks for innovation.

analysis.methods: This study adopts a quantitative, cross-sectional research design using a survey-based approach to examine the relationships among social network use, digital distraction, and innovation performance. Given the objective of testing theoretically grounded relationships and mediation effects, a correlational design is considered appropriate (Hair et al., 2019) . The target population consists of managers and employees of small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) in the Jeddah region of Saudi Arabia, selected due to their critical role in innovation and economic development within emerging economies. A sample of 375 respondents was determined using the Cochran formula to ensure adequate statistical power, and stratified random sampling was employed to enhance representativeness across firms and organizational roles. Data were collected a structured questionnaire comprising four sections: demographic information, social network use (measured a researcher-developed scale), innovation performance (measured using the scale developed by Baker and Sinkula, 1999), and digital distraction (measured using the scale proposed by Zanet et al., 2019). All constructs were assessed using a fivepoint Likert scale ranging from 1 ("strongly disagree") to 5 ("strongly agree"). Content validity was established through expert evaluation to ensure the relevance and clarity of measurement items, while reliability was assessed using Cronbach's alpha coefficients, with all constructs exceeding the recommended threshold of 0.70, indicating acceptable internal consistency (Nunnally & Bernstein, 1994) . The collected data were analyzed using SPSS and SmartPLS software, employing variance-based structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM), which is particularly suitable for complex models, mediation analysis, and predictive research contexts (Hair et al., 2021; Henseler et al., 2015) . The analysis was conducted in two stages, including the assessment of the measurement model (reliability and validity) and the evaluation of the structural model (hypothesis testing and mediation analysis).

In terms of education level, 61% had a bachelor's degree, 32% a master's degree and 7% a doctorate. This statistic indicates sufficient experience and university education of the respondents, which makes the sample suitable for analyzing organizational innovation. At the same time, excessive or unstructured use of these platforms can generate digital distraction, which undermines employees' focus and reduces innovative performance (Brooks, 2015; Cao & Yu, 2019) . Empirical results confirm that social network use has a positive and significant effect on innovation, supporting prior research that emphasizes their role in accelerating information flow and fostering creativity (Parvin et al., 2016; Kapoor et al., 2018) . However, the study also shows that social networks significantly increase digital distraction, which in turn has a negative impact on innovation. These findings align with previous studies indicating that frequent interruptions and multitasking reduce cognitive efficiency and creative output (Junco, 2012; Rosen et al., 2013) . Importantly, the results reveal that digital distraction plays a significant mediating role in the relationship between social networks and innovation. This suggests that the overall impact of social networks is not purely beneficial but depends on how effectively their use is managed within organizations. In other words, social networks simultaneously create opportunities for innovation and risks that may hinder it, which is consistent with the "bright" and "dark" side perspectives in digital technology research. Despite its contributions, this study has several limitations. The sample is limited to small and mediumsized enterprises in the Jeddah region, which may affect the generalizability of the findings. In addition, the use of self-reported questionnaire data may introduce response bias. Furthermore, the study focuses only on digital distraction as a mediating variable, while other potentially relevant mechanisms, such as organizational culture or knowledge management capabilities, were not examined. Future research is encouraged to replicate this study in different geographical and industrial contexts to enhance generalizability. Researchers may also explore additional mediating and moderating variables, such as organizational resilience or absorptive capacity, and employ longitudinal or mixed-method approaches to better capture the dynamic effects of social network use on innovation over time. From a managerial perspective, the findings suggest that organizations should adopt a balanced and strategic approach to social network use. This includes implementing guidelines to regulate usage, reducing unnecessary notifications, promoting professional platforms, and training employees in digital time management and attention control. abstract_text: This article investigates the current state and foreseeable trajectory of artificial intelligence (AI), focusing on its principal application domains and the governance challenges they raise. A qualitative secondary data methodology is adopted, synthesising peer-reviewed academic literature, industry reports, and publications by international organisations including the OECD and the World Economic Forum, with priority given to sources published between 2018 and 2024. AI creates the greatest value where tasks are well defined, datasets are large and accurate, and performance metrics are clear. Across healthcare, finance, transportation, education, manufacturing, energy, and agriculture, measurable improvements in efficiency, accuracy, and cost have been documented. Cross-cutting risks—including algorithmic bias, privacy erosion, labour displacement, and concentration of AI capabilities—require active governance responses. The article proposes targeted policy recommendations at international, national, and organisational levels.

abstract_text: Artificial intelligence is no longer limited to specialized technical settings. Students use it to summarize readings, generate outlines, draft essays and prepare for exams. Professionals use it to write reports, polish emails, analyze information, build presentations and support everyday decisions. People also encounter AI generated text, images, videos, recommendations and automated replies across social media, search engines, learning platforms and workplace tools often without knowing where human judgment ends and machine output begins. Critical thinking is more than the ability to find an answer. It involves questioning assumptions, weighing evidence, comparing viewpoints, identifying bias, recognizing uncertainty, evaluating credibility and making independent judgments. These skills matter in education, professional work, research, media literacy, public communication and ethical decision making. They become even more important because polished content can look convincing even when it is incomplete, biased, unsupported or wrong in an AI rich information environment. This proposed chapter will examine how this shift is changing the way people think, learn, reason, create and make decisions.

abstract_text: Objective: This study aims to investigate how using generative AI such as ChatGPT influences users' cognitive dependency that results in cognitive offloading and deskilling. Background: Generative AI, specifically LLM (Large Language Model)'s use had been rapidly growing in the creative domains such as writing. Some studies suggest that using LLM, or mainly, ChatGPT can support idea generation and expedite learnings, while others warn that users may experience deskilling and weakening on critical thinking. Most of the discussions on this topic have approached from the educational perspective focusing primarily on the ethical implications or the quality of outcome. On the other hand, relatively little attention has been paid to the process of using LLM and how human cognitions are affected. Method: A total of 64 creative essays were collected from 32 University students. These students either used or not used ChatGPT to write the essays. Three writing experts (who identifies their job as a "writer" and has more than 5 years of writing experience) rated the essays on the number of assertions, the number of opposing views, the number of detailed cases introduced, concept quality, sense of agency, and structure diversity. For analysis, the study saw the difference between ChatGPT using group and no support group using paired-sample t-test. Results: The results showed statistically significant differences between AI vs non- AI assisted groups. Participants who used ChatGPT during writing had used more counterclaims (p<0.001), while participants who wrote without ChatGPT demonstrated significant higher levels of authorial agency (p<0.001). Some marginal trends were found in the logical complexity, showing higher number of case use and complexity for the non-AI assisted group. Conclusion: This study suggests that while generative AI can support humans, it may also potentially reduce and deskill individual cognitive abilities when articulating their arguments. In conclusion, this study suggests the need for generative AI systems from human factors perspective, so that the human-AI interaction helps support productivity while maintaining users' cognitive engagement and human agency. Application: The results of this study may contribute to the development of AI interfaces and human-AI interaction design (AX), that support productivity while reducing deskilling and cognitive offloading.

abstract_text: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has entered education faster than the theoretical and methodological frameworks used to evaluate it. This critical integrative review asks a more consequential question than whether GenAI ‘works’: under what pedagogical conditions can it augment learning without displacing learner agency, epistemic responsibility, and higher-order cognition? A purposive corpus of 56 distinct sources was synthesized, spanning foundational theories of experiential, sociocultural, situated, distributed, social-cognitive, cognitive-load, self-regulated, and technology-mediated learning; established technology-acceptance models; artificial-intelligence-in-education and AI-literacy frameworks; policy guidance; and empirical, systematic-review, and meta-analytic evidence published through 2026. The synthesis indicates that GenAI is most defensibly conceptualized as a fallible cognitive artifact embedded in a distributed learning system rather than as an autonomous epistemic authority. Positive effects on achievement, motivation, engagement, creativity, and higher-order thinking are increasingly supported, but they are conditional on task design, scaffolding, interaction quality, verification practices, AI literacy, and sustained human oversight. Evidence for metacognitive improvement remains weaker, while unstructured use can promote cognitive offloading, overconfidence, dependency, and integrity risks. To integrate these findings, this article proposes the Human–AI Pedagogical Agency Framework (HAPAF), composed of five interacting layers: epistemic positioning, learner agency, interaction design, verification, and governance. The framework reframes effective GenAI integration as an agency-preserving pedagogical design problem rather than a tool-adoption problem.

Foundational theories of experiential, sociocultural, situated, distributed, and self-regulated learning converge on the idea that learners develop through activity, mediation, participation, monitoring, and reconstruction. GenAI is compatible with these traditions when it expands the range of explanations, feedback, representations, and practice available to the learner while leaving epistemic judgment and goaldirected regulation intact. Contemporary theoretical sources were added to explain technology integration and adoption (Davis, 1989; Mishra & Koehler, 2006; Venkatesh et al., 2003) , the development of AI in education (Holmes et al., 2019; Luckin et al., 2016; Ouyang & Jiao, 2021; Zawacki-Richter et al., 2019) , and AI literacy and competency (Miao & Cukurova, 2024; Miao et al., 2024; Ng et al., 2021; Tzirides et al., 2024) . The evidence layer prioritized peer-reviewed studies and reviews directly addressing GenAI or advanced conversational AI in educational settings, supplemented by international guidance on ethics and educational governance. The corpus therefore included early conceptual and case-study work (Cotton et al., 2024; Farrokhnia et al., 2024; Kasneci et al., 2023; Tlili et al., 2023) , student adoption and perception studies (Chan & Hu, 2023; Stöhr et al., 2024; Strzelecki, 2024; Tiwari et al., 2024) , empirical studies of learning processes and outcomes (Bai & Wang, 2025; Essel et al., 2024; Fan et al., 2025; Ng et al., 2024; Tossell et al., 2024; Urban et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2024; Youssef et al., 2024) , and higher-level evidence syntheses (Albadarin et al., 2024; Baig & Yadegaridehkordi, 2024; Bhullar et al., 2024; Chen & Cheung, 2025; Deng et al., 2025; Li et al., 2026; Liu et al., 2025; Lo et al., 2024; McGrath et al., 2025; Mohebi, 2024; Wu & Yu, 2024) . Global policy and governance sources included UNESCO's ethics recommendation and GenAI guidance (Miao & Holmes, 2023; UNESCO, 2022) . Analysis proceeded through constant comparison across four coding domains: (a) the locus of cognition and knowledge construction, (b) mechanisms of learner agency and regulation, (c) characteristics of human-AI interaction and instructional design, and (d) boundary conditions involving verification, integrity, ethics, and equity. Evidence was then arranged into causal propositions rather than a simple benefits-versus-risks inventory. For example, personalized feedback was coded not as intrinsically positive, but as potentially beneficial when it triggers revision, monitoring, and transfer; reduced mental effort was coded as ambiguous because it can represent either efficient scaffolding or cognitive offloading. This distinction is consistent with contemporary evidence showing that the same GenAI affordance can produce different outcomes depending on task structure and learner behavior. The review has three intentional boundaries. First, it is conceptual and integrative rather than systematic, so the 56-source corpus should be understood as theoretically purposive rather than exhaustive. Second, the unit of analysis is pedagogical interaction with GenAI, not the technical benchmarking of language models. Third, the framework does not assume that evidence obtained with one product or model version generalizes indefinitely to all future systems. GenAI capabilities evolve rapidly; consequently, the more durable object of inquiry is the structure of human-AI pedagogical relations rather than any specific interface. The second result is that reduced effort is pedagogically ambiguous. Cognitive load theory is often invoked to justify AI assistance because a system can remove routine search, formatting, syntax, or procedural burdens. That interpretation is valid when the removed load is extraneous to the learning objective (Sweller, 1988 ). Yet the same assistance can become detrimental when it removes the very cognitive operations the learner is expected to acquire. A statistics student who uses GenAI to format code may preserve conceptual work; a student who accepts an unexplained model specification and interpretation may bypass it. The design question is therefore not how much effort GenAI saves, but which effort it saves. Experimental evidence increasingly supports this distinction. Urban et al. (2024) found that ChatGPT improved the quality, originality, and elaboration of solutions to a complex creative problem and reduced perceived task difficulty and mental effort. Importantly, however, participants showed uncertainty in metacognitive calibration: perceived usefulness could inflate self-evaluation without equivalent accuracy. Essel et al. (2024) , using a pretest-posttest control design, reported changes in critical, creative, and reflective thinking when undergraduates used ChatGPT in a research-methodology course. (2024) demonstrated that prompt engineering can improve information retrieval within a flipped-classroom context, making the quality of interaction itself an instructional variable. Ng et al. (2024) compared a generative AI-based self-regulated-learning chatbot with a rule-based chatbot and found improvements in science knowledge, behavioral engagement, and motivation. Tossell et al. (2024) , however, observed mixed student experiences in an essay assignment that required ChatGPT, illustrating that mandated AI use does not automatically make writing simpler or learning better. analysis.methods: This study adopted a grounded theory approach because it aimed to construct an explanatory model of an emerging educational process. Grounded theory was appropriate because the study sought to explain process-level learning mechanisms grounded in learners' concrete AI-mediated research episodes. GenAI-mediated doctoral learning is a rapidly developing practice for which existing theoretical categories remain incomplete. The study therefore focused on process and mechanism, with close attention to how students interpreted, used, revised, and justified AI-generated outputs in concrete research tasks. The study primarily followed a procedural grounded theory logic while drawing on broader quality criteria for credibility, analytic fit, and theoretical usefulness ( Corbin and Strauss, 1990 ; Chun Tie et al., 2019 ; Charmaz and Thornberg, 2021 ). Cognitive offloading, metacognitive calibration, and self-regulated learning were used as sensitizing ideas rather than as a priori coding categories. These concepts informed the formulation of the research questions and oriented attention to possible learning mechanisms, but the coding structure was developed through open coding, constant comparison, theoretical sampling, and repeated comparison of empirical incidents, artifact episodes, analytic memos, and emerging category relations. The categories reported in the Results section were generated through comparison across interview accounts, AI-use artifacts, stimulated-recall explanations, negative cases, and saturation-test interviews. The categories should be understood as analytically related processes rather than as a fixed sequence that every participant followed in the same order. In some episodes, task-entry scaffolding led to deeper verification. In others, modular generation created premature coherence and required later reconstruction. Some participants moved back and forth between scaffolding, generation, checking, and accountability within the same task. Task-entry scaffolding describes how GenAI helped doctoral students enter difficult research tasks. Participants used AI to map unfamiliar literature, clarify concepts, translate ideas across disciplinary boundaries, and reduce initial writing difficulty. In this use pattern, cognitive offloading lowered entry barriers while preserving the learner's own research judgment. P03, a first-year sociology doctoral student, described AI as a reading map: “ Before reading a dense theoretical article, I ask a GenAI tool to outline the main debate and explain the key concepts. I do not use the answer as a substitute for the article. It is more like a map. After I get the map, I know where to pay attention when I read the original text .” (P03[Interview]) The artifact provided by P03 showed a prompt asking AI to summarize a theoretical debate and identify key conceptual tensions. In the stimulated-recall discussion, P03 explained that she used the response to mark sections of the original article for close reading. This episode shows AI functioning as an entry scaffold because the output helped the participant approach the original text more strategically while keeping the original text as the primary object of learning. Task-entry scaffolding also appeared in cross-disciplinary work. P10, a materials science doctoral student, explained: “ My project involves materials chemistry and mechanical behavior. Sometimes I understand the experiment but not the theoretical explanation from another field. I ask AI to explain the mechanism in simpler language or compare two possible explanations. It helps me cross the language boundary between fields .” (P10[Interview]) P10′s artifact included an AI-generated comparison between two mechanisms explaining material fatigue behavior. In stimulated recall, he marked several phrases as “too general” and explained how he checked them against recent domain papers. AI supported interdisciplinary translation, while field-specific verification remained central. Writing-entry support was another common form of scaffolding. P07 noted: “ I usually write the paragraph myself first. Then I ask AI to make the expression clearer. If I let AI write first, the paragraph becomes too general. If I write first and then use AI, it helps me express my own meaning better .” (P07[Interview]) These cases show how doctoral students used AI to orient attention, clarify terminology, compare possible explanations, and polish self-generated writing. Task-entry scaffolding therefore represents productive cognitive offloading, because GenAI reduced extraneous entry difficulty while preserving learner-controlled reading, verification, and reconstruction. This pattern appeared across literature orientation, concept clarification, cross-disciplinary translation, and writing-entry support, with discipline-specific variation in the form of scaffolding. Participants reported using AI to generate conceptual frameworks, method suggestions, thesis structures, hypotheses, chapter outlines, and polished paragraphs. These outputs often looked coherent and professional, and their implications for learner engagement depended on how students examined and reconstructed the reasoning embedded in them. P05, a management doctoral student, described this experience: “ AI can generate a theoretical framework in seconds. It gives variables, relationships, and even possible hypotheses. When I first see it, I feel the framework is complete. But when my supervisor asks why these variables should be connected, I realize I cannot explain the logic. analysis.discussion: This study examined how doctoral students use GenAI in research-related learning and how AI-generated outputs become scaffolds for inquiry or substitutes for learner-controlled reasoning. The findings indicate that learner-controlled engagement differed according to where cognitive and metacognitive work was located. Stronger evidence of learner ownership appeared when AI reduced entry difficulty while students retained responsibility for reasoning, verification, and reconstruction. Risks to ownership appeared when generated coherence was accepted before students had reconstructed the underlying conceptual, methodological, or argumentative logic. These findings concern process-level patterns of engagement rather than demonstrated improvements in learning outcomes. This study developed a grounded mechanism model comprising task-entry scaffolding, modular generation, metacognitive calibration crisis, critical reconstruction, and research accountability. More learner-controlled engagement was observed when GenAI helped doctoral students enter difficult tasks, compare possible directions, and refine their own thinking while preserving responsibility for verification, reasoning, and reconstruction. Risks to learner ownership appeared when generated coherence was accepted before conceptual, methodological, or argumentative ownership had been formed. The central educational challenge is therefore to support accountable reconstruction by helping learners transform AI-supported outputs into owned understanding, calibrated judgment, and defensible research decisions. GenAI-supported doctoral learning should be examined through the reconstruction practices learners use to verify, adapt, explain, and defend AI-supported knowledge work.
analysis.limitations: Several boundaries shape the interpretation of this study. First, the participants were doctoral students from Chinese research universities, where supervisory relationships, publication pressure, English academic writing demands and institutional norms may shape GenAI use in distinctive ways. The model should therefore be interpreted as analytically transferable rather than statistically generalizable. Its most direct transferability is to high-complexity learning contexts where learners must evaluate, adapt, and defend AI-supported outputs. Second, AI-use artifacts and stimulated-recall participation were voluntary. Students willing to share such records may have been more reflective, confident, AI-literate or normatively careful than those who declined. This may have led to overrepresentation of participants who were already able to articulate AI-use decisions. The study addressed this risk through negative-case analysis, including comparison between participants who used AI frequently while maintaining strong reconstruction practices and participants who used AI less frequently while showing limited conceptual or methodological ownership. Future studies could recruit less confident or less AI-literate users more deliberately and examine unsuccessful, hidden, or abandoned AI-use episodes in greater depth. Third, stimulated recall provided richer process data than ordinary interviews, while still relying on retrospective interpretation. Fourth, although the study reports participant-level tool and model/version information, it did not experimentally compare the technical performance of different AI systems, model configurations, prompt settings, subscription tiers, or backend model-selection mechanisms. The model/version information was used as contextual information for interpreting participants' GenAI-mediated learning episodes. Different tools and model families may generate outputs with different levels of fluency, source opacity, factual reliability, and context sensitivity, which may affect metacognitive calibration. Future research could combine interview data with systematic prompt-history collection, model-version logs, and tool-comparison designs to examine how specific model characteristics shape cognitive offloading, calibration crisis, and accountable reconstruction. Fifth, although supervisory accountability emerged as an important category, supervisors themselves were not interviewed. Sixth, the qualitative design did not include direct measures of learning performance, knowledge retention, transfer, or the quality of final research products, nor did it include a comparison group or independent outcome ratings. Accordingly, the findings concern process-level indicators of learner ownership, metacognitive monitoring, verification, and reconstruction rather than demonstrated improvements in learning outcomes. Because the study develops a qualitative mechanism model, future intervention, longitudinal, and mixed-methods studies can operationalize productive offloading, premature coherence, metacognitive calibration crisis, critical reconstruction and accountable reconstruction to test their associations with learning performance, knowledge retention, transfer, and research-product quality over time. Future research could also use writing-version analysis, supervisor-student dyadic data, experimental comparisons, and cross-national samples to examine how GenAI-mediated offloading and accountable reconstruction develop across doctoral trajectories.

abstract_text: Abstract Digital technologies have become indispensable for college teaching, assessment, communication, research and administration. However, frequent notifications, personal messaging, social media use and digital task-switching may interrupt sustained attention. This study examined workplace digital distraction and work productivity among college teachers. Specifically, it assessed the levels of digital distraction and perceived work productivity and analysed the relationship between these variables. A quantitative, cross-sectional and explanatory research design was adopted. Primary data were collected from 148 college teachers using a structured questionnaire and convenience sampling. Frequencies, percentages, mean, standard deviation, Cronbach’s alpha, Pearson’s correlation and simple linear regression were employed for data analysis. Respondents reported a relatively high level of workplace digital distraction (M = 3.7686, SD = 0.11328) and a high level of work productivity (M = 4.3230, SD = 0.18345). Both scales demonstrated good internal consistency, with Cronbach’s alpha values of 0.84 and 0.88, respectively. Workplace digital distraction was moderately and negatively correlated with work productivity (r = −.559, p = 0.000). The regression model was statistically significant, F(1, 146) = 66.419, p = 0.000, and explained 31.3% of the variance in work productivity (R² = .313). Workplace digital distraction was a significant negative predictor of work productivity (B = −0.906, β = −.559, t = −8.150, p = 0.000). The findings highlight the importance of notification controls, protected focus periods, digital self-management training and clear institutional communication norms. Colleges should promote the constructive use of digital technologies while reducing avoidable interruptions that may weaken concentration, task completion and teaching-related efficiency.

abstract_text: The rapid integration of digital technologies into educational environments has created new opportunities for learning while simultaneously introducing challenges related to students’ attention and engagement. One emerging concern is digital distraction, which may reduce students’ emotional focus during classroom interactions. This study aims to examine the relationship between digital distraction and the decline of students’ emotional engagement in educational settings. A Narrative Literature Review (NLR) approach was employed to synthesize findings from scholarly articles, academic books, conference proceedings, and institutional reports published primarily within the last decade. Data were collected from reputable databases, including Scopus, Web of Science, ScienceDirect, SpringerLink, and Google Scholar, and analyzed using narrative thematic analysis. The findings indicate that digital distraction commonly occurs through social media use, instant messaging, entertainment applications, notifications, and media multitasking. These distractions fragment students’ attention, reduce emotional presence, weaken empathy and interpersonal sensitivity, and diminish participation in classroom interactions. Furthermore, digital distraction negatively affects student–teacher communication, peer collaboration, and overall classroom social dynamics. The study concludes that digital distraction represents not only a technological issue but also a significant social-emotional challenge that requires balanced educational strategies integrating technology management, social-emotional learning, and meaningful interpersonal engagement.

reading.interpretation: This study demonstrates that digital distraction has become a significant challenge in contemporary education, extending beyond issues of academic concentration to affect students' emotional engagement and classroom interaction. The review reveals that social media use, instant messaging, entertainment applications, notifications, and media multitasking are the primary sources of distraction experienced by students. These digital interruptions fragment attention, reduce emotional presence, and limit students' ability to engage meaningfully with teachers, peers, and learning activities. The findings further indicate that digital distraction weakens empathy, interpersonal sensitivity, classroom participation, and collaborative learning. Its effects are evident in both student-teacher relationships and peer interactions, contributing to reduced communication quality, lower engagement, and weaker classroom social cohesion. Consequently, emotional focus should be recognized as a crucial dimension of student engagement that is vulnerable to excessive digital interference. To address these challenges, educational institutions should adopt balanced strategies that combine effective technology integration, classroom management practices, social-emotional learning programs, and opportunities for face-to-face interaction. Such approaches can help students develop digital self-regulation while maintaining emotional engagement and meaningful participation in increasingly digitalized learning environments.

abstract_text: This research adopts a human-centered perspective in which artificial intelligence is conceptualized not as a replacement for human cognition, but as an adaptive partner that supports decision-making while minimizing unnecessary cognitive burden. Generation X knowledge workers, typically defined as individuals born between 1965 and 1980, represent a critical yet underexplored demographic in Human–Computer Interaction and artificial intelligence research. Although this cohort occupies a large share of managerial and decision-making roles, they increasingly interact with AI-driven environments not designed with their cognitive or ergonomic profiles in mind, contributing to elevated technostress, cognitive overload, and perceived loss of control. This paper proposes a Human-Centered AI framework that integrates Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) and Adaptive User Experience (AUX) design to mitigate technostress and improve digital wellbeing. The system combines machine learning-based cognitive state inference with real-time interface adaptation and multi-layered explanation mechanisms, including SHAP, LIME, counterfactual reasoning, and natural language generation. A mixed -methods design was adopted, combining structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM) with a controlled within-subject experiment, complemented by a pilot validation with 28 Generation X participants assessing feasibility, usability, cognitive load reduction, and perceived transparency. Despite rapid advances in AI, little attention has been devoted to designing systems that actively support users' cognitive and psychological wellbeing rather than simply optimizing efficiency. This study shifts the focus from technology-centered innovation toward human-centered AI, proposing that intelligent interfaces should function not only as decision-support tools but also as mechanisms for reducing technostress, preserving human cognitive resources, and promoting sustainable digital work environments.

abstract_text:
This study aims to analyze the influence of AI-Native Collaboration and Digital Nomad Policies on Innovative Work Outcomes and examine the role of Work-Life Boundary Management and Digital Wellbeing Capital as moderating variables at PT Saribunga Indonesia. The research method used was a quantitative approach with an explanatory research design. Data were collected through a Likert-scale questionnaire involving 28 employees as respondents using a total sampling technique (census). Data analysis was performed using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM) with the assistance of SmartPLS through evaluation of the outer model and inner model, and hypothesis testing using bootstrapping of 5,000 subsamples. The results showed that AI-Native Collaboration had a positive and significant effect on Innovative Work Outcomes with a path coefficient of 0.514 and a p-value of 0.024. Meanwhile, Digital Nomad Policies, Work-Life Boundary Management, and Digital Wellbeing Capital did not show a significant direct effect on Innovative Work Outcomes. The results of the moderation test also showed that Work-Life Boundary Management and Digital Wellbeing Capital did not moderate the effect of AI-Native Collaboration or Digital Nomad Policies on Innovative Work Outcomes. The research model had high explanatory power with an R² value of 0.881. The study's conclusions indicate that AI-Native Collaboration is the primary factor contributing to increased Innovative Work Outcomes in the studied organizational context, while work policy flexibility and work-life boundary management factors, as well as digital wellbeing, did not yet play a significant role in the research model.
 
Keywords: AI-Native Collaboration, Digital Nomad Policies, Digital Wellbeing Capital, Innovative Work Outcomes, Work-Life Boundary Management

abstract_text: This study investigates the role of artificial intelligence (AI) assistants in teachers' cognitive and metacognitive processes through the lens of cognitive offloading theory. Adopting a phenomenological research design, the study explores how, why, and with what consequences teachers delegate mental tasks to AI. Data were collected through semi-structured online interviews with 17 teachers from various disciplines and analyzed using thematic analysis. Findings reveal that participating teachers regularly use AI assistants for both professional tasks, such as lesson planning, material design, exam preparation, and daily life activities, including information seeking and content creation. Participants perceived AI tools as reducing mental effort and time pressure and increasing their sense of self-efficacy, while their views regarding the effects of AI use on creativity were mixed. However, participatingteachers also demonstrated awareness of the risks associated with over-reliance on AI, particularly its potential to weaken critical thinking and self-evaluation skills, a phenomenon linked to "metacognitive laziness." To mitigate these risks, they employ deliberate strategies such as cross-checking AI outputs with other sources, validating them against prior knowledge, and personalizing content rather than accepting it uncritically. The study concludes that ,according to participants’ accounts, AI assistants function not only as tools for efficiency, but also as resources that participants perceived as potentially influencingteachers’ cognitive habits and perceptions of their professional practice. These findings suggest implications forreconceptualizing AI literacy in teacher education, moving beyond technical proficiency toward fostering metacognitive awareness and self-regulation that empower teachers to make informed decisions about when and how to offload cognition. Participants perceived AI assistants not only as tools for improving efficiency but also as resources that may shape their cognitive habits and perceptions of professional practice. These findings highlight the importance of reconceptualizing AI literacy in teacher education beyond technical proficiency to include metacognitive awareness, critical evaluation, and self-regulation in decisions about when and how to offload cognition.

abstract_text:
Abstract
AI-driven neuromarketing combines behavioural theory, multimodal sensing, statistical inference and machine learning to explain how consumers allocate attention, experience affect and translate internal states into purchase-related decisions. This research book develops an integrated framework that treats gaze, physiological activity, interaction traces, language and observed choice as incomplete but complementary measurements of latent consumer states. It connects experimental design and causal inference with predictive modelling, explainability, calibration, scalable data engineering and responsible governance. Particular emphasis is placed on separating measurement from construct validity, distinguishing prediction from causal explanation, and evaluating models under heterogeneity, missingness and distribution shift. The methodological architecture extends from controlled experiments to real-time analytics and MLOps, while sectoral applications cover retail, e-commerce, media, entertainment, tourism and service experience. Across South Asia, Europe, Africa and the Americas, the framework stresses cultural calibration, privacy-aware deployment, transparent decision support and auditable personalization. The book’s central contribution is a research-to-deployment pathway in which measurement protocols, causal estimands, predictive models, uncertainty diagnostics, governance controls and reproducibility artifacts operate as one coherent neuromarketing system.

abstract_text: Though concerns have been raised about the misuse of AI such as ChatGPT in academic settings, recent research also emphasizes pedagogical potential when its use is carefully guided. Informed by the concepts of desirable difficulty, productive struggle, cognitive offloading, and the theory of planned behavior, the authors designed exploratory interventions during AY2025 to guide Japanese university EFL students’ use of ChatGPT in (a) pre-writing information searches, and (b) AI-supported revision of independently written drafts. Survey data and student assignments highlighted contrasting ways in which AI use was influenced by resource-related factors and task design. The findings suggest how structured, in-class guidance can preserve opportunities for effortful learning while mitigating excessive cognitive offloading to AI. This paper contributes to a theoretical discussion of how AI use can support rather than undermine long-term effortful learning habits in EFL writing. title: From Plausibility to Verifiability: The PEARLS Framework for Developing Epistemic Agency in Generative AI-Mediated Higher Education
preview: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has sharply reduced the cost of producing fluent explanations, syntheses, analyses, code, and recommendations, but it has not reduced the intellectual work required to establish whether those outputs deserve belief or use. abstract_text: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has sharply reduced the cost of producing fluent explanations, syntheses, analyses, code, and recommendations, but it has not reduced the intellectual work required to establish whether those outputs deserve belief or use. This asymmetry creates a plausibility-verifiability gap: an AI-generated artifact can display the linguistic and structural markers of expertise while the evidence, provenance, and limitations needed to warrant reliance remain difficult to inspect. Existing AI literacy and evaluative-judgement frameworks specify broad competencies for critical and responsible engagement, yet students and novice users still need an actionable method for evaluating a particular AI-mediated artifact. To address this gap, this conceptual paper introduces and theoretically grounds the PEARLS framework, an artifact-level verification protocol organized around six interdependent dimensions: Process, Evidence, Access, Reproducibility, Legitimacy, and Source. The framework integrates insights from epistemic cognition, epistemic vigilance, cognitive offloading, calibrated trust, evaluative judgement, and open-science principles to treat AI output as a provisional knowledge claim whose warrant must be assembled and examined. It further advances verification-driven learning as a pedagogical mechanism through which learners develop expertise by iteratively focusing consequential claims, tracing and testing their warrant, judging uncertainty and legitimacy, acting on the results, and reframing subsequent inquiry. Five interdisciplinary cases - psychology theory, educational statistics, computer science, history, and health sciences - demonstrate how the relative emphasis of the six dimensions varies with disciplinary standards and the consequences of error. The paper concludes by deriving implications for assessment design and proposing a research agenda encompassing construct validation, intervention studies, disciplinary calibration, equity, and human-AI interface design. PEARLS is therefore offered as a theoretically informed and practically usable scaffold for preserving human epistemic responsibility as knowledge production becomes increasingly AI-mediated.

abstract_text: This study examined the relationship between digital distractions, students' focus, and academic performance among Grade 6 pupils. Digital distractions, operationally defined in this study as interruptions caused by social media usage, online and offline gaming, video and music streaming, and messaging notifications, were examined in relation to students’ focus and academic performance. This study examined how exposure to digital devices affects learners’ concentration and academic outcomes in an elementary school context. A descriptive-correlational research design was employed, and data were collected through a validated survey administered to 51 Grade 6 pupils from three selected elementary schools using stratified proportional sampling. The findings revealed that students experienced high levels of digital distraction, with messaging applications and chat notifications identified as the most prevalent sources. In terms of student focus, learners demonstrated low focus, suggesting that exposure to digital distractions adversely affects concentration during academic tasks. Regarding academic performance, most students maintained outstanding academic achievement, suggesting that distractions had noticeable but not severely damaging effects on their grades. Statistical analysis further indicated significant relationships between digital distraction and student focus, as well as between digital distraction and academic performance. Overall, the study concludes that digital distractions are prevalent among elementary learners and have significant implications for students’ focus and academic outcomes, underscoring the need for responsible and regulated use of digital technologies in educational contexts.

abstract_text:
Introduction 
                     Writing with generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) can improve a supported product without necessarily strengthening the competence that remains after support is removed. This study examined that distinction through a layer-sensitive account of cognitive offloading. 
                   
                   
                     Methods 
                     In this eight-week quasi-experimental classroom study, 180 Chinese undergraduates from six intact English academic-writing classes entered the study and 168 completed the protocol. Two classes were assigned to each of three conditions: no-AI writing, bounded AI support with compulsory reflection, and open AI collaboration. Students completed a baseline task, three intervention assignments, and a supervised Week 8 independent no-AI near-transfer task. 
                   
                   
                     Results 
                     
                      Open AI collaboration had the highest observed supported-writing mean (
                       M 
                      = 4.02), although the class-clustered open–bounded contrast was imprecise (adjusted difference = 0.21, 95% CI [0.06, 0.36], wild-cluster
                       p 
                      = 0.064). At Week 8, the bounded-support condition showed higher adjusted outcomes than open collaboration in writing quality (difference = 0.27), higher-order thinking (0.35), argument depth (0.42), and independent revision quality (0.39); exact wild-cluster
                       p 
                      values ranged from 0.050 to 0.063. Within the 112 AI-exposed students, open collaboration involved more prompts, greater text incorporation, less self-generated text, and deeper idea and reasoning offloading. An adjusted associative decomposition showed that open collaboration predicted higher aggregate offloading (
                       a 
                      = 0.77,
                       SE 
                      = 0.06), which was associated with lower Week 8 higher-order thinking (
                       b 
                      = −0.45,
                       SE 
                      = 0.08); the bootstrap indirect estimate was −0.34, 95% CI [−0.48, −0.21]. Self-regulated writing attenuated, but did not eliminate, this negative association.
                     
                   
                   
                     Discussion 
                     Because conditions were allocated by only six intact classes and the bounded condition combined delegation restrictions with compulsory reflection, the results are interpreted as classroom-level, mechanism-consistent associations rather than definitive causal effects. The findings distinguish performance achieved with GenAI from competence demonstrated independently after support is removed.

abstract_text: This chapter gives a detailed analysis of embodied AI and its transformational potential in the area of human-robot collaboration, grounded in Agentic AI and the Attention Economy paradigms. There exists a synergy of physical embodiment, real-time decision-making, and multimodal perception in Embodied AI, enabling the robots to execute operations in a state of uncertainty in the absence of humans. Autonomous, context-aware behavior in the form of the Agentic AI idea allows the machines to anticipate, perceive, and respond to the actions of humans in a manner independent of explicit supervision. Simultaneously, according to the Attention Economy, human cognitive load becomes the highest priority, allowing AI systems to harmonize their behavior with the focus and attention of humans. Under an assumed cluttered and dynamic scenario, a controlled experiment validates a modular system framework of perception, agentic decision-making, and attention model modules. Several use cases such as healthcare, Industry 4.0, education, and disaster relief are shown in demonstration, detailing how effective the system can be in maximizing collaboration, efficiency, and safeness. Societal and ethical issues ranging from explanations, privacy, and job displacement to regulating AI are listed as key drivers toward safe AI deployment. Lastly, the chapter concludes with the definition of the trends of the future in multimodal AI and universal regulations toward the enabling of sustainable, ethical adoption in real-world scenarios.

abstract_text: Medical gas pipeline systems are a mission-critical component of healthcare infrastructure because they provide uninterrupted delivery of oxygen, medical air, nitrous oxide, vacuum, and related gases to clinical environments where failures can directly affect patient safety. Conventional monitoring and maintenance practices, while essential, often depend on periodic inspection, fixed alarm thresholds, and manual documentation, which can miss subtle degradation such as slow leaks, sensor drift, intermittent communication faults, and localized performance loss. This chapter presents an integrated framework for AI-enabled instrumentation in medical gas safety that combines sensing, calibration, connectivity, analytics, compliance, and workflow integration into a single intelligent monitoring architecture. The chapter begins by examining the sensing foundation of medical gas systems, including pressure, flow, concentration, and temperature measurement, as well as alarm panel design and redundancy strategies. It then describes calibration, commissioning, and maintenance practices that support measurement fidelity and operational reliability across the system lifecycle. Building on this foundation, the chapter explains how IoT-enabled communication layers and edge-cloud data architectures enable continuous telemetry, remote visibility, and scalable system integration. The chapter further discusses real-time dashboards, alarm prioritization, automated escalation, and workflow integration to ensure that analytic outputs translate into actionable clinical and engineering responses. Finally, the chapter addressescyber security, redundancy, reliability, and the emerging role of digital twins as future enablers of simulation, scenario testing, and hospital-wide safety analytics. Overall, the chapter proposes a practical roadmap for transforming medical gas infrastructure from a reactive utility into a proactive, data-driven safety system that supports resilience, compliance, and improved patient outcomes.

abstract_text: The study aims to understand the impact of artificial intelligence (AI) and virtual reality (VR) on critical thinking (CT) skills of the students and working professionals of Uttarakhand, India. The data was collected from 380 respondents who completed questionnaires, of which 357 were valid respondents and used SmartPLS 4 to perform the partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM) technique. The results indicate that AI and VR can directly enhance students’ critical thinking and boost learning engagement (LE) and cognitive offloading (CO). The study demonstrated the positive effect of learning engagement on critical thinking and significant negative effect of cognitive offloading on critical thinking. All four specific indirect effects were found to be significant, but engagement and offloading effects were largely offsetting. Therefore, the total indirect effects of AI and VR were not statistically significant, implying a mediator effect rather than non-mediating effects. The study combines Student Involvement Theory and Cognitive Load Theory to illuminate the differences in technology -critical thinking outcomes in different contexts. The results imply that access to AI and VR tools is not enough; pedagogical practices that enhance the engagement of learners and reduce over-cognitive offloading should be developed. The model accounted for 16.8% of variance in critical thinking and thus is not an exhaustive model of critical thinking development, but instead, it points to mechanisms.

analysis.methods: This study adopts a quantitative, cross-sectional survey design to examine the associations between emergent digital technologies (artificial intelligence and virtual reality) and cognitive mechanisms (cognitive offloading, learning engagement and critical thinking). A survey approach was selected because it permits simultaneous estimation of multiple direct and indirect paths in a single specification. The theoretical basis for the model is set out in Section 3.1. A convenience sampling method was used. Data were collected through an online survey from students and working professionals engaged in technology-enabled learning environments. The inverse square root method was used to determine the minimum sample [50] : assuming an effect as weak as 0.15, a 5% significance level and 80% statistical power, the method indicated a minimum of 275 responses. A total of 380 responses were collected and 357 were retained for analysis after data cleaning. The realised sample comprised 153 students (42.9%) and 204 professionals (57.1%); the composition is reported in Table 2 . Eligibility required that respondents were currently studying or working in a setting in which AI or VR tools formed part of the learning or training process; no minimum frequency-of-use threshold was imposed. Because exposure was not screened at a defined level, respondents with limited direct experience of either technology may be represented in the sample, and this is declared as a measurement validity limitation in Section 8. Data was collected over two-month period from November 2025 to January 2026 using the structured questionnaire administered through Google forms. The questionnaire was distributed to target respondents through email and personal contact. A total of 400 invitations were distributed, of which 380 responses were received resulting in response rate of 95%. Of the 380 responses 23 responses were excluded because they were incomplete resulting in 357 usable responses for final analysis. To assess potential nonresponse bias, early and late responses were compared on key demographic and study related variables. The result shower no statistically significant differences between early and late respondents, indicating that non response bias was unlikely to materially affect the finding Because all constructs were measured from a single self-report instrument at one point in time, common method bias was assessed by two procedures. Harman's single-factor test was performed first. Exploratory factor analysis using principal components extraction with varimax rotation returned exactly five factors with eigenvalues above unity, matching the five theorized constructs. The first factor had an eigenvalue of 8.585 and accounted for 34.340% of the total variance, well below the 50% threshold. When all items were then constrained to load on a single unrotated factor, that factor again explained 34.340% of the total variance. The five extracted factors collectively explained 70.898% of the total variance. The scree plot in Figure 2 shows the eigenvalue discontinuity after the fifth component. On this evidence, no single factor accounts for a majority of the variance, and common method bias is unlikely to be a material concern. In addition to Harman's test, common method bias was assessed through full collinearity VIF values (Table 3 ) [51] . All values lie well within the 3.3 threshold, further indicating that common method bias is not a concern.
analysis.discussion: This study examined the effects of AI-and VR-based tools on critical thinking, with cognitive offloading and learning engagement modelled as mediators. Both technologies exerted significant positive direct effects on critical thinking, learning engagement had a positive effect, and cognitive offloading a negative one. First, AI-enabled tools had a significant direct effect on critical thinking, consistent with prior findings [16, 54] . VR-based tools likewise showed a direct effect, in line with work arguing that immersive environments raise engagement, stimulate curiosity and thereby support critical reasoning [55-58]. However, the magnitude of these direct effects was modest relative to the effects that AI and VR exerted on the mediators (f 2 = 0.014 and 0.044 for AI→CT and VR→CT, against f 2 = 0.195 and 0.092 for AI→LE and VR→LE). The relationship is therefore better understood as operating mainly through engagement and offloading than as a strong standalone effect. Second, the mediation results clarify a pattern that initially appears counterintuitive. While the total indirect effects were not significant, all four specific indirect effects were. Learning engagement positively mediates the relationships between AI, VR and critical thinking [59, 60] , whereas cognitive offloading mediates them negatively, at nearly equal magnitude and opposite sign. Combined, the two routes cancel, producing a non-significant total indirect effect. Reporting only the total indirect effect would therefore have concealed two real and opposing processes; decomposing into specific indirect effects was necessary to reveal them. The positive mediating effects of engagement align with the longitudinal evidence of the reciprocal effects between engagement with study and CB [5] . The findings hint that if the digital tool is purposefully created to enrich learning activities, then it can also be used to foster students' critical thinking through its richness. Third and most importantly for the broader literature, the CT → CO path makes an adjustment between two directly conflicting prior findings, as detailed in Table 1 . According to Gerlich [8] the act of offloading is detrimental to critical thinking and according to Wang [25] the act of offloading does foster learning of critical thinking through the cognitive self-efficacy. The current outcome, favouring the former and against the latter. This conflict is a useful one (not a awkward one). This model does not contain cognitive self-efficacy as an explicit intervening factor for offloading since it builds one's self-efficacy and persistence, whereas Wang's model does. Reconciliation is contingent-with the shedding of the threat to critical thinking also going is a necessary increase in self-efficacy and/or of self-regulated use. The reconciliation of the two sets of results presented here is a proposed one that has not been tested in the present study, but rests on the premise that, besides, the measurement of self-efficacy was not considered relevant to this study. The most direct extension of this work would be to specify this with an offloading route and self-efficacy route, for testing. Combined, the results suggest a two-way sword effect of using AI or VR which can help develop critical thinking skills, but can also reduce critical thinking skills if used incorrectly or distractedly. Finally, the contribution of the critical thinking is quite limited (only 16.8% of variance): AI, VR and engagement and offloading explained less than one-fifth. This should be read as a substantive limitation of the model rather than as an incidental statistic. Numerous pedagogical, dispositional and contextual determinants of critical thinking are not represented in the framework, and the reported effects, though statistically significant, address only a limited portion of the phenomenon. This study examined the effect of AI-and VR-based tools on learners' critical thinking and the routes through which that effect is carried. Both technologies exert a positive but modest direct effect on critical thinking, while their more substantial influence operates indirectly positively through learning engagement and negatively through cognitive offloading. Because these two indirect routes are of similar magnitude and opposite direction, they offset one another in the total indirect effect, a pattern consistent with competitive mediation. The finding is therefore not that AI and VR fail to influence critical thinking indirectly, but that they influence it through two compensatory mechanisms operating simultaneously. Theoretically, the study integrates Astin's Student Involvement Theory and Sweller's Cognitive Load Theory within a single specification, each licensing one of the two routes, and thereby offers an explanation for why technology-mediated learning produces inconsistent findings across the literature. Practically, the results indicate that AI and VR are neither inherently beneficial nor inherently harmful to critical thinking: their effect depends on how they are integrated into the learning process. The potential use of interactive and participative use to promote engagement seems to foster critical thinking while passive and/or uncritical reliance to promote offloading seems to impair critical thinking. A uniform effect of these technologies cannot be claimed since the influence of these technologies depends upon two interacting psychological mechanisms whose equilibrium is either sharpening or dulling in critical thinking skills for students.
analysis.limitations: While this work fits into the conversation on AI, VR and critical thinking, there are some areas that need to be noted as a limitation. Sampling. The findings are based on convenience sampling, and so may not be generalizable. The external validity would be enhanced with probability sampling. Cross-sectional design. The data were collected at one time only, which precludes making causal inferences. To document the temporal order of engagement, offloading and critical thinking processes, longitudinal designs are needed. Common method variance. All constructs were measured with a single self-report instrument administered at one time point. Although Harman's single-factor test and full collinearity VIF values indicate that common method bias is unlikely to have materially distorted the estimates, a single-source design cannot exclude it entirely. Future work should collect predictor and outcome measures from separate sources or at separated time points. Instrumentation. The artificial intelligence and cognitive offloading scales were both adopted from a single source instrument [8] . Although the discriminant validity evidence reported in Section 5.5 supports their empirical separation, constructs sharing an instrument may share method-specific variance, and independent replication using scales from separate developers would strengthen confidence in the AI→CO estimate. Exposure screening. Eligibility required involvement in a technology-enabled learning setting but imposed no minimum frequency-of-use threshold for AI or VR. Respondents with limited direct experience of either technology may therefore have rated their use, which is a measurement validity limitation. Future studies should apply an explicit exposure criterion or report a sensitivity analysis restricted to active users. Group heterogeneity. The sample pools students and working professionals in a single model. Measurement invariance across these two groups was not tested and no multi-group analysis was conducted, so it cannot be confirmed that the measurement model operates equivalently in both. Future research should conduct MICOM testing followed by multi-group analysis, or restrict the sample to one population. Unmodelled controls. Age, gender and frequency of AI and VR use were not entered into the structural model as control variables. Usage frequency in particular is a plausible confound for every path, and re-estimating the model with these controls is a necessary robustness check. Endogeneity and reverse causality. The design is cross-sectional and single-source, while the theoretical relationships are plausibly reciprocal -engagement may raise critical thinking and higher critical thinking may sustain engagement. Reverse causality therefore cannot be excluded, and all reported paths should be interpreted as associational rather than causal. Future work should apply a Gaussian copula test or an equivalent endogeneity diagnostic. Explanatory scope. The model accounts for 16.8% of the variance in critical thinking. Important determinants -among them prior ability, instructional quality, disciplinary context and assessment design -are not represented. Single-country context. The study reflects a single national setting. Education systems, technology adoption and cultural norms differ across countries and may strengthen or weaken the modelled relationships, so cross-cultural and multi-country replication is recommended. Beyond addressing these limitations, three extensions follow directly from the findings. First, the competing-route account should be tested by specifying cognitive self-efficacy alongside offloading, which would allow the Gerlich-Wang disagreement to be adjudicated within one model. Second, AI literacy and self-regulated learning should be introduced as moderators of the offloading route, since both are central to the sources on which the present argument draws and both are plausible boundary conditions on whether offloading harms reasoning. Third, experimental manipulation of tool configuration -for example contrasting an AI interface that requires justification of accepted output against one that does not -would permit causal inference that the present design cannot support.

abstract_text: The Normalisation of Atrocity and Injustice: AI, Social Media and the Politics of Attention is a Neo-Situationist research polemic examining how artificial intelligence, social media, platform capitalism and the contemporary attention economy reshape questions of agency, responsibility, labour, knowledge, childhood and political judgement. The book develops its argument from a central problem: what becomes normal before society has decided whether it should be normal? It argues that artificial intelligence occupies a politically useful contradiction. AI systems are marketed through the language of reasoning, agency, autonomy and collaboration, yet can be rhetorically reduced to passive tools when questions of authorship, ownership, liability or institutional responsibility become inconvenient. At the same time, increasingly powerful forms of cognitive infrastructure are concentrated within privately governed systems built upon accumulated human language, knowledge, culture and expertise. Drawing on the Situationist tradition, the work extends the critique of the spectacle into algorithmically mediated attention. It examines the normalisation of atrocity through continuous feeds, the commodification of attention, AI-mediated cognitive enclosure, labour displacement and productivity, the attribution of agency and responsibility, childhood exposure to social media and AI, political and military uses of artificial intelligence, and the emergence of increasingly rich psychographic infrastructures. Rather than presenting AI itself as the enemy, the book repeatedly follows the causal chain of ownership, control, benefit, decision and capacity to intervene. The book deliberately combines research evidence with détournement, visual argument, compression, repetition and polemical rhetoric. Its form is intended to reproduce and then interrupt aspects of the attention economy it criticises. It introduces the term Rechenschaftsgeist: the reckoning that begins when an historical moment is forced to account for what it has normalised. The work was developed through sustained collaboration between Eric J. Needham and ChatGPT (Z0), with the AI contribution explicitly disclosed. Responsibility for publication, evidential selection, political and ethical judgement, and the final text remains with Eric J. Needham.

abstract_text: This chapter explores the integration of generative artificial intelligence (AI) in higher education through metacognitive reflection and human–AI interaction. While AI tools like ChatGPT offer educational possibilities for idea generation and drafting, they also pose risks of cognitive overreliance and passive acceptance of algorithmic outputs. Using a qualitative multiple case study at two universities, the research examines how undergraduate and graduate students use AI and perceive its role in learning. Findings reveal patterns: graduate students often use AI as a collaborative partner for higher-order design tasks while undergraduates tend to rely on it for execution-oriented tasks and structural organization. Reflective journaling is highlighted as a tool for making processes visible and fostering self-regulated learning. The chapter concludes with pedagogical implications, suggesting structured scaffolding through models like the 4R framework and process-oriented assessments to cultivate students' epistemic responsibility and critical engagement in AI-integrated environments.

abstract_text: Generative artificial intelligence (genAI) can make complex cognitive tasks easier, but it remains unclear how relying on such support affects people's ability to reason independently afterwards. We investigated whether using genAI to solve a complex reasoning task influences subsequent reasoning, memory, and effort when the technology is no longer available. In a preregistered laboratory experiment with a final sample of 193 participants, we used a three-stage relational reasoning task developed for the study, in which participants learned and reasoned about a network of fictional entities and their relationships. During the first stage, participants completed the task either with or without access to ChatGPT, while performance incentives were independently manipulated. All participants then completed a more complex reasoning task based on the same relational network without genAI support, followed by a memory test. GenAI support improved accuracy during the initial task and reduced perceived difficulty. In the subsequent unaided reasoning task, prior genAI use was associated with some evidence of poorer independent reasoning. GenAI use was also associated with weaker adjustment of effort to incentives and task difficulty once the tool was removed. No clear effects were observed on later memory. Overall, the findings suggest that genAI can facilitate performance while it is available, but may also alter how users process task-relevant information and regulate effort during subsequent independent performance.

abstract_text: This chapter examines how the rapid adoption of generative AI can be incorporated into language teacher education. Theoretical frameworks, such as sociocultural theory, metacognition, critical digital pedagogy and intercultural communicative competence, were drawn upon to provide a theoretical basis for a framework with three orientations (thinking with, against, and beyond AI). These orientations provide a lens through which AI is viewed as a tool for dialogue, as an area of critical reflection and as an opportunity to redesign language teacher education from a human-centered perspective. The chapter synthesizes current conversations on the pedagogical and ethical issues arising from the integration of AI into language teacher education and offers suggestions for incorporating best practices.In summary, the innovative use of AI in language education is advocated as well as placing an emphasis on teacher judgment, learner agency and intercultural awareness in the development and use of AI in language education.
