abstract_text:
Abstract 
                 The integration of Generative Artificial Intelligence (Gen AI) into higher education is reshaping how students learn, reason, and produce knowledge. As learners rely on AI systems for tasks associated with interpretation, synthesis, and problem-solving, cognitive activity is becoming progressively distributed across human and technological systems through processes of cognitive offloading. However, present scholarship has largely framed this development through competing narratives of educational enhancement and cognitive decline, paying limited attention to how its consequences are shaped by institutional conditions, pedagogical practices, and inequalities in knowledge production. Addressing this gap, this paper examines cognitive offloading as a contextually mediated epistemic practice within low-resource higher education environments. The study employs a conceptual and critical analytical methodology to develop a continuum model positioning AI-mediated cognitive offloading between adaptive cognitive augmentation and epistemic dependency. The analysis suggests that Gen AI can expand educational participation, improve access to academic support, and compensate for institutional and infrastructural constraints. However, sustained reliance on AI-generated outputs may weaken reflective judgment, metacognitive engagement, interpretive reasoning, and intellectual autonomy. The paper advances two conceptual contributions. First, it develops the concept of cognitive debt to explain the gradual accumulation of diminished critical engagement resulting from repeated delegation of cognitive labor to AI systems. Second, it introduces the curiosity paradox, whereby technologies that facilitate inquiry may simultaneously reduce the uncertainty, persistence, and exploratory effort that sustain learning. The paper concludes by proposing a context-sensitive framework for AI integration grounded in guided engagement, cognitive resilience, epistemic justice, and the inclusion of knowledge systems.

analysis.methods: This study employs a conceptual and critical analytical methodology to examine cognitive offloading in AI-mediated higher education, with particular attention to low-resource educational contexts. Rather than investigating the phenomenon through experimental or survey-based methods, the study engages in interdisciplinary theoretical inquiry to analyze how Gen AI is reshaping cognition, learning, curiosity, and epistemic agency within contemporary educational environments. This approach is appropriate because the central concerns of the paper, that is, cognitive offloading viz., cognitive debt, curiosity, intellectual autonomy, and epistemic dependency, are considerably conditioned by empirical variables and conceptual and normative questions concerning the nature, purposes, and future of education in an increasingly AI-mediated world. However, conceptual analysis is employed to clarify and examine the relationships among the key constructs informing the study, including cognitive offloading, distributed cognition, cognitive debt, curiosity, epistemic dependency, and pedagogical scaffolding. Critical analysis, in turn, is used to evaluate the educational, philosophical, and political implications of these concepts within AI-mediated learning environments. Thus, instead of testing causal hypotheses, the methodology seeks to interrogate underlying assumptions, identify conceptual tensions, and develop a context-sensitive framework for understanding the opportunities and risks associated with human-AI cognitive relations in higher education. Our choice of this methodological orientation responds directly to limitations identified within the existing literature. Current scholarship on AI in education has generated important empirical insights regarding technological adoption, learning outcomes, and student behavior. However, much of this work remains fragmented across disciplinary boundaries and frequently evaluates AI through binary narratives of enhancement or decline. Consequently, insufficient attention has been given to how cognitive offloading intersect within educational environments characterized by institutional scarcity, infrastructural limitations, and unequal participation in global knowledge production. Addressing these gaps requires an analytical framework capable of integrating insights from cognitive science, educational theory, philosophy of technology, critical AI studies, and decolonial scholarship. Accordingly, the study proceeds through four interrelated analytical stages. Many AI systems are designed to maximize speed, convenience, and cognitive efficiency. Educational environments, however, depend upon processes that often require uncertainty, struggle, revision, and sustained inquiry. Institutions should therefore explore pedagogical models that intentionally preserve forms of productive friction within AI-mediated learning. Examples include requiring students to critique AI-generated outputs, compare multiple responses, justify disagreements with algorithmic recommendations, reconstruct reasoning pathways, and reflect on alternative interpretations. Such practices preserve the "desirable difficulties" associated with durable learning and help prevent the gradual displacement of analytical and interpretive capacities (Bjork et al., 2011) .
analysis.results: Our analysis indicates that cognitive offloading in AI-mediated higher education is best understood as a relational and contextually contingent phenomenon in contrast to a fixed consequence of technological adoption. Its educational significance emerges through the interaction of cognitive practices, pedagogical structures, institutional conditions, and epistemic environments. Four interrelated findings emerge from the analysis.
analysis.discussion: The findings challenge dominant narratives that frame Gen AI in higher education as either an unequivocal catalyst for educational transformation or an inevitable source of cognitive decline. Instead, the analysis shows that the implications of cognitive offloading are contingent upon the institutional, pedagogical, and epistemic contexts within which human-AI interaction occurs. Consistent with broader critiques of technological determinism in educational technology research, the educational significance of Gen AI cannot be understood independently of the social and structural conditions that shape its adoption and use (Selwyn, 2019; Zawacki-Richter et al., 2019) . A central contribution of this study is its reconceptualization of cognitive offloading as a contextually mediated educational practice as against a universally beneficial or harmful phenomenon. In lowresource higher education environments, AI systems frequently function as compensatory cognitive infrastructures that help students navigate structural constraints such as inadequate academic support, overcrowded classrooms, limited library resources, and uneven access to scholarly materials (Altbach et al., 2019) . Under such conditions, the delegation of cognitive labor to AI systems often reflects institutional necessity over intellectual disengagement. This finding extends existing understandings of cognitive offloading by demonstrating that the educational consequences of delegating cognitive tasks are inseparable from broader questions of educational inequality and access (Risko & Gilbert, 2016) . At the same time, the analysis reveals a fundamental tension at the heart of AI-mediated learning. While Gen AI can broaden access to information, academic assistance, and personalized learning opportunities (Kasneci et al., 2023; Luckin et al., 2016) , it may also encourage forms of dependence that weaken the cognitive processes higher education seeks to cultivate. This tension is captured through two interrelated concepts developed and extended in this paper: cognitive debt and the curiosity paradox. Concerning the concept of cognitive debt, the study provides a useful framework for understanding the long-term consequences of sustained reliance on AI-generated outputs. Similar to technical debt in software development, cognitive debt accumulates when immediate gains in efficiency are achieved at the expense of deeper cognitive engagement. Repeated outsourcing of reasoning, synthesis, memory, and evaluative judgment may gradually diminish the cognitive capacities required for independent inquiry and critical reflection (Sm´arason, 2026; Watts, 2025) . Emerging empirical evidence further supports these concerns. For example, and as said earlier, Kosmyna et al. (2025) found that individuals relying heavily on large language models exhibited reduced neural connectivity, weaker memory recall, lower cognitive engagement, and diminished ownership of written outputs compared with those relying on search engines or unaided reasoning. Within higher education, cognitive debt therefore represents a reduction in cognitive effort as well as a potential weakening of intellectual autonomy and epistemic agency over time. Closely related to cognitive debt is the curiosity paradox in AI-mediated learning. Educational theory has long regarded curiosity as a foundational driver of meaningful learning, inquiry, and intellectual development (Dewey, 1938; Loewenstein, 1994) . We have also established that recent scholarship similarly argues that curiosity thrives through exploration, uncertainty, and sustained engagement with unanswered questions rather than the immediate acquisition of information (Mishra & Henriksen, 2025) . Gen AI simultaneously expands and constrains these conditions. On one hand, it lowers barriers to inquiry by providing rapid access to explanations, ideas, and learning resources, thereby enabling students to explore topics that might otherwise remain inaccessible. On the other hand, the immediacy and fluency of AI-generated responses may reduce the productive uncertainty, interpretive struggle, and exploratory persistence through which deeper curiosity develops. In this sense, Gen AI can both stimulate and suppress curiosity by fueling exploration while potentially weakening the very cognitive habits that sustain long-term intellectual inquiry. The significance of these dynamics becomes clearer when viewed through the broader purposes of higher education. Education has traditionally been concerned with the transmission of information and with the cultivation of intellectual autonomy, critical reasoning, reflective judgment, and epistemic agency (Biesta, 2015) . Learning therefore involves active participation in processes of questioning, interpretation, evaluation, and meaning making. The findings suggest that Gen AI can support these educational aims when integrated as a scaffold for learning but may undermine them when it becomes a substitute for cognitive effort. This distinction resonates with sociocultural theories of learning, which emphasize that educational tools should support not to replace the developmental processes through which understanding emerges (Vygotsky, 1978; Wood et al., 1976) . The discussion also highlights the importance of examining AI-mediated cognition through a decolonial lens. Dependence on Gen AI is not simply a cognitive issue but an epistemic and political one. Many contemporary generative systems are trained predominantly on datasets reflecting global North perspectives, linguistic norms, and knowledge traditions. Consequently, increasing reliance on such systems risks reproducing forms of epistemic dependency by privileging dominant knowledge systems while marginalizing local, indigenous, and context-specific forms of knowledge (Birhane, 2023; Couldry & Mejias, 2019; Mohamed et al., 2020) . In low-resource educational contexts, where AI systems often function as primary sources of academic support, this dynamic raises important concerns regarding epistemic justice, knowledge diversity, and intellectual self-determination. These findings consequently reinforce the argument that educational inequalities are not merely material but epistemological. Structural disparities influence both access to educational resources, and whose knowledge becomes visible, authoritative, and cognitively internalized within AI-mediated learning environments. Without critical intervention, AI systems may inadvertently deepen existing asymmetries in knowledge production by positioning globally dominant epistemologies as default sources of intellectual legitimacy (Birhane, 2023; Mohamed et al., 2020) . Against this backdrop, the continuum model developed in this paper offers a more nuanced framework for understanding human-AI educational relations. Surely, it is easier, we assume, to treat cognitive offloading as a condition to be either embraced or resisted, but this model conceptualizes it as a dynamic process situated between adaptive cognitive augmentation and epistemic dependency. The location of AI use along this continuum is influenced not by the technology itself but by the pedagogical, institutional, and epistemic conditions governing its use. Educational environments that promote critical interrogation of AI outputs, metacognitive reflection, contextual reasoning, and active knowledge construction are more likely to position Gen AI as a tool for cognitive augmentation. abstract_text: Generative AI has revolutionized the results of alliteration in higher education industry. These instruments are, nowadays, flag bearers of instant information development and personalised assistance. This study investigates the double impact of Generative AI on the learning engagement and critical thinking of high education students. Utilising secondary sources and thematic exploration, this study has assessed how increased adoption of generative AI has impacted students' active thinking, independent learning, and educational engagement. The outcomes of this study indicated that GenAI can be a functional tool that is a learning facilitator and probable cause of cognitive offloading among learners. This depends on the perspective of learners’ usage of Generative AI. However, this research concludes that Generative AI is a strategic resource for critical thinking but can also impede it when used as a substitute for cognitive effort. authors: Sonam Bansal and Vijay Kumar Lamba

Intelligent tutoring systems, adaptive learning platforms, learning analytics, automated feedback, conversational agents and generative AI are creating new possibilities for personalized and interacti…
abstract_text: Artificial Intelligence (AI) has rapidly evolved from a specialized computational technology into an increasingly important component of higher education, influencing teaching, learning, assessment and academic support. Intelligent tutoring systems, adaptive learning platforms, learning analytics, automated feedback, conversational agents and generative AI are creating new possibilities for personalized and interactive learning. At the same time, the rapid integration of AI has raised important concerns regarding student engagement, critical thinking, academic independence, AI literacy, teacher competence, digital infrastructure and responsible use. Existing research provides evidence of considerable educational potential, but findings remain fragmented across AI technologies, pedagogical approaches, disciplines and learning outcomes. This review critically examines the emerging literature on AI-based pedagogy in higher education, with particular emphasis on its relationship with student engagement and critical thinking. It further investigates the roles of AI literacy, perceived usefulness, teacher competence, AI-related technological-pedagogical knowledge, digital infrastructure and institutional readiness in determining the effectiveness of AI-supported learning. The review is conceptually grounded in Artificial Intelligence in Education (AIED), the Technological Pedagogical Content Knowledge (TPACK) framework, AI literacy and technology-adoption perspectives. The conceptual focus is consistent with the original manuscript, which identified AI literacy, perceived usefulness and digital infrastructure as important antecedents of AI-based pedagogy and positioned student engagement and critical thinking as major educational outcomes. A structured literature-review methodology is adopted to identify, screen, organize and thematically synthesize relevant research, with particular attention to AI-enabled personalization, adaptive learning, intelligent tutoring, generative AI, student engagement, critical thinking, AI literacy and institutional readiness. The review distinguishes between technological interaction and meaningful cognitive engagement, recognizing that frequent AI use does not necessarily indicate deeper learning. Similarly, AI may support critical thinking when used for questioning, comparison, evaluation and reflection, but may weaken independent reasoning when students simply delegate cognitive tasks to AI. The review proposes an AI–Pedagogy–Engagement–Critical Thinking (AI-PECT) framework in which AI capabilities influence educational outcomes through pedagogical mediation and learner agency, while AI literacy, teacher competence, infrastructure, assessment design and ethical governance operate as important contextual conditions. The review argues that the educational value of AI depends less on the presence of AI technology itself and more on how deliberately, critically and responsibly it is integrated into teaching and learning. The findings provide a foundation for educators, institutions and policymakers seeking to move from simple AI adoption toward meaningful, human-centred and intellectually responsible learning.

abstract_text: Abstract Workplace mental health challenges are disproportionately affecting young female knowledge workers, who report elevated levels of stress, anxiety, and emotional strain within high-pressure organisational cultures. Large language model (LLM)-based chatbots have the potential to support positive psychology in the workplace by supporting strengths-based thinking, cognitive reframing, and fostering purpose, gratitude, and optimism. This mixed-methods study investigates how women aged 25–34 are using LLM-based chatbots as digital coping tools within knowledge-intensive work environments. While 82% reported using LLMs for work-related tasks, 29% had used them for workplace mental health support. Participants described LLMs as reducing cognitive load and providing accessible, stigma-free spaces for reflection amid demanding schedules. However, concerns around trust, data privacy, and the absence of human empathy limited deeper engagement, with participants emphasising the need for gender-sensitive and psychologically informed design. Notably, general-purpose LLMs were used more frequently than dedicated mental health apps, suggesting the emergence of dual task–wellbeing roles for workplace AI systems. These findings position generative AI not merely as a productivity tool but as an emergent, informal wellbeing infrastructure, raising important implications for organisational responsibility, ethical AI governance, and the design of inclusive human–AI support systems for young working women.

analysis.methods: The most frequently highlighted theme here was the need for chatbots to reflect the workplace realities of young women, providing support that is both personalised and empathetic, and attentive to genderspecific challenges shaping daily professional experiences. This section outlines the methodological approach used to investigate the ways in which young female workers experience and perceive the use of LLM-based chatbots for workplace mental health support. It describes the ethical considerations, subject scope and guiding research questions, before detailing the research design, participant recruitment process, survey materials, and analytical procedures of the study. The section concludes with an overview of both quantitative and qualitative data analysis strategies. Collectively, this methodology evidences the commitment of the study to rigour and ethical integrity, while affording space for exploring the possibilities and challenges suggested by this emerging area of digital mental health research. Participants were recruited in August 2023 via Prolific 55 , a reputable online crowdsourcing platform recognised as a high-quality, efficient medium through which to conduct behavioural and mental health research. These considerations are vital when nuanced, demographic-specific recruitment and data integrity are central to the research process 56 . Prior to full-scale distribution, seven pilot studies of 45 participants were conducted to determine average completion times; refine question wording; and optimise technical operation. 1. Age 25-34 years (inclusive) 2. Self-identified as female 3. Employed full-time 4. Having residence in the UK Participants received monetary compensation ranging from £1.00 to £1.50 for their time. Of 200 participants who completed the survey, 31 were excluded based on the following predefined criteria: duplicate responses; irrelevant answers to open-ended questions; responses that were overly brief or non-informative, completion times below five minutes; male gender identification; and non-targeted age group. The resulting sample included 169 female workers aged 25-34, representing diverse industries. The largest sectors included human health and social care (16.6%), education (16.6%), and professional, scientific, and technical activities (10.1%). Occupation types skewed towards skilled, non-manual roles: professional (39.6%), associate professional (28.4%), and managerial (14.2%), with sales and customer service accounting for 12.4%. Participants were primarily employed in the private (50.9%) and public (41.4%) sectors, with smaller proportions in non-profit (5.3%) and freelance/self-employed roles (2.4%). Working arrangements included hybrid (49.1%), on-site (36.1%), and fully remote (14.8%). Almost half of participants (45.0%) were employed by large organisations with over 1,000 employees. This sample provides a representative cross-section of young female workers in the UK, encompassing a range of organisational contexts, job roles, and workplace arrangements, and affording a meaningful exploration of mental health experiences and technology adoption behaviours. An online survey format was selected for both practical and methodological reasons. This approach enables efficient recruitment across multiple sectors, simplifying logistics and facilitating timely data collection. Importantly, the online format enhanced participant anonymity, a factor known to be critical when addressing sensitive topics such as mental health, reducing social desirability bias 57 . Meanwhile, the use of open-ended questions within a context of anonymity and convenience encourages participants to articulate nuanced experiences naturally and expansively, complementing quantitative insight in order to better understand the participant's experience of engaging LLM-based tools for mental health purposes, and draw out design implications. Survey development was informed by prior research on workplace mental health, the use of DMHIs broadly, and the use of LLM-based chatbots specifically 5, 31, 37, 38, 58 . Survey items were designed to capture both behavioural engagement and attitudinal drivers of adoption. To complement these structured measures, open-ended questions were included following Braun and Clarke's (2006) qualitative framework, enabling participants to share lived experiences and expectations beyond the constraints of numerical scales. The first part of survey consisted of 20 structured questions, organised into five domains: 1. Demographics: age; gender; industry; job role; organisation type and size; and working arrangement. 2. Perception of workplace mental health supports: managerial support; workplace culture; and employer initiatives. 3. Use of non-DMHIs: experiences and types of non-digital mental health interventions (e.g., physical activity, in-person counselling, mindfulness, and peer support). 4. Use of DMHIs: experiences; types of digital mental health interventions and digital devices (e.g., smartphone applications, wearable devices, or web-based resources); source of discovery; current usage, usage frequency and usage intentions; and willingness to share mental health-related data with employers. 5. Use and perception of LLM-based chatbots: experience using for work and workplace mental health purposes; perception of comfort, trust, willingness to use as a workplace mental health support, privacy concerns, and complementarity with human support; and desired functionality. This was followed by five open-ended exploratory questions: (1) the lived experience of participant workplace mental health challenges; (2) prior experience with DMHIs; (3) the perceived benefits of LLMbased chatbots as a workplace mental health support; (4) the perceived barriers to LLM-based chatbot adoption; and (5) suggestions for feature development to better support the mental wellbeing of young female workers in the workplace. Participants were provided with an anonymous link to a survey hosted on Qualtrics 59 , a secure and widely used platform in social and health research. On accessing the survey, participants were asked to review the information sheet and consent form, marking a confirmation checkbox accordingly, thereby confirming that informed consent was obtained from all participants and/or their legal guardian(s), before completing six sections: ( 1) demographic questions; (2) items on perception of workplace mental health supports; (3) use of non-DMHIs; (4) use of DMHIs; (5) use and perception of LLM-based chatbots; and (6) open-ended questions. After completion, participants were thanked and directed to a confirmation page.

analysis.discussion: This study examined how young female workers in the United Kingdom engage with LLM-based chatbots for workplace mental health support, highlighting both gender-specific and transferable design implications. Participants reported repurposing general-purpose LLMs to manage stress, regulate emotions, and organise workloads, demonstrating user-driven adaptation beyond their initial productivity-oriented purpose. This dual use reflects the evolving role of AI in professional environments, where tools can simultaneously address practical tasks and mental wellbeing. Beyond task support, participants' use of LLM-based chatbots also demonstrated potential to foster positive psychology in the workplace by enhancing resilience, emotional regulation, reflective capacity, and strengths-based coping strategies-aligning with the introduction's emphasis on digital interventions that not only reduce distress but actively cultivate employee engagement and flourishing. Analysis revealed two interrelated dimensions: gender-specific considerations and broader, transferable implications for workplace populations. Although the study focused on young women, many findings are applicable across demographics, particularly regarding the balance of trust, empathetic interaction, practical utility, and hybrid AI-human approaches, consistent with broader digital mental health research. Young female workers actively seek mental health support even in organisations perceived as promoting wellbeing, highlighting the need for gender-and user-sensitive design. Specific stressors identified included imposter syndrome, workplace inequality, burnout, anxiety in hierarchical or male-dominated contexts, and biological influences such as hormonal cycles. LLM-based chatbots that acknowledge these lived experiences are more likely to be perceived as relevant, empathetic, and supportive, suggesting that systems incorporating gender-sensitive guidance may enhance engagement. Prior research indicates that DMHIs tailored to contextual and user-specific factors improve adherence and perceived utility 31, 32 , aligning with Human-Centred Design (HCD) principles that emphasise alignment with social, psychological, and environmental contexts of users 33 . Beyond functional assistance, participants valued empathetic and nuanced communication. Research suggests that women are particularly attuned to relational and emotional cues in both face-to-face and digital interactions 34 . Effective workplace chatbots must therefore extend beyond information provision to acknowledge emotional states, validate experiences, and offer reassurance. Empathy in AI-mediated support has been associated with stronger engagement and greater perceptions of legitimacy and trustworthiness35. In workplace contexts, where psychological safety and perceived judgment are salient, empathetic communication may be critical for adoption 35 . Participants further emphasised integrating chatbots into existing workplace systems, such as workload management tools, while maintaining strong privacy protections. Clear guidance, transparent communication of system limitations, and structured onboarding were seen as essential. These findings align with HCD and the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM), which highlight perceived usefulness and ease of use as central to adoption 33, 36 . When tools are embedded into workflows and endorsed organisationally, they are more likely to be perceived as legitimate components of workplace wellbeing ecosystems. Designing gender-sensitive LLM-based chatbots calls for empirically grounded frameworks that integrate contextual, psychosocial, and biological factors. For employers, integrating chatbots tailored to young women offers a practical avenue to enhance workplace wellbeing and demonstrate commitment to equity and inclusion. Effective deployment requires technological infrastructure, staff training, transparent governance, and alignment with human support systems. At a societal level, investing in empathetic and inclusive AI may help reduce gender-related disparities in mental health and workplace participation, fostering healthier and more equitable professional environments. Responsibly designed chatbots can extend beyond individual support to function as tools of organisational and social change. Alongside gender-specific considerations, participants highlighted transferable challenges influencing adoption across diverse groups. Key barriers included concerns regarding privacy, limited empathy, and the reliability of information and advice. Prior research indicates that reliability fosters cognitive trust, empathy cultivates affective trust, and privacy ensures moral and legal trust. These 'trust factors' provide a multidimensional foundation for technology adoption in sensitive domains such as mental health 37, 38 . The Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology (UTAUT, 2003), and its health technology extensions, consistently show that trust mediates behavioural intention and actual use. For LLM-based technology, reliance on trust is amplified by hallucinations, biases, and unpredictable outputs. Combined with privacy risks, users bear the burden of validating information 39, 40 , highlighting the importance of trust for safe, ethical use. Privacy was the most prominent barrier to uptake, centring on concerns about data storage, access, sharing, and potential misuse of confidential information. Although anonymity was recognised as facilitating disclosure, participants feared data breaches or unintended exposure to managers or colleagues, consistent with literature emphasising confidentiality as critical for DMHI adoption, particularly in workplace contexts where disclosure carries professional risk 12 . Participants expressed ambivalence: while more comfortable sharing sensitive information with LLM-based chatbots than with colleagues, they remained wary of how data might be used or governed. Nearly half reported discomfort sharing personal information, whereas comfort was higher for voluntary or work-related data, such as workload indicators (30.0%) and self-reported stress (29.5%). These findings highlight a central design tension: anonymity can reduce stigma and create a safe reflective space, yet insufficient organisational transparency may erode trust. Robust safeguards, including transparent data policies, end-to-end encryption, and user control, are therefore essential for adoption, consistent with HCD principles emphasising clarity, accountability, and user empowerment 33 . Another uptake barrier was the inability of LLM-based chatbots to replicate human empathy and relational depth. Although LLMs can simulate aspects of cognitive empathy by recognising emotions and offering supportive responses, participants emphasised that the technology cannot match the emotional understanding and interpersonal support by humans 41 . In particular, trust-based 'interhuman bonds' were highlighted as essential not only for effective mental health support, but also for the adoption of the technology 42 . This aligns with Bickmore and Picard's [2005] work on relational agents, showing that users value AI companions primarily when they demonstrate empathy, continuity, and sensitivity to emotional states 37 . Human-AI companionship can complement, but not replace, human support in mental health interventions. LLM-based chatbots function effectively as both task and emotional supports. abstract_text:
Abstract 
                   Contemporary generative artificial intelligence software poses a threat to the development of critical thinking skills that sets it apart from the litany of prior technological developments that have raised similar concerns. This article adopts a metacognitive perspective on critical thinking in order to show that AI poses a risk of a critical thinking “death spiral” where AI use degrades critical thinking skill and thereby induces further harmful use. While the evidence on the harmful effects of cognitive offloading on critical thinking is not yet definitive, this article supports the case that AI risks undermining critical thinking abilities by appealing to two lines of evidence. The first is the alignment of features of contemporary AI software with psychological biases that will incline us to trust AI more as our reasoning capacities are degraded. The second draws on social epistemology to show that in the case of expertise identification, consideration of opposing perspectives, and use of evidential “stoppers,” AI undermines social practices and conventions that are constitutive of critical thinking. In light of these considerations, a precautionary principle requires that we do not teach AI skills as part of critical thinking skill development, at least until such time as we have stronger empirical evidence on how to do so without eroding the metacognitive capacity to recognize the right contexts for using rational strategies.

abstract_text:
Abstract 
                 This study investigates mechanisms and predictors associated with patterns and frequency of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) use among pre-service teachers. Traditional technology acceptance models often pay limited attention to context-specific issues such as cognitive offloading and institutional conditions for transparent AI use. Structural Equation Modeling (SEM) was applied to a subsample of active GenAI users (N = 629) drawn from a broader institutional sample of pre-service teachers (N = 695). The UTAUT framework was extended by incorporating perceived rules clarity, psychological safety, self-reported cognitive offloading, and pedagogical readiness conceptualized as AI-TPACK self-efficacy. The results indicate a strongly efficiency-driven pattern of GenAI use: Performance Expectancy (PE) emerged as the only significant UTAUT predictor of usage frequency (β = 0.66, p < 0.001), whereas Effort Expectancy, Perceived Academic Authority Influence, and Facilitating Conditions showed no significant independent associations. Perceived rules clarity was strongly associated with psychological safety (β = 0.61, p < 0.001). Usage frequency was positively associated with self-reported cognitive offloading (β = 0.55, p < 0.001). AI-TPACK self-efficacy was positively associated with performance expectancy of GenAI (β = 0.20, p < 0.001), but it was not directly associated with lower self-reported cognitive offloading (β = 0.01, p = 0.839). These findings suggest that pre-service teachers’ perceived pedagogical readiness to work with AI may increase performance expectations, but does not automatically translate into lower self-reported reliance on GenAI for cognitively demanding study tasks. The study highlights the need for teacher education programmes to combine clear institutional rules, transparent AI-use practices, and metacognitive AI literacy.

analysis.methods: The study employs a quantitative cross-sectional survey design. Its aim is not only to provide a descriptive analysis of the use of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI), but primarily to test complex relationships between latent variables using Structural Equation Modeling (SEM). This approach enables robust testing of a theoretical model that integrates an adapted technology acceptance framework (UTAUT) with pedagogical and psychological constructs: AI-TPACK, cognitive offloading, and psychological safety. Data were collected through an online questionnaire survey administered via the MS Forms platform. The target population consisted exclusively of students enrolled in teacher education programmes, that is, pre-service teachers, at the Faculty of Education, Masaryk University. Data collection targeted students in these programmes across all forms of study, both full-time and combined, including lifelong learning programmes aimed at obtaining a teaching qualification. The instrument was distributed through official institutional communication channels using the university information system between 3 January 2026 and 17 February 2026. Participation was voluntary, anonymous, and without any external incentives. The average completion time was 9 minutes and 33 seconds. The questionnaire began with informed consent and emphasized that the use of GenAI was not normatively evaluated in the context of the study, thereby reducing the likelihood of social desirability bias. The questionnaire was distributed by e-mail to the entire population of students in teacher education programmes (N = approximately 4,300). Data collection yielded 695 valid responses, representing an estimated response rate of approximately 16%. The study uses a large institutional sample of students in teacher education programmes at a single faculty of education. However, given the voluntary nature of participation and the response rate of approximately 16%, the risk of non-response bias cannot be excluded. The electronic data collection tool did not allow incomplete responses to be submitted for key constructs, thereby preventing the occurrence of missing values (missing data = 0%). Given the absence of missing values in this analytical sample, it was not necessary to test missingness mechanisms (MCAR/MAR/MNAR) or to apply advanced imputation techniques, such as FIML. The original dataset contained 698 responses. Systematic data cleaning was subsequently conducted. Three cases were excluded from the analysis due to extreme and invalid values indicating careless completion, specifically unrealistic age values. The final sample for analysis therefore consisted of N = 695 pre-service teachers in full-time and combined forms of study. The respondents' mean age was M = 24.3 years (SD = 6.62), ranging from 18 to 57 years. The higher maximum age and higher standard deviation are due to the presence of students in combined forms of study and in lifelong learning programmes, which is typical of Czech faculties of education. Of the total number of 695 respondents, women constituted the majority (n = 523; 75.3%), whereas men accounted for a smaller share of the sample (n = 172; 24.7%). The marked predominance of women in the sample (75.3%) is consistent with the national trend of feminization of the teaching profession and the demographic composition of faculties of education in the Czech Republic. In terms of study phase, the largest share consisted of students in bachelor's degree programmes (52.2%), followed by students in follow-up master's programmes (30.2%) and five-year master's programmes (17.6%). The detailed demographic composition of the research sample is summarized in Table 1 . The datasets analysed during the current study are not publicly available due to the need to protect respondents' privacy, but may be made available from the corresponding author upon reasonable request.
analysis.discussion: This study aimed to examine the predictors and mechanisms of generative artificial intelligence This study examined the relationships between the use of generative artificial intelligence, technology acceptance constructs, perceived clarity of institutional rules, psychological safety, AI-TPACK selfefficacy, and self-reported cognitive offloading among pre-service teachers. The results suggest that GenAI use in teacher education cannot be understood merely as a matter of technical availability or general digital competence. In the tested model, Performance Expectancy emerged as the dominant factor associated with usage frequency (β = 0.658, p < 0.001), whereas Effort Expectancy, Perceived Academic Authority Influence, and Facilitating Conditions were not independent statistically significant predictors. GenAI use in this sample is therefore associated primarily with the perceived usefulness and efficiency of the tool. A second important finding is the strong positive association between perceived clarity of institutional rules and students' psychological safety when using GenAI (β = 0.607, p < 0.001). This result supports the conclusion that institutions should not leave GenAI use under implicit, inconsistent, or individually interpreted expectations. Clear rules alone do not resolve all issues of academic integrity, but they create conditions for more transparent communication about when AI use is legitimate, when it requires disclosure, and when it already replaces the student's own work. The results further show a positive association between the frequency of GenAI use and self-reported cognitive offloading (β = 0.554, p < 0.001). This relationship cannot be understood as direct evidence of a decline in cognitive abilities or learning quality, but it suggests that more intensive GenAI use may, for some students, be associated with a higher tendency to delegate certain study-related cognitive operations to an external tool. This points to a key pedagogical challenge: distinguishing the productive use of GenAI as support for learning from situations in which the tool replaces processes required for understanding, argumentation, and professional judgement. The pattern of relationships between AI-TPACK self-efficacy, Performance Expectancy, and cognitive offloading is particularly important. AI-TPACK self-efficacy was positively associated with Performance Expectancy (β = 0.197, p < 0.001), but was not significantly associated with lower levels of self-reported cognitive offloading (β = 0.013, p = 0.839). This result suggests that declared pedagogical readiness to work with GenAI may be linked to higher Performance Expectancy of the tool, but in this model it did not emerge as a factor associated with lower offloading. The supplementary analysis also showed a substantial difference between students' self-efficacy for personal study-related AI use and for its didactic integration into future teaching (Cohen's d z = 1.59). In other words, among pre-service teachers, personal experience with AI does not automatically translate into confidence that they can integrate it meaningfully and didactically into teaching. Two practical implications for teacher education follow from these findings. First, the development of AI literacy should not be reduced merely to the technical operation of tools or to general training in digital competencies. The preparation of pre-service teachers should also include a metacognitive and ethical dimension: the ability to recognize when AI supports learning, when it merely accelerates routine work, and when it may replace cognitive processes that should be part of one's own learning. Second, institutional policy should combine clear institutional rules with a safe space for transparent disclosure of AI use. In connection with the discussion on academic integrity, Academic Integrity Reporting (AIR) appears to be a suitable framework, shifting attention from mere detection to disclosure of use, interpretation of intent, feedback, and remediation (Peterson, 2025; An et al., 2025) . In this conception, the role of instructors is not limited to sanction-based control, but also includes guidance, critical validation, and support for responsible AI use. Institutional support should therefore aim to create conditions that may strengthen students' psychological safety and enable transparent disclosure of AI use to become part of dialogic assessment rather than a stigmatizing admission (AlBlooshi, 2026; An et al., 2025) . The study therefore suggests that it is important not only to teach students how to use GenAI, that is, to build AI-TPACK, but also to develop a responsible approach to their own learning. Future research should further test the identified relationships using longitudinal or experimental designs and complement self-report data with more objective indicators of learning quality, process data, or analyses of student outputs. Particular attention should also be paid to the design of academic tasks that allow GenAI to be meaningfully integrated without replacing key phases of learning, as well as to the group of students who consciously reject AI for ethical, environmental, or professional reasons.
analysis.limitations: The results of this study must be interpreted with awareness of its methodological, contextual, and conceptual limitations. First, the research is based on a cross-sectional design and uses self-report instruments. Although Structural Equation Modeling makes it possible to test theoretically specified relationships between latent variables, it does not allow strict causal conclusions to be drawn. The identified relationships should therefore be understood as directional associations interpreted within the proposed model, rather than as evidence of causal mechanisms. Since all main variables were measured through a single questionnaire at the same time point, common method bias cannot be fully excluded. The study is also based on data from a single faculty of education, which, together with the specific Czech cultural and institutional context, limits the generalizability of the results to different national, institutional, or educational systems. Given the voluntary nature of participation and the response rate of approximately 16%, the risk of non-response bias must also be acknowledged, as students with different levels of interest in GenAI, different experiences with these tools, or more pronounced attitudes may have been represented unevenly in the sample. Second, the study did not measure objective learning outcomes, the quality of student work, or the actual processes of working with GenAI. The observed relationship between frequency of use and self-reported cognitive offloading therefore cannot be interpreted as evidence of an actual "cognitive cost" of GenAI, a decline in critical thinking, or deterioration in academic performance. To examine these effects more directly, a longitudinal, experimental, or mixed-methods design would be necessary, including objective learning outcomes, process data, or analysis of student outputs. A major conceptual limitation is also the fact that the instrument used does not allow for a fine-grained distinction between adaptive offloading, that is, the strategic delegation of routine load in order to free up capacity for more complex cognitive operations, and maladaptive offloading, in which GenAI replaces one's own understanding, argumentation, or independent task solving. Similarly, AI-TPACK in this study was operationalized as self-efficacy, not as an objectively measured pedagogical, technological, or ethical competence. The interpretation of the results is further limited by the marginal fit of the structural model and by the rapidly changing GenAI environment, in which tools, institutional rules, and student practices are evolving quickly.

abstract_text: Abstract The human–robot ratio is a useful design heuristic for supervisory robot control. However, advances in AI, computation, and reliable autonomy enable existing systems to extend beyond hierarchical supervision to more flexible organizations of interdependent team members. The human–robot ratio can be misleading for such organizations, so there is a need for a new way to understand teams of interdependent humans, robots, and AI agents. We propose the attention‐demand economy , a graph‐theoretic abstraction in which agents generate and transform attentional demands subject to bounded capacity. This abstraction exposes nonlinear scaling behavior, cascading supervisory requirements, and coordination bottlenecks that are masked under models that rely solely on the human–robot ratio. We demonstrate how the model can be used to (1) develop new system‐level metrics and (2) discover the source and extent of cascading failures. This paper also shows how a radar chart can be used to understand the overall difficulty of managing a human–robot team. The paper briefly demonstrates how the radar chart can be used to design the attention‐demand model. The primary message of this paper is a call to shift from optimizing human–robot ratios to designing organizations with justified attention flows.

abstract_text: The rapid integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) into education has transformed the way students learn, solve problems, and access information. AI-powered tools such as ChatGPT, Gemini, Microsoft Copilot, and intelligent tutoring systems have emerged as valuable learning companions, providing instant explanations, personalized guidance, and academic support. However, the increasing dependence on these technologies has raised concerns about cognitive offloading, a phenomenon in which individuals rely on external tools to perform cognitive tasks that would otherwise require memory, reasoning, or critical thinking. This paper provides an analytical review of recent research to examine whether AI is causing students to think less or enabling them to learn differently. By analyzing existing studies, the paper explores the impact of AI-assisted learning on critical thinking, memory retention, problem-solving abilities, creativity, academic performance, and learner autonomy. The findings indicate that while AI can enhance personalized learning, improve accessibility, and reduce cognitive workload, excessive dependence may weaken deep learning, independent reasoning, and long-term knowledge retention. The study concludes that AI should be viewed as a supportive educational partner rather than a replacement for human thinking. A balanced approach that combines AI-assisted learning with active cognitive engagement is essential to ensure meaningful learning and the development of higher-order thinking skills in the age of artificial intelligence. Keywords: artificial intelligence; AI in Education; Cognitive Offloading; Critical Thinking; Student learning

abstract_text: The issue of academic stress and constant connectivity to digital devices is a growing concern in higher education, and students' reactions to this stress are likely to impact their engagement, learning experiences and academic results. While there has been some scholarship on academic stress, on the use of the smartphone, on digital distraction, and on engagement with learning, there has been less scholarship on how these factors are linked and intertwined as part of the contemporary university learning environment. This gap is filled by this qualitative study that uses an interpretivist approach to explore the scholarly literature on how academic stress, digital distraction, student engagement, and learning outcomes relate. This study uses documentary analysis and thematic analysis of the existing peer-reviewed literature with an emphasis on literature from the past few years in higher education, educational psychology and digital-learning scholarship. The four interconnected patterns revealed by the thematic synthesis include: academic stress as a demand that reduces cognitive and emotional resources; digital distraction as a competing demand that fragmentates attention and can lead to disengagement; students' engagement as a learning process which is mediated by behavioral, emotional, and cognitive conditions; and learning outcomes as a result of the cumulative interaction between the demands of academic stress and the self-regulatory resources of students. In recent times, there's also growing evidence that overuse of the smartphone and digital multitasking can have a negative impact on academic performance, while strategic and goal-oriented technology use can enhance engagement (Martin et al., 2025; Troll et al., 2021). The literature also indicates that academic stress can adversely affect engagement and academic functioning, yet the relationship between academic stress and the respective outcomes can vary depending on the contextual and individual resources (Wunsch et al., 2021). Findings align with a demands–resources perspective of student wellbeing and engagement, suggesting that a combined analysis of academic and digital pressures is relevant. In practice, the study highlights the importance of institutional strategies that rely on student-centered engagement with the subject, a supportive learning environment, digital self-regulation, and workload management.

The synthesis suggests that academic pressure and technology use are not two distinct effects on learning, but rather they have educational meaning in how they interplay with a student's attention, feelings, motivation, ability to self-regulate, and engagement with learning. The main point is that academic pressure may diminish the psychological resources that support longer-term learning and digitally mediated distractions can further break them down. These pressures can build up, impacting on engagement in behaviour, emotions and cognition, which can have implications for concentration, learning retention, motivation, perseverance and learning quality generally. The evidence, however, refutes the technological determinism and the idea that academic stress is always and everywhere a source of poor learning. The implications vary significantly based on context, coping skills, digital behaviours, pedagogical approaches, and institutional support (Hsieh, 2025; Nkomo et al., 2021; Wunsch et al., 2021) . Based on the thematic synthesis, engagement seems to play a special role in this relationship. Students who are academically stressed might be emotionally drained, on the other hand, notifications, social media, entertainment, and multitasking can vie for focused attention that is needed for sustained academic processing. The findings of this study prove that mobile-phone distraction can affect students' immediate recall ability, highlighting the need to safeguard students' attentional resources when learning ( Chen et al., 2025) . But it can also enable communication, collaboration, information and meaningful participation when integrated purposefully into learning activities, through digital technology (Nkomo et al., 2021) . What is important is not the technology itself but whether its use facilitates purposeful engagement or creates cognitive and behavioral competing demands. Theoretically, the study is an integrated interpretation of student learning in discussing the student learning process by integrating Stress and Coping Theory, Cognitive Load Theory, Self-Regulated Learning Theory and Student Engagement Theory. These viewpoints collectively imply a learning outcome is forged through the dynamic interplay of academic requirements, coping capacities, attentional abilities, regulatory mechanisms, and involvement with learning contexts. This is a holistic view, which goes beyond looking at academic stress, smartphones or engagement as stand-alone variables. It also emphasizes the need to think about the kinds of engagement that are not necessarily the same as the kinds of learning that it is assumed they will bring. The conceptualization and measurement of engagement in technology-mediated learning (TML) has also been found to be a lot different across existing studies (Nkomo et al., 2021) . The development of behavioural participation, emotional involvement, and cognitive investment in a changing academic and digital environment should therefore be explored and researched further in higher education. The applications are as significant. Universities should steer clear of policies that only ban the use of the cell phone or that blame students for distracting themselves. Rather, institutions should put in place comprehensive wellbeing and learning strategies that integrate wellbeing and stress-management, digital self-regulation, healthy technology, distraction-aware learning spaces, supportive teaching and institutional wellbeing policy. Academic advising and counseling services can be used to provide effective suggestions for adapting to workload, tests, procrastination, and competing demands. Teachers can create learning tasks that promote continued engagement without undue disruptions to technology. Institutions can also offer guidance on how to manage notifications, practice focused learning, use social media responsibly, and how to balance connect and recover. Such interventions should take into account the fact that students' self-regulatory skills are shaped by their academic context and that whilst selfcontrol may be a personal responsibility, it is also a contextually influenced skill. The results highlight that students are aware of the importance of making informed digital habits a habit for themselves. Adjusting to a better environment can be achieved by silencing unnecessary notifications, setting periods for focused study, limiting technology use during leisure time, organizing workloads, taking breaks when necessary, and seeking assistance if workloads become too high. However, individual strategies should supplement not supplant institutional responsibility. Universities play an important role in developing realistic workloads, facilitating assessments in a supportive manner, providing easy access to counselling, psychologically supporting classrooms and establishing a learning environment that acknowledges students' cognitive and emotional needs. There are a number of caveat. The study was a qualitative one of the type documentary and so relied solely on previous studies of the students and on secondary literature. The synthesis is not able to identify cause and effect links among academic stress, digital distraction, engagement, and learning outcomes. Second, because of the varying definitions, measurement tools, educational setting, and methodology applied in the existing literature, it is not easily possible to compare the results. Third, while this review was primarily based on recent scholarship, the evolving technology landscape of digital makes it possible that evidence can become outdated as new platforms, applications, and patterns of technology use emerge. Finally, the credibility of documentary interpretation is always dependent upon the use of researcher judgements, even when such efforts have been made as systematic source selection, thematic comparison, and reflexivity. Documentary synthesis should thus be complemented by qualitative interviews and focus groups which would give further insight into how students themselves construe academic pressure, digital distraction, coping, and engagement, and, hence, how they speak about them. Longitudinal research can explore these relationships over the semesters and over testing periods more of the time than cross sectional research. Cross-cultural studies are also required since the academic and technological practices, institutional support systems and conceptions of students' wellbeing differ between societies. This study might provide information on the extent to which the patterns found in this study may be widely generalizable or strongly influenced by specific educational and cultural environments. Finally, the study findings suggest that to enhance learning outcomes in a digitally saturated environment in higher education, attention must be given to the entire learning ecology of the student. Academic stress and digital distractions should be treated together as they can merge in the way students engage with the digital world. abstract_text: The integration of AI in higher education presents both opportunities and challenges, reshaping how students learn, collaborate, and produce knowledge. While AI offers benefits such as personalized feedback and expanded access to information, it also introduces risks, including cognitive offloading and the potential erosion of critical thinking. This chapter advocates for a shift towards critical AI literacy, which extends beyond technical proficiency to encompass analytical evaluation, ethical engagement, and metacognitive reflection. Set within the context of an online asynchronous course redesigned to prepare students for academic success with AI technology, the chapter explores design experiences, implementation strategies, and their implications. Further, the authors distill a framework for learning experience design focused on cultivating AI literacy. The chapter underscores the need for reflective engagement with AI and the development of pedagogical frameworks to ensure students are prepared for responsible, thoughtful participation in an AI-mediated world.

venue: International Journal of Computer Information Systems and Industrial Management Applications
preview: The study investigates how social media notification design shapes young consumers’ emotional and behavioural responses across the dominant platforms of Instagram, Facebook, YouTube and Twitter. Extending affect infusion theory, interruption science and digital choice architecture, the research introduces and validates micro-regret as an immediate, interruption-induced emotional reaction that arises prior to cogniti…
abstract_text: The study investigates how social media notification design shapes young consumers’ emotional and behavioural responses across the dominant platforms of Instagram, Facebook, YouTube and Twitter. Extending affect infusion theory, interruption science and digital choice architecture, the research introduces and validates micro-regret as an immediate, interruption-induced emotional reaction that arises prior to cognitive message processing. A cross-sectional survey of 300 young Indian social media users is analysed through structural equation modelling. Results demonstrate that four notification design attributes; frequency, timing, modality and persuasive message framing significantly increase micro-regret, which in turn negatively affects brand attitude and purchase intention while elevating disengagement behaviours. Mediation analyses confirm micro-regret as a central affective pathway linking design level features to downstream consumer outcomes. The study presents novel theoretical contributions by reconceptualising regret as a pre-decisional micro-emotion, reframing notification design as an affective architecture, and positioning disengagement as an emotional self-preservation strategy. Managerial implications highlight the need for emotionally sensitive notification systems, reduced digital intrusiveness and ethical attention practices. The research advances an emotionally grounded understanding of digital consumer behaviour in a hyper-connected environment.

title: The Unpriced Externality: Toward a Data and Attention ESG (DAESG) Framework for AI Governance
preview: Digital ecosystems collapse the same way physical ecosystems do: through extraction that outpaces regeneration. abstract_text: Digital ecosystems collapse the same way physical ecosystems do: through extraction that outpaces regeneration. This paper argues that attention extraction and data-commons depletion constitute unpriced externalities in AI and platform governance, analogous to the unpriced carbon externalities that preceded the emergence of environmental, social, and governance (ESG) accounting. Two extraction vectors are identified: attentional extraction, evidenced by engagement-maximizing design features now subject to regulatory scrutiny, including the European Commission's July 2026 preliminary finding that Meta's Facebook and Instagram breach the Digital Services Act through addictive design; and data-commons extraction, evidenced by model collapse, the documented degradation of AI systems trained on recursively generated synthetic data. The paper argues that both vectors reflect a deeper structural pattern: a decoupling of reward from risk, in which the party capturing the value of extraction is not the party bearing its cost. Building on this diagnosis, the paper proposes DAESG: a three-layer accountability framework, comprising disclosure, standards, and capital allocation, structured to give financial governance functions a basis for treating digital ecosystem extraction as a material, disclosable, and manageable risk. The paper distinguishes DAESG from existing “Digital ESG” (DESG) literature, which addresses how digitalization improves corporate ESG performance rather than the extraction risks of digital ecosystems themselves.

This paper has proposed DAESG as a first structured response: a three-layer disclosure, standards, and capital allocation framework, explicitly distinguished from the existing DESG literature, intended to give financial governance functions a working basis for treating digital ecosystem extraction as a risk that can be measured, limited, and, through capital allocation, re-coupled to the party responsible for generating it. title: From Gradual Release of Responsibility to Gradual Release of Technology: A Case for the Staged Use of AI in Formal Education
abstract_text: Debate over the role of generative artificial intelligence in formal education is marked by sharply divergent claims about its effects on student learning. Much of this disagreement reflects a failure to distinguish immediate performance gains from durable learning. This article addresses a central gap in the literature by focusing on when and how students should be permitted to rely on AI. It introduces the Gradual Release of AI-Technology (GRAIT) model, extending Pearson and Gallagher’s gradual release of responsibility to the staged use of cognitively substantive AI-technologies in formal education. The model distinguishes gradual release of responsibility, which concerns who performs the cognitive work, from gradual release of technology, which concerns when and how that work may be scaffolded, augmented, or offloaded. Three phases are proposed: independent cognition, where foundational knowledge and skill are developed without AI substitution; shared (entangled) cognition, where AI is introduced through constrained, teacher-guided interaction; and offloaded cognition, where learners strategically delegate and reallocate aspects of thinking once risks to learning are minimal and opportunities emerge elsewhere. Progression depends on demonstrated knowledge, skill proficiency, and epistemic readiness. The central question is not whether students should use AI, but who should use it, when, how, and under what conditions it should be embraced or avoided.

This randomized controlled experimental study examined the impact of intermittent digital distraction on cognitive executive functions within simulated social and work environments. The primary objective was to evaluate potential cognitive interference induced by audiovisual stimuli across behavioral (error rate), neurophysiological (spectral EEG parameters), and subjective (perceived workload via NASA-TLX) dimensions. The experimental protocol utilized a battery of psychodiagnostic tasks assessing working memory (Dual N-back), inhibitory control (Stroop task), and selective attention (d2-R), synchronized with continuous 7-channel EEG recording via the LSL protocol. Data were analyzed using Generalized Linear Mixed Models (GLMM), ANCOVA, and Spearman partial correlations. analysis.methods: The scientific research is conceived as a complex experimental design carried out in a controlled environment of a psychological laboratory with the aim of objectifying the impact of intermittent digital distraction on executive functions in a heterogeneous sample of students and employees. The main methodological pillar is the integration of a proprietary software application that synchronizes behavioral psychodiagnostic tasks (Dual N-back, Stroop test) with continuous neurophysiological recording using a 7-channel EEG system Brain Products X.on. The experimental procedure simulates common digital interference in real time through standardized audiovisual notifications with an intensity of 60 dB, which are inserted into the process at pseudo-random intervals. The accuracy of data collection is ensured by the LSL protocol, which allows for rigorous segmentation of neurophysiological markers, namely spectral analysis of fm-Theta and Alpha rhythms, as well as analysis of event-related potentials (P300 amplitude). Objectively measured parameters of executive error rate and reaction times are supplemented in the final phase with subjective scaling of mental load using the NASA-TLX questionnaire and measurement of residual capacity of selective attention using the d2-R test. The research sample ( n = 87) consisted of male ( n = 12) and female ( n = 18) psychology teachers aged 19–24 (AM = 21.4; SD = 1.2) from the University of Constantine the Philosopher in Nitra, who were selected for our research by purposive sampling. Our research also included male ( n = 16) and female ( n = 13) managers from various companies aged 28–54 (AM = 41.2; SD = 7.8) who participated in the research based on an online call. Ordinary employees from various companies ( n = 28) aged 24–58 (AM = 36.7; SD = 9.4) also participated in the research. We randomly divided the research participants into an experimental ( n = 45) and a control ( n = 42) group by drawing lots. The study took place in the psychological laboratory at the Department of Educational and School Psychology, Constantine the Philosopher University in Nitra, Slovakia. Data collection was carried out over a period of 4 months, from October 2024 to March 2025. The laboratory environment was sound-attenuated, temperature-controlled ( 21 ∘ C − 22 ∘ C ), and maintained under constant artificial lighting to minimize external sensory noise. The experimental protocol consisted of a battery of five methods ordered by cognitive demand and measurement goal, with an emphasis on objectifying working memory and inhibition processes. The duration of the measurement for one participant was 30 min. This multimodal task is considered one of the most demanding paradigms for measuring working memory ( Jaeggi et al., 2008 ). It requires simultaneous processing of auditory and visual stimuli, while activating the fronto-parietal network, especially the dlPFC and ACC ( Kerns et al., 2004 ). The method tests the limited capacity of working memory slots ( Cowan, 2001 ) through the processes of updating, inhibition and attention switching. A multidimensional rating scale ( Hart, 2006 ) serves to objectify the subjective perception of cognitive load. It tracks six dimensions: mental, physical and time demands, performance, effort and frustration. The regression coefficient for the difference between groups remained non-significant [ b = −6.91, SE = 10.11, t (77) = −0.68, p = 0.496, 95% CI (−27.04, 13.22)] after controlling for all covariates. Among the included covariates, age ( p = 0.461), gender ( p = 0.944), education ( p = 0.675), and accuracy in the Stroop task ( p = 0.129) showed no significant effect. In contrast, accuracy in the Dual N-back task was a significant predictor of concentration performance [ F (1,77) = 4.64, p = 0.034, partial n 2 = 0.57, b = 54.70, SE = 25.40, t (77) = 2.15]. analysis.discussion: The interpretation of the findings in the framework of the presented scientific research brings a comprehensive view of the dynamics between digital interference and the executive apparatus of the human brain. When analyzing the first research question (RQ1), which examined the error rate in tasks focused on working memory and inhibitory control under the influence of audio-visual distraction, the results indicate a remarkable ability of short-term adaptive resilience of the executive system. Although Ward et al. (2017) postulate that the suppression of irrelevant stimuli itself consumes a critical amount of energy and leads to cognitive drain, our participants were able to maintain performance accuracy even under experimental conditions. This phenomenon can be explained through the lens of Kurzban et al.’s (2013) cognitive effort model, according to which subjective psychological experience and mobilization of internal resources enable the suppression of distractors without immediate performance degradation. In practice, it was shown that participants perceived digital notifications as unwanted noise and consciously increased cognitive input to eliminate the error rate, which is also confirmed by the observed “floor effect” in the Stroop task. However, the higher error rate in the Dual N-back test compared to the Stroop test ( p < 0.001) indicates that the working memory updating processes are more executively demanding than pure motor or cognitive inhibition, although in neither case did distraction cause system collapse. Reflecting the findings of Aron et al. (2014) , the absence of prolongation of reaction times suggests that the hyperdirect rIFG-STN pathway was not paralyzed by the presence of digital stimuli, which indicates the stability of cognitive control across demographic covariates such as education or gender, thereby partially correcting the assumptions of Knox and Wolohan (2014) about the influence of cognitive reserve on short-term resilience. In the second research question (RQ2), which monitored the stability of concentration in the d2-R test after exposure to distractions, it was shown that cumulative cognitive fatigue did not leave a significant trace in the subsequent selective attention ability ( p = 0.496). This result is scientifically intriguing, especially in the context of Cowan’s model (2011), which assumes that the suppression of distractors occupies slots in working memory, which theoretically should lead to subsequent exhaustion. However, our data suggest the presence of cognitive plasticity and compensation ( Ding et al., 2025 ), where the increased alertness (arousal) induced by distraction persists and paradoxically stabilizes subsequent performance. The key finding of VO2 remains that the strongest predictor of concentration in the d2-R test was accuracy in the Dual N-back test ( p = 0.034), confirming that individual working memory capacity and prefrontal circuit stability are more dominant for performance than external stimuli. From a neuropsychological perspective, this implies that individuals with a more robust central executive are able to switch more effectively between demanding cognitive operations and routine administrative control, with this stability acting as a protective factor against residual fatigue from digital interference. The third research question (RQ3) focused on the relationship between error rate and subjectively felt mental effort (NASA-TLX), with the results yielding a differentiated picture depending on the type of task. A significant correlation between error rate and subjective load (effort ρ = 0.34; frustration ρ = 0.41) was confirmed exclusively in the Dual N-back test. We explain this finding through metacognitive processing ( Menon and D'Esposito, 2022 ), where participants were clearly aware of moments of failure and loss of continuity during demanding information updating, which led to an increase in perceived frustration. On the contrary, this correlation was absent in the Stroop and d2-R tests, suggesting that inhibition processes controlled by more autonomous rIFG-STN pathways ( Aron et al., 2014 ) may not be perceived by consciousness as enormously demanding unless they lead to massive interference. Thus, digital distraction appears to increase the “cost of performance” especially where there is a direct competition for slots in working memory ( Ward et al., 2017 ), while during routine administrative tasks individuals may not be aware of the latent weakening of their attention, which may be a risk factor in a real work environment. The fourth research question (RQ4) investigated the existence of a specific neurophysiological profile associated with increased error rates. The analysis encountered methodological limitations in the form of extreme multicollinearity between theta and alpha activity (r > 0.98), suggesting that in our experimental setting these bands represented a common neurophysiological substrate of cortical excitation. Nevertheless, the results yielded a crucial finding about the stability of the alpha rhythm in the experimental group ( p = 0.002). Instead of the expected fragmentation of attention, intermittent distraction led to a significant increase in the stability of alpha activity, which we interpret as a neurophysiological “shield” or state of hyper-focus ( Ashinoff and Abu-Akel, 2021 ). This sensory gating mechanism ( Klimesch, 2012 ) allowed participants to suppress digital stimuli as irrelevant noise, thereby proactively protecting the attention devoted to the primary task ( Braver, 2012 ; Anderson and Levy, 2009 ). The stabilization of parietal neuronal networks thus serves as a reactive tool for selective resource targeting in the short term. The last research question (RQ5) analyzed the correlation between subjective workload and neurophysiological parameters (fm-Theta and Alpha). While no relationship was found in the Stroop task, a significant negative correlation was identified between perceived effort and parietal alpha activity in the Dual N-back task ( ρ = −0.31). Lower levels of alpha activity at high perceived workload indicate that the central executive had to make a massive effort to maintain the goals in memory ( Klimesch, 2012 ). However, an interesting finding is the absence of an increase in fm-Theta activity in the experimental group, which contradicts the models of Langner et al. (2018) and Guo et al. (2018) . This fact suggests that participants habituated to the distraction very quickly and their ACC did not evaluate it as a priority cognitive conflict ( Goldin-Meadow et al., 2001 ). Paradoxically, at higher perceived effort, fm-Theta activity even decreased ( r = −0.31), indicating that at maximum concentration the brain suppressed the monitoring of the external environment in favor of the primary goal. title: Impact of Smartphone Multitasking on Self-Reported Attention and Memory Difficulties among Indian Undergraduate Students
